parts.overview:
agents, code: This part covers two crates. `ostra-agents` embeds the repo's `assets/` folder in the binary and turns it into what every execution receives: the agent definition from `agent.toml`, the system prompt rendered with the tool names of the executor, the typed `Label: value` spawn block, and the repo brief appended to the first message. `ostra-code` is the code navigation layer: a table-driven tokenizer for 22 languages, an incremental per-project index of names, definitions and imports, a dependency and reference graph, the eight code tools agents call, and a provider chain (a project's own command, language servers over LSP, then the built-in index) that serves the Files view and the editor. `ostra-engine` (`factory.rs`) builds each spawn from `ostra-agents`, `ostra-workspace` reads agent definitions to validate settings, and `ostra-server` wires `ostra-code` into the REST API and into the `CodeNav` trait that native and harness executors use. `ostra-agents` depends only on `ostra-core`; `ostra-code` depends on `ostra-core` and `ostra-sandbox`, because language servers and command providers run under the workspace sandbox. The prompts, judges, references and skills themselves belong to the assets area; this part describes how they are loaded and rendered.

core: ostra-core is the shared domain crate of Ostra. It depends on no other Ostra crate, and every other crate (store, sandbox, policy, tools, providers, agents, engine, executors, MCP, code index, workspace, server) builds on its types. It defines identifiers, agent names, capabilities, executor kinds, pipeline enums and stages, the append-only session event log and gate payloads, the `submit_<agent>` payload schemas, the `Executor` and `ExecutionHost` traits, global and workspace settings with route resolution and save-time validation, the project profile, every path Ostra derives, the canonical tool-call and policy-decision shapes, MCP tool naming, subagent coordination and project management tool inputs, typed research/spec/plan documents, documentation books with BM25 search, code navigation contracts, workspace artifacts, model pricing, and the REST and WebSocket data types that ts-rs exports to `web/src/api/gen/`. The crate also holds small OS helpers: process-tree control, shell lookup, and git config overrides. Its functions are synchronous and pure except where a section says it reads or writes files or starts a process; async code lives in the crates that call it.

engine: ostra-engine is the code that runs one Ostra session, which is one user request taken through research, spec, fact-check, plan, build, review, test, and documentation. A session is an append-only event log; `SessionState::fold` turns the log into state, the pure function `next_steps` turns state into the next steps, and the `Engine` runner performs those steps and appends the events that result. Models do the work inside stages through executors, and they answer a small set of named judgment questions (judges); code holds every gate and every limit. The crate knows no executor, provider, or HTTP server: it reaches them through the `Services`, `SpawnFactory`, and `Executor` traits, and ostra-server wires the real implementations. It depends on ostra-core (events, DTOs, traits), ostra-store (SQLite), ostra-agents (prompts and typed spawn blocks), and ostra-sandbox (host commands and git repair). Its sections below cover the fold, the planner, judges and YOLO, the runner, subagent coordination, the init flow, the spawn factory, the view projections, and the tests.

exec-harness, exec-native, mcp, notify, policy, providers: This area holds the crates that run one leaf agent and keep it inside Ostra's rules. `ostra-policy` decides, for every canonical tool call, whether it is allowed, needs the user, or is denied. `ostra-providers` streams model responses from Anthropic and OpenAI behind one neutral interface. `ostra-exec-native` is the native agent loop built on those two plus `ostra-tools`. `ostra-exec-harness` runs the same agents inside installed CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Antigravity) under a PTY and routes every tool call back through the policy by a hook bridge. `ostra-mcp` is the client for workspace MCP servers with OAuth sign-in, and `ostra-notify` sends Web Push messages without OpenSSL. The engine reaches executors only through the `Executor` trait of `ostra-core`, and `ostra-server` wires these crates to HTTP routes, the approval cards, the MCP connections and the push subscriptions.

sandbox: ostra-sandbox is the kernel-enforced boundary under every command Ostra runs for an agent or a project. The policy layer (ostra-policy) judges tool calls by the paths they name, which a shell can hide; this crate makes the operating system enforce the same boundary: the host is read-only, only an execution's own roots are writable, Ostra's data and the user's credentials are hidden, and the network leads out only through an egress proxy that Ostra controls. It has three layers. A `Profile` describes one execution's boundary without naming a backend. A `Backend` (bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt through `sandbox-exec` on macOS) renders the profile into a wrapped command. The `sys` module is the only code that calls the kernel, with one `Os` implementation per operating system. Around these sit the egress proxy (`egress.rs`), the `ostra sandbox-init` helper with its seccomp filter (Linux), decoy credential files that signal a containment probe, process tracking (`Members`), host commands for programs Ostra starts for a project, and save-time validation of sandbox settings. The crate depends on ostra-core for config types, paths, and the `ExecutionHost` trait. It is called by ostra-exec-native and ostra-tools (the native Bash tool), ostra-exec-harness (harness CLIs), ostra-engine (format commands and cache cleanup), ostra-code and ostra-server (language servers, code providers, MCP stdio servers, startup cleanup, the `sandbox-init` subcommand), and ostra-workspace (settings validation and status). Those areas are documented by their own writers.

server: The server area is the `ostra` binary and library in crates/ostra-server. It is the only process an Ostra user starts. It binds an HTTP listener (default 127.0.0.1:7878), authenticates browsers with a one-time token that is exchanged for an HttpOnly cookie, serves the embedded React console, and exposes the REST API under /api, the multiplexed WebSocket at /ws, and the local-only harness callbacks under /internal. It wires the real implementations of the traits the engine (ostra-engine), workspaces (ostra-workspace), and tools (ostra-tools) declare: Services, WorkspaceHost, CodeNav, McpConnector, ManageConnector, and CoordConnector. It owns the server-side features that need process-wide state: the sign-in registry, the per-workspace engine hub, the MCP gateway with OAuth, the git clone and git dock commands with saved credentials, the project file views with change attribution, the code-index providers, the Sessions tree and search, workspace artifacts, the master key that seals stored secrets, and harness setup terminals. Other areas own the engine, executors, policy, sandbox, tools, providers, code index, MCP client, workspace logic, and storage; this area calls them and names them in each section's boundaries.

store, tools, workspace: This area covers three Rust crates. `ostra-store` keeps Ostra's durable state in SQLite: each workspace's database (the session event log plus the tables materialized beside it for the console), the machine-wide registry (workspace list, push subscriptions, key-value rows, encrypted credentials), and each project's lesson memory. `ostra-tools` implements the native tools that agents call (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob, WebFetch, Skill, Report, Document, Memory, MemoryRecall, DocsSearch, and the Windows PowerShell and Cmd shells), their JSON-schema definitions, and the traits through which the server supplies code navigation, MCP, project management, and subagent coordination. `ostra-workspace` owns one open workspace: its settings and validation, its projects, the approval records that keep commands from folder files from starting, workspace creation and deletion, and the stored console layout. The crates depend downward on `ostra-core`; `ostra-engine` and `ostra-exec-native` use the store and tools, and `ostra-server` wires the real implementations into `WorkspaceHost`, the connector traits, and the registry's encryption key.

web: The web console is the React 19 single-page app in web/. It is the browser UI of the ostra server: a person uses it to start tasks, answer gates, watch executions and terminals, read specs, plans and documentation books, browse and edit project files, change workspace settings, and set up a workspace. It is built with Vite into web/dist, which the ostra binary embeds (crates/ostra-server/src/assets.rs) and serves next to the REST API under /api and the WebSocket at /ws. All types come from ts-rs bindings generated by ostra-core into web/src/api/gen, and all visual components come from @ostra/design. The code splits into an API layer (client.ts, socket.ts, mock/), shared live data (lib/store.ts, lib/live.ts), a desktop shell with editor-style tabs (shell/), a mobile shell for viewports up to 720 px (mobile/), one screen per resource type (screens/), and feature modules (features/context, features/docs, features/gates). Per the project rules the UI is kept compiling against API changes and is not polished, because it will be redesigned later.

design, site, assets: This part covers three folders that contain no Rust logic: assets/ (the text Ostra gives to models), design/ (the @ostra/design React component library and CSS tokens), and site/ (the public homepage and docs site). The assets folder holds 14 agent prompts with their agent.toml definitions, 10 judge prompts, 7 stack references, the meta-author skill, a capability-to-tool mapping, and 3 prompt fragments; the ostra-agents crate embeds them in the binary, renders each prompt for the executor that will run it (native, claude, codex, grok or agy), and writes references, skills and rendered agent instructions under the data directory. The design package is imported by web/ (the console) and by site/, never the reverse, and it also holds the Markdown and Mermaid renderer that the site docs and the console documentation books share. The site builds two static pages, a homepage with an embedded mock console and a docs page that renders the repository's own Markdown at build time. Other areas own the engine that spawns agents and asks judges, the core submit schemas the prompts describe, the server that embeds the web build, and the browser tests that check the site.

tests: The tests/ folder holds four independent suites. tests/conformance/main.rs is the engine conformance binary: 126 fixtures that build an event history for a session, fold it with SessionState::fold, and assert the exact list of next steps the pure planner returns, one or more per HANDOVER or Ultracode rule. tests/browser is a Playwright suite that starts a scratch ostra server, a fake Anthropic API, an attacker web server and a static copy of the site, and proves that agent text, repo text, terminal output, cross-origin requests, the sign-in token, uploads and browser storage cannot run script or change server state. tests/evals holds TOML and fixture data for four live, paid evals (judges, advisor, coordination, test stage) that are run by test files under crates/ostra-server/tests. tests/windows-probes is a standalone Rust program, outside the cargo workspace, that measured the Windows sandbox design on a throwaway VM. The suites talk to the other areas only through their public surfaces: the engine crate API, the ostra binary and its REST routes, the embedded web build, and the site build.

docs, other files: This part of the book covers everything in the ostra repository that is not a crate, a browser package, the agent assets or the tests: the 34 Markdown files in docs/, the three root design documents (README.md, HANDOVER.md, CLAUDE.md), the Cargo and npm workspace configuration, the build and run scripts, the login-service installers for Linux, macOS and Windows, and the Docker image. Readers are people who build, install, run or document Ostra, and agents that need to know where a fact is written and which command produces the binary. The docs are plain Markdown that GitHub shows as it is and that the site package renders at build time through a navigation list in site/src/docs/pages.ts. HANDOVER.md is the behavior spec, CLAUDE.md holds the contributor patterns, and the scripts turn the npm workspace (design, web, site) and the Cargo workspace (15 crates) into one release binary, target/release/ostra, that embeds web/dist. This area describes the crates, web, design, site, assets and tests only at their boundary with these files; the other areas of the book document them.

sections.title: Agent definitions and effort
sections.purpose: Loads the 14 agent definitions from `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml` once per process and answers what an agent may do and how hard it reasons on a given executor. The engine, the workspace settings checks and the prompt renderer read these values whenever they need an agent's tier, timeout, capabilities or effort.

owns: The `AgentDef` shape and the `agent.toml` key names (`description`, `default_tier`, `timeout_seconds`, `capabilities`, `effort`).
The effort fallback rule in `effort_for`: executor table, then `native`, then `Effort::High`.
does_not_own: The `AgentName`, `Capability`, `Tier`, `Effort` and `ExecutorKind` types (core area, `crates/ostra-core`).
Routing a tier to a model and the complexity-based effort override (`resolve_effort` in `ostra-core` config, called from `ostra-engine` `factory.rs`).
Enforcing `timeout_secs` on a running execution (executor areas: `ostra-exec-native`, `ostra-exec-harness`).
The text of the `agent.toml` files (assets area).

assumptions: Every entry of `AgentName::ALL` (14 names) has `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml` with all five keys. `load_defs` returns an `AgentsError` otherwise and `defs()` panics with `embedded agent definitions are invalid`, so a bad file is a build defect found by this crate's tests, not a runtime condition.
Assets are embedded with `rust_embed` (`#[folder = "../../assets"]`), so a changed `agent.toml` takes effect only after a rebuild.
The `effort` table may omit an executor table; `effort_for` covers the gap.
Callers treat the returned `&'static AgentDef` as read-only.

business_flow.action: Asks `agent_def(agent)` for one agent.
business_flow.outcome: The first call in the process parses all 14 `agent.toml` files and stores the map in a `OnceLock`; later calls read the stored map.

business_flow.action: Asks `effort_for(agent, executor)`.
business_flow.outcome: The effort of the executor's table is returned; when the table has no key, the `native` value is returned; when that is missing too, `Effort::High`.

business_flow.action: Uses the workspace's `resolve_effort` first and `effort_for` only when settings give no value.
business_flow.outcome: Workspace settings override the definition's effort.

sections.title: Prompt rendering per executor
sections.purpose: Turns an agent's `prompt.md` into the system prompt for one executor. The prompts are written with `{{tool_*}}` tokens that name each tool by what it does; rendering replaces them with the tool names of the native executor or of one harness (Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Agy) and prepends shared guides. `ostra-engine` calls `render_prompt` for every spawn.

owns: The order in which output rules, guides, the prompt body and the harness tool vocabulary are joined.
The token-to-mapping-key table (`TOKENS`) and the capability-to-tool-name mapping read from `assets/tool-mapping.toml`.
The text of the generated `## Tool vocabulary` section, including the fixed paragraph that forbids a harness from starting its own subagents.
does_not_own: The text of the prompts, `output-rules.md`, `code-tools.md`, `coordination.md` and `tool-mapping.toml` (assets area).
Registering the tools with a provider or an MCP server (executor areas and `ostra-tools`); this crate only names them.
Deciding which executor an agent runs on (workspace settings and engine).

assumptions: Every `{{token}}` a prompt or guide uses exists in the context built by `Mapping::context` (the 28 `tool_*` tokens and `assets_dir`). The environment uses `UndefinedBehavior::Strict`, so an unknown token is an `AgentsError::Template` error with the asset path.
`assets/output-rules.md`, `assets/code-tools.md` and `assets/coordination.md` exist at the asset root; a missing file is `AgentsError::Missing`.
`assets/tool-mapping.toml` is valid; `mapping::get` panics with `assets/tool-mapping.toml is invalid` otherwise.
`set_assets_dir` ran before the first render when a non-default assets directory is wanted, because `assets_dir()` is read on each render and the `assets_dir` token holds that path.
A prompt never contains a literal `{{` or `{%` that is not a token; tests assert that no rendered prompt contains either.

business_flow.action: Calls `render_prompt(agent, executor)` while building a spawn.
business_flow.outcome: The prompt source is read from the embedded `agents/<name>/prompt.md`.

business_flow.action: Builds the template context: each `tool_*` token resolves to a tool name for the executor's table, and `assets_dir` is the assets path.
business_flow.outcome: A key with no entry for the executor falls back to the key text itself, for example `read`.

business_flow.action: Renders the body, then prepends `code-tools.md` when the agent has the `code` capability and `coordination.md` when it has `coordinate`, then prepends `output-rules.md`.
business_flow.outcome: Every prompt starts with the output rules, which forbid text outside tool calls.

business_flow.action: For a harness executor, renders a tool vocabulary section and places it before everything else.
business_flow.outcome: The harness model sees a table that maps each capability to the tool names of its own CLI.

diagrams.title: Order in which render_prompt assembles the text
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  p[Read agents/name/prompt.md] --> c[Build context from tool-mapping.toml]
  c --> r1[Render body with minijinja strict]
  r1 --> q1{Has code capability?}
  q1 -->|yes| g1[Prepend code-tools.md]
  q1 -->|no| q2
  g1 --> q2{Has coordinate capability?}
  q2 -->|yes| g2[Prepend coordination.md]
  q2 -->|no| o
  g2 --> o[Prepend output-rules.md]
  o --> e{Executor}
  e -->|Native| n[Return body]
  e -->|Harness| v[Prepend tool vocabulary]

subsections.title: Tool mapping and tokens
subsections.purpose: Defines how a capability becomes a tool name on each executor. `Mapping::tool(capability, executor, agent)` reads `[capabilities.<key>]` in `assets/tool-mapping.toml` and substitutes `{agent}`, `{op}` and `{Op}`.

owns: The 28-entry `TOKENS` table and the substitution rules for `{agent}`, `{op}`, `{Op}`.
does_not_own: The tool names themselves (data in `tool-mapping.toml`, assets area).
The operation lists `CODE_TOOLS` (8 operations), `PROJECT_TOOLS` (2) and `COORD_TOOLS` (3) (core area).

assumptions: A capability key has an entry for each executor table it is used on; otherwise `tool` returns `None`.
`{agent}` is replaced by `AgentName::snake()`, so `submit_{agent}` becomes `submit_code_reviewer` for the code-reviewer.
For a key with an operation (`code:callers`), the operation text gets its first letter uppercased for `{Op}`, which gives `CodeCallers` on the native executor.

business_flow.action: Splits `capability` at the first `:` into key and operation.
business_flow.outcome: `code:callers` gives key `code` and operation `callers`.

business_flow.action: Looks up `capabilities[key][executor.tier_table()]` and replaces `{agent}`, then `{op}` and `{Op}`.
business_flow.outcome: A tool name or, for some capabilities, a prose instruction such as `Read on the skill's SKILL.md`.

subsections.title: Harness tool vocabulary section
subsections.purpose: Builds the `## Tool vocabulary` section that opens a harness executor's prompt, because harness CLIs name their tools differently from the names the prompts were tuned on. Native prompts do not get it.

owns: The section text, the table of capabilities the agent has plus `submit`, the strategy selection, and the closing `Done!` instruction.
does_not_own: The strategy texts (`[strategies.skill]`, `[strategies.ostra_tools]`, `[strategies.write]` in `tool-mapping.toml`, assets area).
Starting the harness or registering the `ostra` MCP server (`ostra-exec-harness`).

assumptions: `HarnessKind::display_name` and `HarnessKind::as_str` exist; the latter is the strategy table key.
The agent's capabilities come from `agent_def(agent).capabilities`; the vocabulary lists exactly those plus `submit`.
A harness replies `Done!` after `submit_*` is called; the engine reads the result from the submit call only.

business_flow.action: Writes the heading and one sentence naming the harness.
business_flow.outcome: The model learns it runs under Ostra in that harness.

business_flow.action: Adds one table row per capability plus `submit`; for `code`, `manage_projects` and `coordinate` it joins the tool names of every operation with `, `.
business_flow.outcome: For example the `code` row lists all 8 code tools.

business_flow.action: Appends each strategy text for the harness, skipping `skill` unless the agent has the `skill` or `read` capability and `write` unless it has `write` or `edit`; `ostra_tools` is always included.
business_flow.outcome: The model knows how to load skills, edit files and reach Ostra's MCP tools on that CLI.

business_flow.action: Appends the paragraph that forbids the harness's own subagents, then the instruction to reply only `Done!` after the submit call.
business_flow.outcome: Delegation goes only through Ostra's subagent tools, and no output tokens are spent on a final message.

sections.title: Asset lookups and materialization
sections.purpose: Gives the rest of the program read access to the embedded judge prompts, stack references and bundled skills, and writes the references, skills and per-agent instructions to a folder on disk so that agents can read them with file tools. The server calls `set_assets_dir` and `materialize_assets` at startup.

owns: The assets directory setting (`set_assets_dir`, `assets_dir`) and the `{{assets_dir}}` text replacement in references and skills.
Which files are written by `materialize_assets`: `refs/*`, `skills/*`, and `agents/<name>.md`.
The stack-reference rule in `stack_names`.
does_not_own: The asset content (assets area).
Choosing the data directory (`ostra_core::paths::data_dir`, core area).
Calling order at startup (`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`, server area).

assumptions: `set_assets_dir` is called once, before any call of `reference`, `embedded_skill`, or a render; it returns `false` when already set and keeps the first value. `reference` and `embedded_skill` cache their maps on first use with the directory known at that moment.
Embedded assets are UTF-8; a non-UTF-8 file is an `AgentsError::Parse`.
The caches (`judge_prompt`, `reference`, `embedded_skill`) leak their strings with `Box::leak` once per process; the amount is bounded by the number of assets.

`materialize_assets` renders each agent's instructions for the native executor, so `agents/<name>.md` uses native tool names whatever executor a run uses (Rule O5: the advisor reads a failed agent's own instructions).
A reference is a stack seed only when its first line starts with `# Stack Reference:` and its name does not start with `_`.

business_flow.action: Calls `set_assets_dir(assets)` and then `materialize_assets(&assets)` at startup.
business_flow.outcome: The directory is fixed for the process and the files exist on disk.

business_flow.action: Collects every embedded file under `refs/` and `skills/` with `{{assets_dir}}` and `{{ assets_dir }}` replaced by the directory, and renders `agents/<name>.md` for all 14 agents.
business_flow.outcome: A list of (target, content) pairs.

business_flow.action: Reads each target and skips it when the content is identical; otherwise creates parent folders and writes it.
business_flow.outcome: Only changed files are rewritten; the returned list names them, and a second run returns an empty list.

business_flow.action: Uses `reference_path(name)` for `Stack reference:` lines and `instructions_path(agent)` for the advisor.
business_flow.outcome: Agents get absolute paths under the assets directory.

sections.title: Typed spawn parameters
sections.purpose: Represents the `Label: value` block that starts every agent run as one Rust struct per agent and per initializer mode, so that a required parameter is a non-`Option` field and a missing one does not compile. The engine's `factory.rs` maps planner inputs onto these structs, calls `render`, and uses `to_json` for the recorded params.

owns: The struct for each agent, the six initializer mode structs, and the exact label order each renders.
The contract table (`PARAMS`, `contract`) that `parse_block` uses to validate a block.
does_not_own: Choosing the values and naming every report path (`paths::report`; engine area, `ostra-engine/src/factory.rs`).
The prompts that read these labels (assets area).
Submit schemas for what agents return (`ostra-core/src/submit.rs`, core area).

assumptions: Paths are absolute. The engine names every path; `parse_block` rejects a relative `Workspace root`, `Repo root`, `Session dir` or `Report file`.
`projects_in_scope` renders as `key -> path` lines.
`Repo key` is a lowercase slug (`ostra_core::slug::is_project_key`).
The spawn block is the start of the first message; it ends at a line `---` or a line starting with `## ` where the repo brief begins.

business_flow.action: Builds the struct for the planner's `SpawnInputs`.
business_flow.outcome: The compiler enforces the required parameters.

sections.title: Language table and tokenizer
sections.purpose: Splits source text into typed tokens for 22 languages without a parser, for colored display in the Files view and as the input of the outline, index and graph. The tokenizer never fails: text it does not understand is skipped.

owns: The `Lang` table (`lang.rs`): comment and string syntax, keywords, builtin types and constants, definition keywords, the extension-to-language map.
Token positions: byte offsets, 1-based lines, 0-based UTF-16 columns.
The rule that a multi-line comment or string becomes one token per line.
does_not_own: Definitions, imports and supertypes (Outline section, `code-outline`).

assumptions: Paths use `/` separators and are project-relative; `for_path` splits on `/`.
Source is valid UTF-8 text; the index reads files with `String::from_utf8_lossy`. Byte offsets are stored as `u32`, and files above 1 MiB (`MAX_FILE_BYTES`) are never tokenized.
A 4-byte UTF-8 sequence counts as 2 UTF-16 columns, which matches the browser and language servers.
A backtick string always spans lines; `'` starts a character literal only (Rust lifetimes are handled by the lexer).

business_flow.action: Finds the language with `lang::for_path(path)` from the extension or file name.

sections.title: Per-project code index
sections.purpose: Keeps, for each project, the names each file mentions, its definitions and its imports, never its text. Usages, dependencies, symbol search and the graph are answered from it. A query re-reads only the files that mention the asked name. The `Indexes<K>` registry builds one index per project on first use and keeps it current from write touches and a periodic disk check.

owns: `ProjectIndex` storage, name interning, postings, the `sync` and `link` steps, and the byte and file caps.
`Indexes<K>`: slots per project key, the dirty set, and the decision when to sync fully.
Symbol search scoring (`name_score`).
does_not_own: The project file list and the file watcher that calls `touch` (server area: `crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs`, `files`).
Graph queries (`code-graph`) and type-aware usages (`code-usages`), which are further `impl ProjectIndex` blocks.
Running index work off the async runtime: callers use `spawn_blocking`.

assumptions: All `Indexes` methods that build or query an index are blocking; the first call for a project reads every source file. `NativeProvider` and the server's `CodeTools` call them inside `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`.
The file list `Arc<FileIndex>` changes identity (a new `Arc`) when the file set changes; the registry compares with `Arc::ptr_eq`.
Edits made outside Ostra are noticed at the next full check, at most 30 seconds later (`FULL_SYNC`); writes made through Ostra call `touch` for immediate refresh.
Entry ids only grow: a removed file keeps its slot with `alive = false`, which keeps posting lists sorted by appending.
A file with a NUL byte in its first 8,000 bytes is treated as binary and not indexed.

business_flow.action: Calls `Indexes::with(key, root, list, f)`.
business_flow.outcome: The slot for `key` is created if needed; a changed root resets it.

business_flow.action: Takes the dirty set, refreshes the resolver (cached by file list identity), then syncs fully when the list changed or the last full sync is older than 30 seconds, else syncs only the dirty paths.
business_flow.outcome: The index matches the disk.

business_flow.action: Drops entries for removed files, stats the listed files in parallel, and re-analyzes files whose size or mtime changed.
business_flow.outcome: New entries with names, mentions, definitions (with one-line signature), imports and supertypes.

business_flow.action: On the first query after a change, resolves every import to a target and builds importer maps; discards the graph.
business_flow.outcome: `deps` and the graph can answer.

business_flow.action: Runs `f` on the `&mut ProjectIndex` under the slot lock.
business_flow.outcome: The answer of one query.

  e -->|yes| f[Remove entry]

Supertype hops in member lookup are capped at 8 (`MAX_SUPER_DEPTH`).
In Jvm and C families a bare name inside a class body can mean a member of that class, unless a local declaration of the same name precedes it in the method.

sections.title: Dependency and reference graph
sections.purpose: Derives a file-to-file graph from the index without reading files, and answers structural questions with it: neighbors, reach, paths, cycles, packages, callers, callees, impact and implementations. It also builds the node and edge data of the graph views in the Files view. The graph is built on the first query after a link and dropped by the next link.

owns: Edge construction from import targets and name mentions, and the rule for which file a mention means (`resolve`, `tier`, `nearest`).
All graph query methods on `ProjectIndex` and the layout columns of the views.
Test-file and hub-file detection by path.
does_not_own: The index storage and sync (`code-index`).
The text rendering of answers for agents (`code-agent-tools`).
Drawing the graph in the browser (web area).

assumptions: The graph depends on the index being synced just before the query; `Indexes::with` guarantees that.
Names are matched by text. A name defined in more than 3 files (`MAX_DEF_FILES`) links none of them unless the mentioning file imports the defining file directly.
Single-character names never create edges.

A file is a test file when a folder is named test, tests, __tests__, spec, specs, testdata or fixtures, or the name contains `.test.` or `.spec.`, starts with `test_`, or ends with `_test.go`, `_test.py`, `_test.rs`, `_spec.rb`, `_test.rb`, `Test.java`, `Tests.java`, `Test.kt`, `Tests.cs`, `Test.php`.
A hub file is an index module (stem `lib`, `main`, `mod`, `index`, `__init__`) or any file with an `export * from`.

business_flow.action: Runs `link`, then `build_graph` when no graph is cached.

business_flow.action: For each file adds an edge to every resolved import target, an edge with names for every mention that resolves to another file, and for a folder import (a Go package) edges to the files whose names are used, or to the whole folder when none is used.

business_flow.action: Walks `out` or `inn` edges with `steps`, which follows an edge only if it has names or is a real import not into a hub.
business_flow.outcome: Neighbors, reach, paths, units, cycles.

business_flow.action: Use `usages`, group references by the innermost enclosing definition, and for impact repeat per hop.
business_flow.outcome: Definitions that use a symbol, hop by hop.

sections.title: Code provider chain
sections.purpose: The Files view asks a chain of providers for four request kinds (file, usages, deps, symbols) and takes the first answer. The server builds the chain per request in this order: the project's own `code_provider` program, then each `language_servers` entry, then the built-in index. A provider answers `null` (`Ok(None)`) to leave a request to the next one; a failed or invalid answer also falls through, and the answer that is shown carries the reason as a warning.

owns: The `CodeProvider` trait, `ask`, `Answer`, `NativeProvider`, `CommandProvider` and the validation of external answers (`parse_answer`).
The stamping of the provider name and warnings on answers.
does_not_own: Building the chain from project settings on each request (server area, `crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs`, `ask`).
The wire types `ProviderRequest`, `CodeFile`, `CodeUsages`, `CodeDeps`, `CodeSymbols` and `PROTOCOL_VERSION` = 1 (core area, `ostra-core/src/code.rs`).
The sandbox that confines the program (`ostra-sandbox::host_command`).

assumptions: The native provider is last in the chain, so a request that every other provider declines is answered by the index. If the chain is empty or everything declines, `ask` returns `No code provider answered this request.`
Settings are read per request, so saved provider settings apply to the next request.
An external provider reads one JSON object from stdin and writes one JSON value to stdout; it may exit without reading its input.
Paths in external answers are project-relative, without `..`, `.`, a leading `/`, a backslash or a NUL, and lines are 1-based.

business_flow.action: Builds a `ProviderRequest` with `version`, project `root` and the operation fields.
business_flow.outcome: A validated request.

business_flow.action: Calls each provider in order.
business_flow.outcome: `Ok(Some)` returns at once; `Ok(None)` moves on; `Err` records a problem and moves on.

business_flow.action: Stamps the answer with the provider's name and prefixes recorded problems to the warning.
business_flow.outcome: The browser shows which provider answered and why earlier ones did not.

business_flow.action: Runs the index query in `spawn_blocking`.
business_flow.outcome: Always an answer for a readable project.

sections.title: Language server providers
sections.purpose: Runs language servers over the Language Server Protocol for projects that list `language_servers` in their settings. A pool starts a server on the first request for one of its languages, keeps it while it is used, and stops it after 10 minutes without requests. File answers overlay the server's semantic tokens and outline on the built-in answer, so imports and any colors the server leaves out still come from the tokenizer.

owns: `LspPool` (process lifecycle, limits), `Client` (JSON-RPC framing and routing), `LspProvider` (requests and conversion), and outside-file handling.
Conversion between LSP and Ostra types (`convert.rs`).
does_not_own: The `LanguageServerConfig` type: `command`, `languages`, `timeout_secs` (default 10), `initialization_options` (core area, `ostra-core/src/config.rs`).
Sandbox profiles and process confinement (`ostra-sandbox`, sandbox area); this crate calls `host_command`.
Which chain position a server takes and the HTTP endpoints for outside files (server area).

assumptions: A server must count columns in UTF-16. `initialize` advertises only `utf-16`; if the server answers another `positionEncoding`, `start` closes it and returns ``<name> counts columns in <encoding>. Ostra needs a server that counts them in utf-16.``

The server runs under the workspace sandbox because it runs the project's build scripts and macros. The pool entry remembers the sandbox settings it started under; changed settings replace the server on the next request.
Servers report canonical paths, so `Server` keeps both the root and its canonical path and accepts URIs under either.
Files are sent as UTF-8 text under 1 MiB (`MAX_FILE_BYTES`); otherwise the error is `Cannot read <path> as UTF-8 text under 1 MB.`
Documents opened in a server are identified by the hash of their text; a changed hash sends `didChange` with the full text.

business_flow.action: Finds or creates the entry for (project key, command), evicts stale or over-limit entries, and starts the server in a spawned task, waiting at most the provider's `timeout_secs`.
business_flow.outcome: A running `Server`, or `<name> is still starting. Ask again in a moment.` while the start continues for the next caller.

business_flow.action: Syncs the document (`didOpen`, `didChange`, `didClose` for the least recently used beyond 32 documents), then sends the request.
business_flow.outcome: The server answers.

business_flow.action: Converts the answer to Ostra types and adds a note when the server is still loading the project.
business_flow.outcome: An `Answer` with a warning such as `<name> is still loading the project, so this answer may be incomplete.`

business_flow.action: Every 60 seconds stops entries idle for 10 minutes or stale.
business_flow.outcome: Idle servers are closed with `shutdown` and `exit`.

subsections.title: Files outside the project
subsections.purpose: A server may answer a definition inside a library source (a `file://` URI in a package cache) or a class inside a jar (jdtls `jdt://contents/...`). jdtls serves jar classes through `java/classFileContents`; Ostra sets `extendedClientCapabilities.classFileContentsSupport` to true in `initializationOptions` for servers whose languages include `java`, unless the project sets it.
A file:// path under the home folder is shown with `~`; a `/C:/x` Windows URI loses its leading slash.

sections.title: Crate role and module map
sections.purpose: ostra-core holds the types and pure rules that every other Ostra crate shares. It exists so the engine, executors, policy layer, server, and browser agree on one definition of each id, event, setting, path, and payload. It is compiled into every other crate, and it never calls into them.

owns: The 28 public modules declared in `lib.rs` and the re-exports `AgentName`, `Capability`, `InitializerMode`, `ExecutorKind`, `HarnessKind`, the six id types, `Complexity`, `Effort`, and `Tier`.
The `#[ts(export)]` marking of every type the browser receives, and the export directory setting `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` in `.cargo/config.toml`.
The `test-prices` Cargo feature that exposes `pricing::install_test_prices` to other crates' tests.
does_not_own: Session state folding, the planner, and the runner (ostra-engine).
Running tools, providers, or harness processes (ostra-tools, ostra-providers, ostra-exec-native, ostra-exec-harness).
Policy guards and bash parsing (ostra-policy); this crate defines only the `ToolCall` and `PolicyDecision` shapes.
SQLite storage (ostra-store) and the HTTP server (ostra-server).

assumptions: No other Ostra crate is a dependency of ostra-core, so a capability the engine needs from another crate becomes a trait method declared here or in the engine (CLAUDE.md, crate direction rules).
`.cargo/config.toml` sets `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` to `web/src/api/gen` (relative) and `TS_RS_LARGE_INT` to `number`, so `u64` fields export as TypeScript `number`.

Windows-only code (`junction`, `windows-sys` with `Win32_Foundation`, `Win32_Security`, `Win32_System_JobObjects`, `Win32_System_Threading`) compiles only under `cfg(windows)`; Unix builds use `libc`.
Other crates that need install_test_prices enable `features = ["test-prices"]` on ostra-core in their dev-dependencies (ostra-exec-native, ostra-providers, ostra-exec-harness).

sections.title: Execution contract: specs, results, deltas, and the Executor trait
sections.purpose: `exec.rs` is the contract between the engine and whatever runs an execution, the native loop or a harness PTY. It defines what an execution receives (`ExecutionSpec`, `ExecContext`), what it returns (`ExecutionResult`, `Usage`), what it streams (`ExecutionDelta`), and the two traits: `Executor` runs, and `ExecutionHost` is the set of callbacks the engine gives the executor.

owns: The field set of `ExecContext`, which the policy layer uses to judge each tool call.
`Usage` accumulation rules and `ExecutionStatus::is_terminal`.
The `Executor` and `ExecutionHost` trait signatures and their default method bodies.
does_not_own: Implementations: `NativeExecutor` (ostra-exec-native), `HarnessExecutor` (ostra-exec-harness), `EngineHost` (ostra-engine runner), plus test doubles.
Building a spec from planner inputs (spawn factory in ostra-engine).
Policy decisions from a context (ostra-policy).

assumptions: `ExecutionStatus::is_terminal` is true for every status except `Running`, so `Waiting` counts as terminal for that method.

`ExecutionHost::record_message`, `transcript`, `yolo`, and `wait_for_wake` have default bodies (no-op, empty list, false, `None`), so a host that needs none of them implements only `emit` and `ask_permission`.
`Usage::input_tokens` excludes cache reads and writes; every provider's and harness transcript's usage is normalized to that before pricing (comment in `pricing::cost`).
`Usage::context_tokens` is the latest request size, so `add` replaces it only when the incoming value is above zero.
Fields added to `ExecContext` after its first version carry `#[serde(default)]`.

business_flow.outcome: The spec names the route, effort, and sandbox choices for this run.

business_flow.action: Runs the spec through `Executor::run(spec, host, cancel)` and calls `host.emit` for each delta
business_flow.outcome: The engine persists and broadcasts every delta.

business_flow.action: Asks `host.ask_permission(call, reason, rule)` when policy says ask
business_flow.outcome: The host waits for a browser answer, or answers at once under YOLO.

business_flow.action: Returns an `ExecutionResult`
business_flow.outcome: The engine appends `ExecutionFinished` with the status, submit payload, final text, usage, and error.

sections.title: Global config and workspace settings
sections.purpose: Three TOML files configure Ostra: the global `config.toml`, a workspace's `.ostra/workspace.toml`, and a project's `.ostra/project.toml`. This section covers the first two and the loading and saving helpers. Settings are read fresh per execution and validated at save time, never resolved silently at spawn time.

owns: The structs `GlobalConfig`, `WorkspaceSettings` and their defaults, including the seeded workspace routes.
`load_toml`, `load_toml_required`, `save_toml`, and `ConfigError`.
Merge rules: `PermissionRules::merged`, `SandboxConfig::for_workspace`, `WorkspaceSettings::instructions_for`.
does_not_own: Where the files live (the paths section).
The registry that keeps sandbox, tool enforcement, and saved credentials outside `workspace.toml` (ostra-store).
Reading files per execution and calling validation (ostra-workspace `validate_settings`, ostra-server).

assumptions: A missing file loads as `T::default()` in `load_toml`; any other read error is `ConfigError::Io`, and a parse error is `ConfigError::Parse` with the path.
`save_toml` writes `<name>.toml.tmp` and renames it over the target, so a reader never sees a partial file; it creates missing parent directories.

The workspace fields `sandbox_mode`, `tool_enforcement`, `sandbox_network`, `sandbox_allowed_hosts`, `sandbox_decoys`, `sandbox_loopback`, and `sandbox_blocked_ports` live in the registry and never in `workspace.toml` (Rule A2, doc comments).

sections.title: Route resolution
sections.purpose: `resolve_route` turns a route key (an agent name or `judge`), a phase complexity, and the settings into one executor and one concrete model. It runs at validation time for every route key and at spawn time for each execution, with the same code in both places.

`executor_override` replaces the routed executor (a harness failure re-routed to native).

sections.title: Path resolution, secrets, and private files
sections.purpose: The guards and the sandbox compare paths, so this module makes the comparison strict. It resolves a path the way the kernel would, lists the credential locations no agent may read, and creates files and directories readable only by their owner.

owns: `resolve`, `normalize`, `is_inside`, `fold`, `strip_verbatim`, `canonical`, and the Windows path problem checks.
`HOME_CREDENTIALS`, `secret_paths`, and the owner-only file and directory helpers.
`link`, the cross-OS link creation.
does_not_own: Deciding to deny a tool call (ostra-policy `guards.rs`, which calls `resolve`).
Hiding paths inside the sandbox (ostra-sandbox).

assumptions: On Unix, `resolve_posix` follows each symlink, dangling ones included, before a later `..` applies, with at most 40 link expansions; a link cannot make a path look inside a root when the write lands outside it.
`normalize` is lexical only and touches no file system.
`is_inside` expects absolute, normalized paths; on Windows it folds case and separators, as NTFS does.

On Windows, `windows_path_problem` flags NT object paths, `\\host\share`, device namespace paths, drive-relative paths such as `C:foo`, and alternate data streams; `is_reserved_device` flags `CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `COM1` to `COM9`, `LPT1` to `LPT9`, `CONIN$`, `CONOUT$` (not `NUL`); both return false or `None` on Unix.
`dot_dot_after_link` (Windows) reports a `..` right after a junction or symlink, because Win32 and POSIX-style programs open different files.
On Windows a new directory inherits its parent ACL, so `create_private_dir_all` sets mode 0700 only on Unix.
`secret_paths` includes the data dir, the file named by `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` when set, and every `HOME_CREDENTIALS` entry under the home folder.

sections.title: MCP tool naming, server validation, and env expansion
sections.purpose: Workspace MCP servers expose tools that every executor can call. This module defines the names those tools carry inside Ostra, the rules for server names, the save-time checks of `mcp_servers`, and the `${VAR}` expansion for header and env values.

owns: The naming scheme `mcp__<server>__<tool>` and the bare form `<server>__<tool>`.
`validate`, `is_server_name`, `serves`, `expand_env`, `expand_refusing`, `expand_with`, `is_literal_value`, `SAVED_SECRET`.

A bare name is at most `MAX_BARE_NAME` (52) characters, because harnesses prefix `mcp__ostra__` (12 characters) and providers cap tool names at 64.

When a tool name has characters outside letters, digits, `_`, `-`, or the combined name is too long, `bare_name` sanitizes it, shortens it, and appends an FNV-1a hash (8 hex digits) of the original, so two tools never share a name.

A literal value (neither empty, `${ostra_secret}`, nor containing `${`) is kept encrypted in the registry; `${ostra_secret}` in `workspace.toml` stands for it.

sections.title: Subagent coordination and project management tools
sections.purpose: Two small toolsets let an agent call Ostra itself. The coordination tools (`SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply`) let agents ask each other questions and wake each other with answers. The management tools (`ProjectList`, `ProjectCreate`) let an agent list projects or create a new one. This section covers their input parsing, limits, and result types.

`AskTarget`, `DeliveryKind`, `RunEnd`, `CoordReply`, `CreatedProject`.
does_not_own: Delivering messages, waking runs, and enforcing the caps (ostra-engine runner and spawn logic, ostra-server bridge).
Creating the folder, git repository, and init session for a project (ostra-workspace and ostra-engine).

A message is non-empty plain text of at most 8000 characters; longer material goes in a file named by path.

subsections.purpose: `apply_update(base, update, remove)` lets an agent send only what changed. Top-level fields in `update` replace the stored fields, and a list whose items all carry an `id` merges by id instead of being replaced.

sections.title: Documentation books
sections.purpose: A documentation book is what the docs stage writes into a workspace. It covers a set of projects; each project is one part of sections and sub-sections, and a book of two or more projects also has a system architecture. The engine writes every book file from the agents' submit payloads, and no agent writes one (Rule B5).

owns: The book model (`Book`, `BookPart`, `DocSection`, `DocSubsection`, `Architecture`, `GlossaryEntry` and related types).
`book_id`, `merge`, `apply`, `write`, `remove`, `read`, `list`, and the Markdown rendering of a book.
`check_documentation`, `check_architecture`, and `check_diagram` (Rules B1 to B4).
does_not_own: Choosing which projects a session documents and when `BookWritten` is appended (ostra-engine runner `perform`).
Reading books for agents (`DocsSearch` tool in ostra-tools and the search section below).
Showing books in the console (ostra-server routes and web).

assumptions: A book id is the sorted, deduplicated project keys joined with `_`, so a later session on the same projects updates the same book (Rule B6); project keys hold no `_`, so different sets stay apart.
An id longer than `MAX_BOOK_ID` (80) is cut and suffixed `_` plus a 16 hex digit FNV-1a hash of the full id.
A valid book id starts with a lowercase letter or digit and holds lowercase letters, digits, `-`, `_`, at most 80 characters.
`BOOK_LOCK` serializes every read-merge-write and removal in this process, so two sessions updating one book keep each other's parts; it does not lock across processes.
`write` removes files of sections that no longer exist and empty directories, so the folder mirrors `book.json`.
A submit with `status` other than `ok` passes validation unchecked.

business_flow.action: Writes `book.json`, `index.md`, `glossary.md`, `architecture.md` when present, and `<project>/<section id>.md` per section

sections.title: Book search (Rule B8)
sections.purpose: `book_search.rs` ranks passages of the workspace's documentation books for a query. A section is cut into small passages; each passage is scored with BM25 over three weighted fields; a unit (section, sub-section, glossary term, architecture aspect, or project overview) is ranked by its best passages. A hit carries only the passages that matched, never the whole section.

owns: `Index::build`, `search`, `render`, `tokens`, `load_books`, `Filter`, `Hit`, `Unit`, `Passage`.
does_not_own: The `DocsSearch` tool that calls it and its permission (ostra-tools, ostra-policy).
Book storage (the books section).

assumptions: The index is built in memory from the books on disk each time; it is not persisted.
A query with no terms left after stop word removal, or an index with no passages, returns no hits.

Terms are lowercased and stemmed with a simple suffix rule (`ies` to `y`, `sses` to `ss`, trailing `s` removed except `ss`, `us`, `is`); an identifier also yields its camelCase and snake_case parts, so `SessionState` matches `session state`.
A unit title counts once for the unit and never picks which passages are shown.
Diagram passages are indexed by their labels and messages without Mermaid keywords and bare node ids.

business_flow.action: Scores each passage, groups by unit, adds title and second-passage score, sorts by score then unit order

sections.title: Process trees, shells, and git overrides
sections.purpose: Three small modules isolate operating system details that agent command execution depends on: stopping a child process and everything it started, finding the right shell, and keeping a repository's own `.git/config` from starting programs when Ostra or an agent runs git.

owns: `proctree::Tree`, `prepare_tokio`, `prepare_std`.
`shells::bash`, and on Windows `git_root`, `powershell`, `cmd`, `NO_GIT_BASH`.
`git::NO_EXEC`, `AUTOMATIC`, `AGENT_CONFIG`, `config_env`, `agent_env`, `blank_filters`, `filter_overrides`, `submodule_filter_overrides`.
does_not_own: Spawning commands and timeouts (ostra-tools Bash, ostra-exec-harness).
Sandbox profiles (ostra-sandbox).
The Git dock operations (ostra-server).

assumptions: On Unix a child leads its own process group (`process_group(0)`), and `terminate` sends SIGTERM and `kill` sends SIGKILL to the group and to the pid.

On Windows a child is created suspended without a console window, assigned to a Job Object with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` and no breakaway, then resumed with `NtResumeProcess`; if assignment or resume fails, the child is resumed and terminated, and an error is returned.
`Tree::terminate` does nothing on Windows, because a console program outside a console of its own has no such request; `end` closes the job and so kills what remains.
`adopt_running` places a running child (a PTY child) in a job, and what it started earlier is not in the job.
On Windows the Bash tool uses Git for Windows' `bin\bash.exe` found by absolute path, because `bash` on `PATH` is often the WSL launcher; on Unix it is `bash` from `PATH`.
`git::AUTOMATIC` adds `core.hooksPath=/dev/null` (an empty directory under the data dir on Windows); agent git keeps hooks because agent commits run the repository's hooks.
`filter_overrides` reads at most `MAX_FILTER_REPOS` (256) repositories and logs a warning when it stops; it blanks every `filter.*.clean|smudge|process` driver except the three git-lfs commands.

sections.title: Engine architecture and the session loop
sections.purpose: The engine turns one user request into a finished session by repeating one cycle: fold the event log into state, ask the planner for the next steps, perform each step, and append what happened as events. Every other section of this part describes one piece of that cycle. Read this section first to see how the pieces connect.

owns: The session lifecycle from `Engine::create_session` to the `SessionCompleted` or `SessionFailed` event
The rule that every state change is an event, and that only `SessionState::apply` changes session state
The rule that only `Inner::append` in runner.rs appends events
The per-session driver task, its in-flight step set, and the parallel execution slot limit
does_not_own: Event, gate, purpose, and DTO type definitions (ostra-core, documented in the core area)
SQLite tables and queries behind `WorkspaceDb` (ostra-store, store area)
Running an agent: the native loop (ostra-exec-native) and the harness PTY executors (ostra-exec-harness) implement the `Executor` trait
Model calls for judges (`Services::judge`, implemented by ostra-server with ostra-providers)
HTTP routes, WebSocket fan-out, and push delivery (ostra-server, server area)
Agent prompts and spawn block rendering (ostra-agents, agents area)
Tool permission decisions and guards (ostra-policy, policy area)

assumptions: One `Engine` exists per workspace, created with the workspace root, the workspace ID, a `WorkspaceDb`, and an `Arc<dyn Services>` (runner.rs `Engine::new`).
A session's state is always reproducible from its stored events; `Inner::load` folds `db.events(id)` when a session is not in memory.

The planner and the fold read no file or setting directly. Facts from outside the log reach them through `PlanCtx` or are recorded in an event (for example `AUTO_FIXABLE_PARAM` in the review execution params).
Appends to one session are serialized by the session's state mutex, so stored sequence order equals fold order.
Tokio is the async runtime: the driver and every step run as `tokio::spawn` tasks.

business_flow.action: Submits a request on the New task form
business_flow.outcome: `Engine::create_session` validates it, creates the session folders, and appends `SessionCreated`.

business_flow.action: Folds the log and calls `next_steps`
business_flow.outcome: The planner returns the steps that can start now, for example a Classify judge call.

business_flow.action: Performs each step in its own task: a judge call, an execution, a gate, or a command
business_flow.outcome: The result is appended as events such as `DecisionMade`, `ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionFinished`, `GateOpened`.

business_flow.action: Appends an event under the session state lock

sections.title: Session state and the fold
sections.purpose: `SessionState` is the whole state of a session, computed only by `SessionState::fold(id, events)` and changed only by `SessionState::apply`. The fold is deterministic: the same events always give the same state, so a server restart replays the log and continues. This section explains the shape of the state and the rules that keep the fold pure.

owns: All session state fields: classification, explore tasks, spec and plan tracks, phases and work loops, gates, decisions, executions, init tracks, notes, budget raise, pause and containment state
The interpretation of every `SessionEvent` (`apply`, `on_started`, `on_finished`, `on_decision`, `on_gate_opened`, `on_gate_answered`)
Derived queries the planner and views call: `full_request`, `open_gates`, `spent_usd`, `can_override`, `forced_executor`, `book_update`
does_not_own: Deciding what to do next (planner, see engine-planner)
Appending events (runner, see engine-runner-lifecycle)
Event type definitions (ostra-core)

assumptions: The fold never reads the clock, files, or settings. Timestamps come from `StoredEvent.at`.

A fact from outside the log that changes how an event folds must be recorded in the event. Examples: `GateAnswered.routed` records whether the answer needed the Route answer judge; the review `ExecutionStarted.params` carries `auto_fixable_ids` because the fold cannot read `project.toml`.
Unknown IDs are ignored, not errors: `GateAnswered` for an unknown or already answered gate returns early; `ExecutionFinished` for an unknown execution returns early.
Events of a session arrive in sequence order starting with `SessionCreated`.
Logs written before later rules exist still fold: serde defaults on judge outputs (`items`, `research`, `forget`, `title`) make old decisions deliver every answer.

Interrupts running executions when delivery is Now; clears `resume_from`; stores an `Amendment` (pending when routed); when not routed, `on_amended` queues research and records a requirement change.
Sets `paused`; pause marks every running execution as interrupting. Resume clears `paused` and `contained`.
Appends the signal; the third signal of one execution (`PAUSE_AFTER` = 3) pauses the session and sets `contained`.
Stores a `DecisionRecord` and calls `on_decision`; an override also stores the new output and reason and sets `overridden`.

Stores an `ExecRecord` with its loop key, removes the purpose key from `resume_from`, records the subagent root when it resumes another run, marks it interrupting if the session is paused, then `on_started` and `coord_started`.
Clears the result and end time, removes the resume and waiting keys, clears the execution's containment signals, then `on_started` with `resumed = true`.

Stores the result. A pause-interrupted run enters `resume_from`; a project-creating run enters `restart_fresh`; a `Waiting` result enters `waiting_keys` and folds as Interrupted; then `on_finished` and `coord_finished`.
Stores a `GateRecord` and records the owning track through `on_gate_opened`.
Ignored when the gate is unknown or already answered; otherwise stores answer, source, reason and calls `on_gate_answered`.
Tracks the running command per project. A Format result stores the exit code (`Some(None)` when skipped). A Stage result moves the matching loop to Done and stores `staged = exit code 0`.
Failed HIGH or MEDIUM findings return to the remaining set, then the loop re-evaluates through `after_findings`.

subsections.title: Spec and plan tracks and fact-check state
subsections.purpose: `ArtifactTrack<T>` holds generation and fact-check state for the spec and for the plan. The planner reads it to decide whether to generate, fact-check, ask questions, or ask for approval. The fold updates it when those executions and gates finish.
assumptions: A fact-check result counts only when its status is Ok and its verdict is not Error (`fact_finished`).
A revision of a spec receives only the answers, changes, and research documents the current version does not reflect yet (`applied` versus `sent` marks), so the agent edits instead of rewriting.

Approval is valid only for the version that passed a fact-check: the fold ignores an approval when the gate is not the asked one, when a run is pending (`needs_run`), or when `passed_current()` is false.

business_flow.action: Spec execution finishes Ok with a readable `GenerateSpecSubmit`
business_flow.outcome: `current` is replaced, `version` increments, `applied` copies `sent`, findings clear, approval is revoked.

business_flow.action: Fact-check finishes with PASS
business_flow.outcome: `consecutive_fails` resets to 0.

business_flow.action: Fact-check finishes with FAIL
business_flow.outcome: `consecutive_fails` increments, the findings text is stored in `pending_findings`, and `needs_run` is set so the owning agent runs again.

business_flow.action: Execution ends with status Error
business_flow.outcome: `artifact_error` retries once (`ERROR_RETRIES`), then stores `failed`.

business_flow.action: A requirement change arrives after the spec exists (Rule D10)
business_flow.outcome: The change is appended to `spec.changes`, `spec.needs_run` is set, the spec approval is revoked, and an existing plan is revoked and marked `invalidated`.

subsections.title: Phases and the work loop (implement, review, fix)
subsections.purpose: Each phase has two `WorkLoop`s, one for implementation and one for tests. A loop holds a `LoopNext` value that says what happens next. The fold moves `LoopNext` when an execution finishes; the planner reads it to spawn the next step. This is where the review cap, autofix, rescue, handoff, and blocker rules live.
assumptions: Only the execution recorded in `WorkLoop.running` may move its loop: `loop_finished` returns if the finishing execution is not `l.running`.
A work pass is an Implementer, WriteTest, PromptGeneration, or Verify run that submits `ImplementerSubmit` or `ReportSubmit`.
A review submit that does not parse fails the loop with the missing-submit message.
The project's auto-fixable rule IDs are read from the review execution's params (`auto_fixable_ids`), never from `project.toml`, so the fold stays pure.
A finding is auto-fixable only when its severity is not BLOCKER, its rule does not start with `SEC-BLOCK` or `PHASE-REQ`, and its rule ID is in the recorded set.

business_flow.action: A work pass ends Ok
business_flow.outcome: The changed files and report path are recorded. The next state is Review, Stage, or Done depending on `ReviewMode`, `stage`, and changed files.

business_flow.action: A review pass ends
business_flow.outcome: `iterations` increments and findings are split: BLOCKER goes alone to a BlockerFix work pass with no cap; auto-fixable findings go to Autofix; HIGH and MEDIUM go to Fix; LOW findings are kept in `leftover_low` and do not block.

business_flow.action: Iterations reach the effective cap with findings left
business_flow.outcome: Without YOLO the loop becomes CapReached and a ReviewCap gate opens. With YOLO the loop becomes Resolve and the ResolveReview judge decides; if resolution stops converging the loop becomes Blocked.

business_flow.action: A work pass submits STUCK
business_flow.outcome: The loop becomes Rescue and the Rescue judge picks explore, rerun, or gate.

business_flow.action: A work pass submits HANDOFF
business_flow.outcome: The loop becomes Handoff; a prompt-generation run follows, then a Resume work pass.

business_flow.action: An execution ends Interrupted
business_flow.outcome: The loop re-runs the in-flight step with `WorkKind::Rerun` and the same instructions.

subsections.title: How gate answers fold
subsections.purpose: A gate is a decision point that stops a stage until the user or YOLO answers. `on_gate_opened` records which track owns a gate; `on_gate_answered` applies the answer. This section lists every gate kind with the answer it accepts and its effect.
assumptions: The answer shape is validated before it is appended (`validate_answer` in runner.rs), so the fold treats an unexpected shape as no choice.
`routed` in `GateAnswered` is computed by `answer_needs_route` before the append; the fold trusts it.
A bare choice (approve, stop, retry, budget raise) has one meaning and is applied as is. Only answers with free text are routed through the Route answer judge (Rule J1).

tables.title: Gate kind, answer, and fold effect
rows: Answers appended to `spec.answers`, `needs_run` set. When routed, held for the Route answer judge.
Answers become a requirement change on the spec (Rule D10).
Approved and current and fact-check PASS: `approve_spec`. Feedback: pushed to `spec.changes`, `needs_run` set. Routed feedback is held.
Approved and current: plan approved and `adopt_plan_phases`. Feedback goes to the spec as a requirement change.
Choice: `stop` or another round, optional text
`stop` sets `stopped`; any other option sets `fail_limit_extra = consecutive_fails`; text becomes a spec change.
`another-pass`: `extra_cap` +1 and a Fix work pass (AwaitRoute when text is routed). Otherwise the loop is Blocked.
`retry`: `extra_cap` = iterations, resolve counters reset, Fix pass with the last review's HIGH, MEDIUM, and BLOCKER findings. Otherwise stays Blocked.
Retry re-runs the step; abandon blocks the loop, stops the spec or plan, abandons an explore, EPA, docs, or architecture stage, or fails an abandoned init.
`native` adds the agent to `native_fallback`, then retries.
Stores decisions on the init track.
No fold effect; the waiting execution receives the answer.
Choice: `raise` with optional dollars, or stop
Raise adds dollars (default: the current limit, minimum 1) plus any overspend to `budget_raised`. Any other choice fails the session.

sections.title: The planner: next_steps and Step
sections.purpose: `next_steps(&SessionState, &PlanCtx) -> Vec<Step>` decides what happens next. It is pure: it performs nothing and changes nothing. The runner performs the returned steps, appends the resulting events, and calls the planner again. Every rule in HANDOVER or Ultracode that decides ordering is implemented here or in the fold and has a fixture in tests/conformance/main.rs.

owns: The ordering of stages per category
The decision to open each gate, call each judge, and spawn each agent
Step identity (`Step::key`) used to avoid starting a step twice
The budget guard and the created-project hold on new work
does_not_own: Performing steps (runner, see engine-runner-lifecycle)
Folding results (see engine-state-fold)
Spawn rendering (engine-factory)
YOLO answers (engine-yolo); the planner only emits `YoloAnswer` steps

assumptions: `PlanCtx` carries the only outside facts: each project's format command (`format_commands`) and the session budget (`budget_usd`, `None` means no limit).
The runner calls `next_steps` on a clone of state taken under the state lock and performs steps afterward; state may have moved on by the time a step runs, so every `perform_*` re-reads state.
Two steps with the same `Step::key` are the same step. The planner removes duplicates within one call, and the runner skips a key that is already in flight.
A session that is not created, is terminal, or is paused yields no steps (Rule P1); pause blocks even YOLO answers.

subsections.title: Stage chain per category
subsections.purpose: `Planner::flows` picks the stage chain from the session's category. Research, spec, and plan stop at their artifact; implement runs the full build; verify, prompt, and quick change run phases only; test and docs run the closing stages.
assumptions: Categories are the `Category` enum from ostra-core: RESEARCH, SPEC, PLAN, IMPLEMENT, VERIFY, TEST, DOCS, PROMPT, QUICK_CHANGE, QUICK_ANSWER.
Explore tasks spawn in every category, because rescue and answer research can arrive during a build.
With no research document the spec is never entered (Rule D1): the planner emits `Fail` with the message that every research task failed or was abandoned.
The Track judge runs only for IMPLEMENT when no track was forced on the New task form.

business_flow.action: RESEARCH: waits for `explore_complete`
business_flow.outcome: Completion judge and `Complete`.

business_flow.action: SPEC: `explore_complete` then `spec_flow(false)`
business_flow.outcome: The spec needs a fact-check PASS but no approval; then completion.

business_flow.action: PLAN: `spec_flow(true)` then `plan_flow`
business_flow.outcome: Both need approval; then completion.

business_flow.outcome: Phases are built from the approved plan or created inline.

business_flow.action: IMPLEMENT: runs created-project init, phases, implementation review, closing stages
business_flow.outcome: Completion when `all_implement_done` holds.

business_flow.action: VERIFY, PROMPT, QUICK_CHANGE: runs phases, completes when every implementation loop is terminal and nothing is running
business_flow.outcome: No spec, plan, or closing gate.

business_flow.action: TEST and DOCS: run closing stages from pre-made Done phases
business_flow.outcome: No closing gate because the category already chose tests or docs.

business_flow.action: QUICK_ANSWER: spawns the quick-answer agent and completes with its answer
business_flow.outcome: No completion judge; the answer text is the report.

subsections.purpose: `spec_flow` and `plan_flow` generate an artifact, ask its open questions, fact-check it, and ask for approval. Each returns true once the artifact is done for the category.

subsections.title: Phase scheduling and loop steps
subsections.purpose: `phases` starts idle phases whose dependencies passed, one implement pipeline per project at a time, and `loop_steps` turns each `LoopNext` into a step. `removed_phases` drops phases that depend on a blocked phase.
assumptions: Rule M2: one implement pipeline per project runs at a time; different projects run in parallel. A project is busy while one of its loops is non-idle and not terminal.
A phase with `depends_on = None` depends on every earlier phase ID (Rule M5). Inline phases chain to the previous ID.
A phase is ready when every phase it depends on has a Done implementation loop (`deps_passed`).
A blocked phase removes every idle phase that depends on it, directly or through other removed phases (Rule D9); independent phases continue.
Agent choice: Initial, or Rerun and Resume when `work_count` is 1 or less, use the loop's `work_agent`; other kinds use `fix_agent`.

business_flow.action: Finds an idle phase with passed dependencies in a free project
business_flow.outcome: `loop_work` spawns the Initial work pass with the phase file, report file, and user notes kept for the implement or tests stage.

business_flow.action: Finds a loop with `running` or an open gate
business_flow.outcome: Returns without a step.

business_flow.action: Finds LoopNext Review
business_flow.outcome: Spawns code-reviewer with pass number `iterations + 1`, changed files, rationale, phase value `N` or `N-tests`, and ledger path.

business_flow.action: Finds LoopNext Blocked not yet announced
business_flow.outcome: Emits `AnnounceBlocked`; after the announcement, without YOLO and with no answered block gate, opens PhaseBlocked (Rule D9).

business_flow.action: Finds LoopNext Failed
business_flow.outcome: Opens ExecutionFailed, or HarnessFailure when the error starts with `harness-`.

business_flow.action: All phases terminal and nothing running
business_flow.outcome: `implementation_review` opens the ImplementationReview gate (Rule F1) or runs the Feedback judge on an unrouted round.

subsections.title: Format, closing gate, tests, documentation, book, and completion
subsections.purpose: After a project's phases pass review, `closing_stages` formats the project once, asks whether to write tests and documentation, runs the test stage, runs the documentation stage, and finally writes the documentation book. `completion` then asks the Completion judge for the report and ends the session.
assumptions: The closing stages start per project only when every non-removed phase of the project has a terminal implementation loop and at least one phase passed.
Format runs once per project (Rule D8) and is not gated; a missing command records `Some(None)`.
An explicit request for both tests and docs replaces the closing gate (Rule T3). Projects reaching the gate together are asked in one batch (Rule T6).
Only phases with `test_policy` Required, or without a plan file, are covered by tests (Rule T4).
An open BLOCKER finding blocks documentation (Hard rule 21).
A book of two or more documented projects also runs the system-architecture agent before the book write (Rule B4).

business_flow.action: Project code is done and format has not run
business_flow.outcome: Emits `Command Format` with the project's configured command.

business_flow.action: No closing choice yet
business_flow.outcome: Collects a `ClosingItem` per project and opens one ClosingGate with `ask_tests` and `ask_docs` flags.

business_flow.action: Tests chosen
business_flow.outcome: Spawns the execution-path analyzer for each covered phase in parallel; after all analyses finish, runs write-test and its review serially in phase order (Rule T4).

business_flow.action: Docs chosen and tests done
business_flow.outcome: Spawns documentation for the project, at most 4 documentation writers at once (Rule B7).

business_flow.action: Every part of the book is written
business_flow.outcome: Spawns system-architecture when there are 2 or more parts, then emits `WriteBook`.

business_flow.action: `all_implement_done`
business_flow.outcome: `completion`: Completion judge, then `Complete` with the judge's report plus a Projects created section (Rule O3).

sections.title: Judges: model decisions the engine asks for
sections.purpose: A judge is a single model call with a forced `decide` tool whose JSON input matches a schema. The engine uses judges only where a decision needs judgment: classification, research sufficiency, track, stakes, routing of free-text answers, feedback, rescue, resolving a capped review, YOLO answers, and the completion report. Each result is stored as a `DecisionMade` event with its reason, and the fold applies it.

owns: Judge output structs and JSON schemas (judge.rs)
Judge user messages built from session state (judge_input.rs)
The judge call loop with retries, validation, and cost tracking (`Inner::call_judge`)
Decision override rules (`SessionState::can_override`, `Engine::override_decision`)
does_not_own: Judge system prompts: `assets/judges/<name>.md`, served by `SpawnFactory::judge_prompt` (ostra-agents, agents area)
The model client that executes the call (`Services::judge`, server and providers areas)
Route resolution for the judge (`resolve_route` in ostra-core)

assumptions: The judge route key is `ostra_core::agent::JUDGE_ROUTE` with default tier Advanced and effort Low.
Every judge output carries a `reason` string; `reason_of` reads it and defaults to empty.
A judge output that parses into its typed struct is valid, with one extra rule: a Feedback output must have at least one target. YoloAnswer output is always valid at this stage and is checked later.
Judge usage cost is kept in memory per session (`judge_cost`) and added to the session row cost; it is not stored in events, so it resets when the server restarts.

business_flow.action: Emits `Step::Judge { judge, subject }`
business_flow.outcome: The runner calls `perform_judge`.

business_flow.action: Builds the user message with `judge_input` and the schema with `output_schema`
business_flow.outcome: The message and a short summary are ready.

business_flow.action: Calls `Services::judge` up to 3 times, sleeping 500, 1000, and 1500 ms after failed attempts
business_flow.outcome: The first output that validates is used.

business_flow.action: Appends `DecisionMade`
business_flow.outcome: The fold applies the decision in `on_decision`.

business_flow.action: All attempts fail
business_flow.outcome: The session fails with the error and a hint to check the judge route's provider key, except Completion (fallback report) and YoloAnswer (a Note; the gate waits for the user).

subsections.title: Answer routing (Rule J1) and added context (Rule C2)
subsections.purpose: When a gate answer or added context carries free text, the Route answer judge decides where each part goes before any agent sees it. Each part is delivered now, remembered for later stages, or discarded. The judge can also queue research and take back notes kept earlier.
assumptions: `answer_needs_route` is true only for answers with content: OpenQuestions with answers; spec or plan approval with non-empty feedback; FactCheckRecurring with text and an option other than `stop`; ReviewCap `another-pass` with text; Stuck `fact` with text; PhaseBlocked `retry` with text; ImplementationReview `feedback`.
A judge that does not name an item delivers it (`item_for` returns Deliver when no part exists).
A single-text answer uses the item ID `answer`; any item counts for it.
Notes get IDs `N1`, `N2` in the order kept; a forgotten note stays in the log and reaches no agent.
A judge may queue at most 3 research tasks per answer (`MAX_ANSWER_RESEARCH`), in projects the session has; an unknown project falls back to the primary project.
Context added before classification is read by the Classify judge with the request; after classification, only RESEARCH, SPEC, PLAN, and IMPLEMENT sessions route added context (`routes_amendments`).

sections.title: YOLO: engine-answered gates
sections.purpose: When a session runs with YOLO, the planner emits a `YoloAnswer` step for every open gate that YOLO may answer, and the runner answers it without waiting. Some gates get a fixed answer, some go to the YOLO judge, and some are never answered by YOLO because they need the user.

owns: `yolo_plan`, `yolo_leaves_open`, `yolo_answer_from_judge` (judge_input.rs)
`Inner::perform_yolo`
YOLO handling of live permission asks in `EngineHost::ask_permission` and `Engine::set_yolo`
does_not_own: The YOLO setting itself: the workspace default (`settings.yolo.default`) and the New task toggle (ostra-workspace and server areas)
Permission policy layers (ostra-policy)

assumptions: A paused session gets no YOLO answers (Rule P1).
YOLO never raises a budget and never retries an execution the user stopped (Rule P4).

The YOLO judge answer is checked by code: an approval needs a fact-check PASS on the current version, a rejection needs feedback, and every open question must be answered; a missing answer falls back to the agent's recommended option.
If the YOLO judge fails or its answer is refused, the engine appends a Note and the gate waits for the user.
