sections.title: Runner: Engine API, driver, and event append
sections.purpose: `Engine` is the public handle the server calls. Internally `Inner` holds the loaded sessions, a broadcast channel, the running-execution map, and the execution slot counter. One driver task per live session calls the planner and performs steps. `Inner::append` is the only way events enter a session.

owns: Session creation, pause, resume, stop, amend, YOLO toggle, gate answering, decision override, execution cancel and resume, and read-only reopen of harness runs
Restart recovery (`Engine::recover`) and offline stop (`stop_session_offline`)
The broadcast of `EngineNotice` values to the server
Gate answer validation (`validate_answer`) and the allow-rule suggestion (`suggest_rule`)
does_not_own: HTTP and WebSocket handling (server area)
Persisted rows (ostra-store)
Sandbox behavior for spawned programs (ostra-sandbox)

assumptions: `Engine` is `Clone`; clones share one `Arc<Inner>`.
The broadcast channel holds 4096 notices; a slow subscriber lags and loses old notices.
Mutex poisoning is ignored (`lock` takes the inner value), so one panicking step does not block a session.
For a pipeline session at least one project must have `.ostra/INVENTORY.md`; otherwise creation fails with a message to initialize a project first.

`stop_session` appends `SessionFailed` first, then cancels tokens, so nothing planned after the stop can start (`append` refuses `ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionResumed`, `CommandStarted` on a terminal session with `EngineError::Ended`).

business_flow.outcome: Each running execution is finished as Interrupted (or Waiting when it waited) keeping its spend, stale permission asks are denied, and drivers restart for unfinished sessions.

sections.title: Spawning an execution
sections.purpose: `Inner::perform_spawn` turns a `SpawnRequest` into a running execution: it waits for a slot, resolves the route, builds the spawn, records the start, runs the executor, and records the result. It also handles resuming a paused run, continuing a conversation, and creating a project.

assumptions: At most `limits.max_parallel_executions` executions hold a slot across the workspace, re-read each time; values below 1 count as 1. A waiting spawn polls every 2 seconds or when a slot frees.
The spawn returns without starting anything if the session is terminal or paused when the slot is acquired.
A resumed run must be for the same agent and have ended Interrupted or Waiting; otherwise the spawn is a fresh run.
A resumed or continued conversation keeps the executor and model it started on, which also keeps the prompt cache.
The skill generation step runs at tier Advanced whatever the agent default.
Claude and Grok harness runs get a `harness_session_id`: the resumed native session ID or a new UUID.
A Review execution always gets `auto_fixable_ids` from the project profile in its params.

sections.title: EngineHost: callbacks from a running execution
sections.purpose: `EngineHost` implements `ExecutionHost` for one running execution. The executor calls it to report output, ask for a tool permission, store messages, read a transcript, and wait for a message. It is how a run talks back to the engine.

owns: Recording activity items, usage, summary lines, and native session IDs
Permission gate creation and the wait for an answer
Containment signal recording
Releasing the execution slot while a run waits for a message
does_not_own: The `ExecutionHost` trait definition (ostra-core)
Permission decisions and guards (ostra-policy, policy area)
Classifying deltas as containment signals (`ostra_core::containment::classify`)

assumptions: A host without a session (a side-panel or read-only reopened run) denies every permission ask.
Executors report usage counted from zero; the host adds `usage_base` so a resumed run continues its total.
Containment signals are recorded at most `PAUSE_AFTER` (3) per execution so a retry loop cannot flood the log.
Appends by the host ignore errors except where noted, because a dropped activity item must not stop a run.

business_flow.action: Calls `emit(delta)`
business_flow.outcome: The execution's summary line, native session ID, usage, and activity item are stored; the item and session cost are broadcast.

business_flow.action: Emits a delta that classifies as a containment signal
business_flow.outcome: The host appends `ContainmentSignal`; the signal that makes the count 3 pauses the session and interrupts running executions.

business_flow.action: Calls `ask_permission(call, reason, rule)`
business_flow.outcome: A Permission gate opens with a suggested allow rule. Under YOLO it is answered AllowOnce at once; otherwise the host waits on a oneshot channel until `answer_gate`, stop, or interrupt sends the answer. A dropped channel means Deny.

business_flow.action: Calls `wait_for_wake()` after asking a subagent
business_flow.outcome: The host returns a pending message or waits for one, releasing its slot while it waits and acquiring a slot again when woken.

assumptions: A format command runs only after the user approved that exact command (Rule A1). An unapproved command is skipped once with the message `FORMAT_NOT_APPROVED` and recorded as a skipped format.

sections.title: Pause, resume, containment, and interrupts
sections.purpose: A session can be paused by the user, by three containment signals from one execution, by added context sent now, or because an agent created a project. In each case the fold marks running executions as interrupting and the runner cancels them; the stage then resumes the same run or restarts it.

owns: The `interrupting`, `resume_from`, `signals`, `contained` fold fields
`Interrupt` reasons and their messages
Cancelling tokens and denying permission asks of interrupted runs
does_not_own: Signal classification (`ostra_core::containment::classify`)
How an executor resumes a conversation (executor areas)
The pause and resume HTTP endpoints (server area)

assumptions: A paused session plans nothing, answers no gate under YOLO, and spawns nothing (Rule P1).

Only a run interrupted by a pause enters `resume_from`; an interrupt for new context clears `resume_from` so stages re-run from their spawn block (Rule C2), because a resumed conversation would not see the new context.
A run that starts in the window before the pause reaches the runner is marked interrupting as well.
A cancelled run whose execution is not marked interrupting stays Cancelled, which the planner treats as stopped by the user (Rule P4).
Continuing after containment is the user's acceptance, so a resumed execution's signal count starts again at 0 (Rule P3).

business_flow.action: Pauses the session
business_flow.outcome: `SessionPaused` marks every running execution as interrupting with Pause; the runner cancels their tokens and denies their waiting permission asks.

business_flow.action: Receives Cancelled from an executor marked interrupting
business_flow.outcome: The status becomes Interrupted with the message `The session was paused.`

business_flow.action: Handles the finished run
business_flow.outcome: The run is stored in `resume_from` under its purpose key; work loops set the in-flight step to Rerun.

business_flow.action: Resumes the session
business_flow.outcome: `SessionResumed` clears `paused` and `contained`. The planner sets `resumes` on the next spawn of that purpose; `perform_spawn` reuses the execution ID and appends `ExecutionResumed`.

business_flow.action: Emits three containment signals in one execution
business_flow.outcome: The session pauses and push notice `Session paused` explains why; the session stage shows which execution to read.

business_flow.action: Sends context with delivery Now
business_flow.outcome: Running executions are interrupted with Context; each re-runs from its spawn block with the context once the Route answer judge decides.

sections.title: Subagent coordination: asks, consults, and pair loops
sections.purpose: `coord.rs` lets running agents ask each other questions (Rule H3) and lets a pair such as author and fact-checker continue one conversation across rounds (Rules H5 to H7). Everything is a pure function of the log: asks, answers, and deliveries are events, and routing is computed from state.

owns: `Ask`, `Route`, `Delivery` and the routing decision
Conversation roots (`subagents`) and continuation rules
Tool call validation for SubagentAsk and SubagentReply (`ask_event`, `reply_event`) and the SubagentList text
does_not_own: Tool names, limits, and input parsing (`ostra_core::coord`)
Waking a run: the planner emits `Deliver` and Consult spawns; the runner performs them
The native and harness executors' wait behavior

assumptions: A subagent ID is the first execution of a conversation; later runs that resume it map to the same root (`subagent_of`).
A native run that asks ends with status Waiting and holds no process; a harness run that asks keeps its process alive and waits for a `Deliver` step.
A Waiting result folds as Interrupted for its stage, and the planner holds the stage's spawn until a message wakes the run in place (`waiting_keys`).
A helper (`explore` only, `HELPER_AGENTS`) may not start helpers, and a Consult run may not ask.
A run that was given a question must answer it with SubagentReply before it asks anything else.

A continuation falls back to a fresh run when the previous run did not end Ok with a submit, the agent differs, the forced executor differs, a harness run has no native session ID, context was delivered after it started, or the conversation already has `MAX_CONVERSATION_RUNS` runs.

sections.purpose: An init session builds a project's skills and inventory: detect the stack, scout components, propose skills, ask the user to approve them, generate each skill, and write the inventory and profile. The same flow runs inside a pipeline session for a project an agent created (Rules O3 to O5), with an advisor agent looking at failed steps before the user does.

sections.title: How the executors, policy, providers, MCP client and push fit together
sections.purpose: This section shows how the six crates of this area cooperate when the engine starts one execution (one run of one leaf agent). It names the two execution paths, native and harness, and the one rule they share: every tool call becomes a canonical `ToolCall` and passes `ExecutionPolicy::check` before it runs. Read it first to find which crate owns a behavior.

owns: The decision for each tool call (policy crate).
The streaming model clients and their error mapping (providers crate).
The native turn loop and the harness supervision loop (the two executor crates).
The MCP client protocol and the Web Push protocol.
does_not_own: The pipeline planner, runner and spawn factory that create `ExecutionSpec` values (engine area, `crates/ostra-engine`).
Tool implementations such as Bash, Read, Edit (tools area, `crates/ostra-tools`).
Sandbox backends, egress proxy and decoy files (sandbox area, `crates/ostra-sandbox`); this area only builds profiles and calls them.
`/internal/policy`, `/internal/mcp`, approval cards, workspace MCP connections, and push subscription storage (server area, `crates/ostra-server`).
Shared types such as `ExecContext`, `ToolCall`, `PolicyDecision`, `Usage`, `GlobalConfig` (core area, `crates/ostra-core`).

assumptions: The engine starts an execution by calling `Executor::run(spec, host, cancel)` from `ostra-core`; it never names a concrete executor (`crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`, `crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/executor.rs`).

Tool calls use Claude Code tool names and input shapes (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebFetch`, and Ostra tools such as `Report`, `Memory`), because `ostra-policy` matches on those names.
An agent ends its run by calling `submit_<agent>`; the engine reads only that payload (`ExecutionResult.submit`).
The server supplies the `ExecutionHost` (events, permission asks, YOLO flag) and the `BridgeServices` implementation; this area only calls their trait methods.

business_flow.action: Starts an execution for a leaf agent with an `ExecutionSpec` whose route names either a native `provider:model` or a harness CLI.

sections.title: Policy engine (ostra-policy)
sections.purpose: The policy engine answers one question for every tool call of every executor: allow, ask the user, or deny with a correction. It applies two layers in order. Layer 1 guards protect the pipeline and cannot be overridden by permissions, users or YOLO. Layer 2 follows Claude Code's permission model of modes plus allow, ask and deny rules. A post-tool observer drives the build streak and the lesson gate.

owns: The decision order of layer 1 then layer 2, and YOLO's effect on asks.
The list of guards, their names and their denial texts.
The permission rule grammar and matching.
The bash parse model and the write-target extraction.
The build streak counters and the lesson gate state for one execution.
does_not_own: Showing an ask to the user and recording the answer (server area and engine area through `ExecutionHost::ask_permission` or `BridgeServices::resolve_ask`).
Recording a lesson (`Memory` tool, tools area and `ostra-store`).
The shape of `ToolCall`, `PolicyDecision`, `RuleRef`, `ToolOutcome` (core area, `crates/ostra-core/src/policy.rs`).
Which settings supply allow, ask and deny lists (core area config and workspace area).

assumptions: Tool calls arrive already canonical: Claude Code tool names and input fields such as `file_path`, `command`, `url`, `cwd` (native executor via `ToolEnv::canonical_call`, harness via adapters).
`ExecContext` is complete when `ExecutionPolicy::new` runs; its `repo_root`, `session_dir`, `session_root` and `workspace_root` are real paths that can be canonicalized (`Roots::new` in `guards.rs`).

An empty `workspace_root` means there is no workspace: the workspace-specific roots (artifacts, books, sessions root, workspace db) stay empty and their checks are skipped (`inside` returns false for an empty root).
`PolicyInputs.build_commands` and `test_commands` come from the project's `project.toml` and are supplied by the caller; the policy never reads the file.
Permission rule strings were validated at settings save; an invalid rule found at run time is logged with `tracing::warn!` and ignored (`parse_rules`).

business_flow.action: Builds a canonical `ToolCall` and calls `ExecutionPolicy::check`.
business_flow.outcome: A `PolicyDecision` of Allow, Ask or Deny, each carrying a `RuleRef` that names the guard or permission rule.

business_flow.action: Runs layer 1 guards first.
business_flow.outcome: A guard denial returns at once and nothing later can allow the call.

business_flow.action: Runs layer 2 permissions when no guard fires.
business_flow.outcome: Deny rules beat ask rules, which beat allow rules, then the mode default applies.

business_flow.action: Converts asks to allows when YOLO is on.
business_flow.outcome: Denials stand; asks and `mode:bypass` allows become an allow named `yolo`.

business_flow.action: Reports each finished call to `ExecutionPolicy::observe`.
business_flow.outcome: The streak may produce a note to append to the tool result or a memory recall request.

concerns.responsibility: Composes layers, holds per-execution state (YOLO, session allow rules, build streak), builds allow-rule suggestions.

subsections.title: Decision order and modes
subsections.purpose: `ExecutionPolicy::check` composes the layers and YOLO. `layer1` runs the guards in a fixed order; `layer2` applies permission rules and the mode default by tool family. This subsection lists the order so a change to one check does not reorder another.

owns: Ordering of guards and layer 2 by tool family.
Mapping of modes to default decisions.
does_not_own: The individual guard texts (subsection on guards).
Rule grammar (subsection on permissions).

assumptions: `PermissionMode` has four values: Default, AcceptEdits, Plan, Bypass (`ostra_core::config::PermissionMode`); YOLO forces Bypass for mode decisions (`ExecutionPolicy::mode`).
The caller refreshes YOLO before each check with `set_yolo(host.yolo())` (native executor does this in `submit` and `tool_end`).
`State` is behind a `std::sync::Mutex`; a poisoned lock is recovered with `into_inner`.

business_flow.action: Parses the command with `bash::parse` when the tool is `Bash`.
business_flow.outcome: The parsed commands are shared by layer 1 and layer 2.

business_flow.action: Layer 1: answer-only runs are refused any write; `Report`, `Document` and manage tools have their own checks; `submit_*` is refused while a reply is owed or a lesson is pending; PowerShell and cmd text is scanned; every write target passes `check_write`; every read path passes `check_windows_path` and `check_read`; Bash passes `check_shell`, `check_shell_reads`, per-target checks and the build streak gate.
business_flow.outcome: The first denial is returned.

business_flow.action: Layer 2 by family: Bash, Edit (Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit, ApplyPatch), Read (Read, Grep, Glob), WebFetch, Skill with a path, tools that change Ostra, and every other tool.
business_flow.outcome: A decision with a rule reference.

business_flow.action: When YOLO is on, turns Ask into Allow with rule `yolo`, and turns an Allow by `mode:bypass` into Allow `yolo`.
business_flow.outcome: Only denials remain as blockers.

flowchart TD
    A[ToolCall reaches check] --> B{tool is Bash}
    B -->|yes| C[bash parse]
    B -->|no| D[layer1 guards]
    C --> D
    D -->|denial| X[Deny with guard rule]
    D -->|none| E[layer2 permissions]
    E --> F{yolo on}
    F -->|no| G[return layer2 decision]
    F -->|yes| H{Ask or mode bypass allow}
    H -->|yes| I[Allow with rule yolo]

tables.title: Layer 2 behavior by tool family
rows: Per target path: deny and ask rules win; allow rules and session allows

A file that runs code later (`runs_code_later`) uses the mode default; a path in the session dir or temp is allowed; AcceptEdits allows paths in the repo; otherwise the mode default. Any deny returns at once; the first ask is kept; otherwise Allow named by the allowing rule, `mode:acceptEdits` or `session-dir`.
Bypass allows with `mode:bypass`; every other mode asks (`mode:default` or `mode:acceptEdits`).
Per simple command: deny across all commands, then ask across all commands, then allow rules and session allows

Unmodelled or unparsed scripts follow the mode; a read-only command with in-scope writes is allowed; AcceptEdits also allows `mkdir`, `touch`, `cp`, `mv` inside repo, session dir or temp; otherwise Bypass allows, Plan denies, Default and AcceptEdits ask.
Only a deny rule can refuse; allow rules are ignored (Rule O1)
Plan denies; every other mode asks with rule `manage`; YOLO answers it.

Known Ostra tools, `submit_*`, harness bookkeeping tools and MCP gateway tools are allowed; in Plan mode an MCP tool is allowed only when its server marks it read-only (Rule M1); an unknown tool gets the mode default.

subsections.title: Layer 1 guards
subsections.purpose: Layer 1 guards refuse a call no matter what permissions, users or YOLO say. Each guard is a port of an Ultracode hook or an Ostra rule and returns a denial whose text gives the correction first, because Grok clips reasons to 256 characters. The `Roots` struct holds the canonical paths all guards compare against.

owns: Guard names, matching and denial texts.
The `Roots` path classification: repo, session, temp, protected, secret, engine state, artifacts, books.
does_not_own: The containment constants `SELF_PROTECTION`, `GIT_METADATA`, `SECRET_READ` (core area, `ostra_core::containment`).
Which agent owns which artifact (core area, `AgentName`).

assumptions: Rule G1: write scope, the report path and self-protection apply only when `ctx.enforce_tool_calls` is true (`Roots.strict`). Ownership, secrets, git metadata and the test-file rule hold without it.
Paths are compared after canonicalization with `ostra_core::paths::resolve`; relative paths resolve against the call's `cwd` field when absolute, else the repo root (Rule C3, `start_cwd`).
A project that itself lives under the OS temp dir is treated as project source, not scratch (`Roots::in_temp`).
Git Bash MSYS paths (`/c/Users/me`) are translated before comparison (`Roots::resolve` via `paths::from_msys`).

subsections.title: Permission rules and matching
subsections.purpose: Permission rules use Claude Code's syntax, `Tool` or `Tool(spec)`. This subsection describes the grammar, how each family matches, and the suggestion an 'always in this workspace' answer adds. Settings validation calls `validate_rule` so a bad rule fails at save time.

owns: Rule parsing, path anchoring, bash spec matching, URL host matching, suggestions.
does_not_own: Where rules are stored and merged (core and workspace areas).
Applying deny, ask, allow order (decision subsection).

assumptions: A rule's tool name must be one of the 29 names in `KNOWN_TOOLS`, or start with `mcp__`, `Other:` or `submit_` (`parse_rule`).
`Edit` rules cover every file-writing tool, and `Read` rules cover Grep and Glob (`family`, `Rule::matches`).
The matcher compares canonical absolute paths; on Windows both pattern and path are lowercased and `\\?\` prefixes are dropped (`glob_path`).
`validate_rule` checks path patterns against placeholder roots `/repo` and `/home/x`, so it validates syntax only.

business_flow.action: Saves a rule such as `Bash(npm run test *)` in settings.
business_flow.outcome: `validate_rule` returns an error message with the fix, or accepts it.

business_flow.action: Matches a rule against a subject: one simple command, a resolved path, a URL, or a tool name.
business_flow.outcome: True when the tool family matches and the spec matches.

business_flow.action: Answers a permission ask with 'always in this workspace'.
business_flow.outcome: `allow_rule_suggestion` produces a rule (for example `Bash(git push *)` or `Edit(/src/**)`) that the caller adds as a session allow rule; no rule is suggested for tools that change Ostra (Rule O1).

tables.title: Rule grammar
rows: Glob over one simple command; `*` matches anything; a trailing ` *` also matches the bare command
Legacy prefix form: the command equals the prefix or starts with it plus a space
Matched against the full words, the words without leading `VAR=value`, and the effective command without wrappers such as `sudo`
Gitignore-style path globs: `//x` absolute, `~/x` under home, `/x` and `x/y` relative to the repo root, a bare name matches at any depth, a trailing `/` adds `**`; `dir/**` also matches `dir`
The URL's host equals the domain or ends with `.domain`; the host is parsed with the same parser reqwest uses
Covers every tool of that MCP server; `mcp__github__search` covers one tool
Matches every use of the tool

is not a tool Ostra knows

subsections.title: Bash parsing and read-only classification
subsections.purpose: `bash::parse` uses tree-sitter-bash to split a command into simple commands in execution order, with redirects, heredoc bodies and the paths each command would create, overwrite, move or delete. The policy trusts a command to run unasked only when it fully understands it; anything else asks. This replaces the regex heuristics of Ultracode's `shell-paths.js` and keeps its rules.

owns: Parse model, write-target extraction, the read-only command list and its hardening rules.
does_not_own: Applying targets to roots (guards.rs `shell_targets`).
Running commands (tools area).

assumptions: The grammar is `tree_sitter_bash::LANGUAGE`; a syntax error sets `Parsed.complete = false` and the policy then asks (Default) or denies (Plan).
Nested parsing of `bash -c`, `eval` and heredoc bodies fed to a shell stops at depth 4 (`MAX_DEPTH`); deeper code marks the parse incomplete.
`cd` and `pushd` are tracked linearly; subshell scoping is not modelled (`command_cwds`); `popd` or a dynamic `cd` target makes the directory unknown (`cwd_unknown`).
Only statements the walker models count as `modelled`; a standalone assignment, `export`, `[[ ]]`, a loop header or a function sets `modelled = false`.

business_flow.action: Calls `bash::parse` on the `command` field.
business_flow.outcome: `Parsed { commands, complete, modelled }`.

business_flow.action: Call `write_targets`, `unresolved_writes`, `command_cwds` and `inline_code`.
business_flow.outcome: Resolved write targets with the `cd` in effect, indexes of commands that write somewhere unknown, and interpreter code text.

business_flow.action: Calls `is_read_only` per command.
business_flow.outcome: A command qualifies only when it has no assignments, runs at word index 0 after no wrapper, has a static name without a `/`, and is in the read-only list with safe flags.

rows: `dest/src_name` when the destination is a directory (`-t`, `--target-directory` and abbreviations, several sources, or a trailing `/`), else the destination; `mv` also targets each source
The file words after the script
`git` write subcommands: checkout, switch, restore, reset, apply, am, stash, clean, rm, mv, merge, rebase, pull, cherry-pick, revert, commit, add
The working tree at the `-C` directory or the cwd

`printf -v`, or a word with `[`, `$` or a backtick
Any argument is dynamic or a glob

subsections.title: Build streak and lesson gate
subsections.purpose: The build module recognizes build and test commands, decides whether an outcome failed, and counts consecutive failures per execution. It warns at 3, refuses further build commands at 5, and, after a pass that follows a real streak, requires the agent to record a lesson before it reports or submits. It ports Ultracode's `build-signal.js`, `build-streak.js` and `build-streak-gate.js`.

owns: Streak counters, thresholds, recovery records and their messages.
does_not_own: Storing the lesson (`Memory` tool, `ostra-store`).
Appending notes to tool results and running recall (executors).

assumptions: Configured commands come from the project profile (`build`, `test`, `test_one`, `lint`, `typecheck`); with none configured, the fallback regex `FALLBACK_BUILD` recognizes common tools such as `cargo`, `mvn`, `gradle`, `npm run`, `pytest`.
A placeholder such as `{MODULE}` in a configured command matches any text (`command_matcher`).
An exit code wins over output text; output markers are used only when no exit code is known (`failed_from`).
`None` from `failed_from` means no evidence (timeout, interruption, or an unknown result with empty output) and the streak is not changed.

business_flow.action: Runs a build or test command through Bash.
business_flow.outcome: `observe` records pass or fail in the `Streak`.

business_flow.action: On the 2nd consecutive failure with a known diagnostic, asks the caller to recall lessons (`Observation::RecallLessons`).
business_flow.outcome: The executor appends matching lessons to the result.

business_flow.action: On failures 3 and 4, adds a note to state the root cause; on failure 5, the gate refuses further build commands and the note tells the agent to submit `stuck`.
business_flow.outcome: The agent must hand back with status `stuck`.

business_flow.action: Passes after at least 3 failures with a known signature.
business_flow.outcome: A `Recovery` is stored as pending and a note demands a `Memory` lesson; `Report` and `submit_*` with status ok are refused until a `Memory` call succeeds or `Report` gives a reason.

sections.title: Model providers (ostra-providers)
sections.purpose: The providers crate gives the rest of Ostra one streaming chat interface over the Anthropic Messages API and the OpenAI Responses API. It resolves API keys, builds requests for each model's capabilities, parses streamed events into neutral blocks, prices usage, retries transient failures before output starts, and offers a scripted provider for tests.

owns: Neutral request, response and error types.
Request bodies, stream parsing, retry, key lookup and base URL resolution.
does_not_own: Which model a route names (core area route resolution).
Prices and limits (core area `pricing`).
The agent loop that consumes responses (`ostra-exec-native`).

assumptions: Only the provider names `anthropic` and `openai` are built from config; any other name in the config is logged and ignored (`Providers::rebuild`).
Model ids are written `provider:model` in routes; `for_model` splits at the first colon.
Pricing, context window and maximum output per model come from `ostra_core::pricing`, which is backed by the models.dev catalog; a missing model has no ceiling and no cost table.
Streams end with `message_stop` (Anthropic) or `response.completed` or `response.incomplete` (OpenAI); a stream that ends earlier is a retryable network error.

business_flow.action: Builds a `ChatRequest` and calls `Provider::chat` with an event sink and a cancel token.
business_flow.outcome: Text, thinking and tool-input deltas stream to the sink while the response accumulates.

business_flow.action: Sends the request with retry; on a retryable error before any content block starts, waits with jittered backoff and sends again.
business_flow.outcome: A `ChatResponse` with content blocks, `StopReason`, `Usage` with `cost_usd`, the answering model and a refusal category when present.

business_flow.action: Calls `structured` for a judge decision.
business_flow.outcome: The tool input of the forced `decide` tool call and the summed usage.

subsections.title: Neutral types and errors
subsections.purpose: The neutral types let the agent loop and judges run unchanged on either vendor. A `ChatRequest` carries system blocks, messages of typed blocks, tool definitions, server tools, effort and tool choice. A `ChatResponse` returns blocks, a stop reason and usage.

A tool-use input whose streamed JSON did not parse is stored as an object with the key `__invalid_json` (`INVALID_INPUT_KEY`); the agent loop answers it with an error instead of running the tool.

subsections.title: Registry, key lookup and structured output

sections.title: Native executor (ostra-exec-native)
sections.purpose: The native executor runs one leaf agent on an API key. It loops model turns, passes every tool call through the policy, runs allowed tools through `ostra-tools`, compacts context near the window, and ends when the agent calls its `submit_<agent>` tool with a valid payload. It returns an `ExecutionResult` with status, submit payload, final text and usage.

owns: The turn loop, turn limits, continuation and reminder turns, compaction trigger, tool dispatch order, submit validation, transcript rebuild.
does_not_own: Tool implementations (tools area).
Policy decisions (policy section).
Provider calls (providers section).
Sandbox mechanics (sandbox area); this crate only builds a profile and starts the egress proxy and decoy watch.

assumptions: `spec.route.model` is `provider:model` and the provider has a key; otherwise the run fails at once with a message naming the provider.
`spec.timeout_secs` is at least 1 (`max(1)`); on expiry the run is cancelled and returns status Error with `timed out after N s`.
The host's `transcript(id)` returns stored `(role, content)` pairs when a run resumes; a `compaction` record replaces every message before it.
Project build and test commands are read fresh from the repo's project profile for every policy input and for build-time accounting.
`MemoryStore::open(memory_db)` works for lesson recall; a failure there silently skips recall.

business_flow.action: Calls `run` with an `ExecutionSpec`.
business_flow.outcome: The run races a cancel token and a timeout; both stop the inner run and wait up to 3 s (`CLEANUP_GRACE`) for tools to die.

business_flow.action: Resolves the provider, opens workspace MCP tools, builds `ExecutionPolicy`, `ToolEnv`, the sandbox, the tool list and the first message (or the resumed transcript).
business_flow.outcome: Tools are the capability tools, the Document tool when allowed, workspace MCP tools, and the submit tool whose schema is `spec.submit_schema` when set.

business_flow.action: Loops up to 400 turns, calling the provider with effort `spec.effort` and the model's whole output limit.
business_flow.outcome: Each response records usage, is saved to the transcript and is handled by stop reason.

business_flow.action: Runs tool calls in order; consecutive read-only calls run concurrently.
business_flow.outcome: Results return as one user message of tool results.

business_flow.action: Calls `submit_<agent>`.
business_flow.outcome: After policy, schema and document checks pass, the run ends with status ok, stuck or handoff; other calls of that turn are answered 'Not run: the run ended with the submit call.'

subsections.title: Compaction, resume and sandbox setup
subsections.purpose: Three mechanisms keep a native run alive across long work and restarts. Compaction replaces the conversation with a summary near the context window. Resume rebuilds the conversation from the stored transcript. Sandbox setup wraps Bash in the execution's sandbox profile.

owns: Trigger and retry rules for compaction, resume message construction, sandbox profile assembly for Bash.
does_not_own: The summary itself (provider `compact`).
Sandbox backends and proxy (sandbox area).

assumptions: Context size is the last response's input plus cache plus output tokens, plus an estimate of four characters per token for messages added since (`context_of`, `estimate_tokens`).
Compaction runs only when the last message is a user turn, because no tool call may be open.
The `[sandbox]` table and the workspace mode are read fresh from the global config for each execution (`sandbox_for`).
The scratch dir (the sandbox's `/tmp` or `TMPDIR`) is deleted when the run ends or its future is dropped (`Scratch`).

business_flow.action: Checks the estimated context against 95 percent of the window before each request.
business_flow.outcome: When reached, and any earlier failed attempt has allowed growth of 2 percent, it calls `Provider::compact` with the fixed instructions.

business_flow.action: Receives a summary.
business_flow.outcome: The conversation becomes the provider's compacted window plus the 'compacted into the summary above' user turn, and a `compaction` record is stored so a later resume starts from it.

business_flow.action: Receives no summary or an error other than cancel.
business_flow.outcome: The run continues without compaction and waits for growth before trying again.

business_flow.action: Resumes with `spec.resume`.
business_flow.outcome: Stored messages are merged per role; open tool calls get an 'Interrupted: this call did not finish.' error result; the resume note, or the default interruption notice, is added. Resuming in place records only the new turn so the replayed prefix hits the prompt cache (Rule P2).

sections.title: Harness executor (ostra-exec-harness)
sections.purpose: The harness executor runs one leaf agent inside an installed CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Antigravity) under a PTY. Every tool call the CLI makes reaches Ostra's policy through a hook command, and Ostra's own tools, including `submit_<agent>`, are served by an MCP stdio shim. The run completes when the agent calls its submit tool, confirmed by the CLI's Stop event where one exists.

owns: Launch plans, PTY handling, hook and MCP message translation, supervision and completion rules, usage following, harness status.
does_not_own: The `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp` routes and the `BridgeServices` implementation (server area).
Sandbox backends (sandbox area).
Policy decisions (policy section).

assumptions: The CLI binary named in `[harness.<name>].command` is on `PATH` (`which::which`); otherwise the launch fails with a `harness-launch:` error.
The `ostra` binary serves `hook` and `mcp-stdio`; its absolute path is `HarnessExecutorConfig.ostra_binary`.
The server's callback URL is `http://<ip>:<port>` when the CLI is sandboxed (`bridge_addr` refuses a host name).
Each execution has one random token, minted in `LiveRegistry::register` from two UUIDs, and every callback must present it.
Flags and payload shapes were checked against claude 2.1.280, codex 0.153.4, grok 1.0.30 and agy 1.2.6 (`launch.rs` module note).

subsections.title: Hook bridge, MCP shim and adapters
subsections.purpose: The bridge is the two-sided link between a running CLI and the server. `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio` are subprocesses the CLI starts; they forward to `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp`. `HarnessBridge` handles those requests on the server side, and a per-harness `Adapter` translates payloads to canonical tool calls and formats the answer in the shape that CLI accepts.

owns: Payload translation, response formats, the list of Ostra tools shown to each run, submit recording.
does_not_own: HTTP routing and local-peer checks of `/internal/*` (server area).
Policy decisions and ask resolution (`BridgeServices` implementation in the server).

assumptions: The bridge never fails open: anything unreadable on a PreToolUse denies, and `ostra hook` prints a deny when the server is unreachable or its answer is unreadable.
`ostra hook` without `OSTRA_EXECUTION` is a no-op (exit 0), because Antigravity's integration is installed globally; `ostra mcp-stdio` without it answers the handshake with no tools.
Authorization needs both the live registry's constant-time token check and `BridgeServices::authorize`.
MCP protocol versions served are 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25; 2026-07-28 is left out on purpose because Claude Code rejects a `tools/list` without fields that version requires.
A harness's hook payload may be in snake_case or camelCase; adapters read both.

business_flow.action: Runs `ostra hook --harness <h> --event <e>` with the payload on stdin.
business_flow.outcome: The subprocess posts a `PolicyRequest` with the bearer token; PreToolUse has no HTTP timeout, other events 60 s.

business_flow.action: PreToolUse: parses the call, counts it, rejects another agent's `submit_*`, calls `policy_check`, resolves an Ask with `resolve_ask`.
business_flow.outcome: Allow, or a deny with the reason and `(Ostra <layer>: <rule>)` appended.

business_flow.action: PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure: parses the outcome and calls `policy_observe`.
business_flow.outcome: Notes return as additional context in the harness's format.

business_flow.action: Stop: forwards to `stop_event` and asks `LiveExecution::on_stop`.
business_flow.outcome: Allow, or a block with the submit reminder for the first 2 Stops without a submit; the third is let through and marks the run as given up.

business_flow.action: Calls an Ostra tool through `ostra mcp-stdio`.
business_flow.outcome: `initialize`, `server/discover`, `ping`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list` and `prompts/list` are answered; other methods return error -32601.

business_flow.action: Calls `submit_<agent>` through MCP.
business_flow.outcome: Coerce, `validate_submit`, `doc::check_submit`, then `record_submit`; the first payload wins and a second is refused.

diagrams.title: PreToolUse handling in HarnessBridge
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
    A[policy request] --> B{token and harness match}
    B -->|no| D1[deny Stop now]
    B -->|yes| C[adapter parse_pre]
    C -->|refuse spawn or question| D2[deny with correction]
    C -->|call| E{other agent submit tool}
    E -->|yes| D3[deny use own submit tool]
    E -->|no| F[services policy_check]
    F -->|Allow| G[allow]
    F -->|Deny| D4[deny with rule text]
    F -->|Ask| H[resolve_ask]
    H -->|allowed| G
    H -->|denied| D5[deny user refused]

tables.title: Adapter differences
rows: `MultiEdit` and `NotebookEdit` map to `Edit`; `LS` maps to `Glob`; `PowerShell` is an opaque shell
An argv array is POSIX-quoted into one command; on Windows a non-POSIX shell becomes the opaque `PowerShell` tool; output carries no exit code
camelCase with snake_case aliases; `use_tool` wraps another tool
Claude-shaped deny with the reason fitted to 256 characters (head plus last sentence)
`toolInputTruncated` past 128 KiB is refused with an instruction to split the call
`toolCall.{name,args}` with PascalCase arguments; `call_mcp_tool` wraps MCP calls
PostToolUse carries no result, so outcomes are marked `result_known: false`; post and stop answers are `{}`

tables.title: Refusals before the policy
rows: Every Ostra agent is a leaf; a delegated task would run outside the guards
Questions go in the submit call; Ostra asks from the pipeline's gate

concerns.responsibility: Server-side handler for policy and MCP requests.
Subprocess entry points; stdio lines in, HTTP posts out, replies on stdout.
`meta`, `parse_pre`, `parse_post`, `pre_response`, `post_response`, `stop_response`.
What the bridge needs from the server: `authorize`, `policy_check`, `resolve_ask`, `policy_observe`, `mcp_call`, `mcp_tools`, `stop_event`.

code_refs.note: Wire shapes, environment names, `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp` paths.

subsections.title: Live execution state and stop handling
subsections.purpose: `LiveRegistry` holds one `LiveExecution` per running harness execution. The bridge writes what arrives (submit payload, session id, transcript path, tool count, stops, waiting flag); the executor reads snapshots and waits for changes.

owns: Per-execution mutable state, stop verdicts, nudge text.
does_not_own: Deciding when the run ends (supervision).

assumptions: The registry entry and its token exist only between `register` and `remove` in `HarnessExecutor::run`.
The first recorded submit wins; later calls return false.
An inspection run (`set_inspect`) expects no submit, so a Stop is never turned back.

business_flow.action: Calls `on_stop` with the last assistant message.
business_flow.outcome: Allow when inspecting or waiting; Allow and `stopped_after_submit` when a submit exists; Block with a nudge for the first 2 stops; then `gave_up`.

business_flow.action: Reads `snapshot`.
business_flow.outcome: A copy of `LiveState`: submit, session id, transcript path, stops, flags, last activity, last message, tool calls, waiting.

tables.title: Nudge text
rows: Call the submit tool now, before stopping, because a run that ends without it is recorded as failed

concerns.responsibility: State, `Notify` wakeups, stop verdicts.
Map by execution id; `authorize` compares tokens in constant time.

subsections.title: PTY session and terminal replay log
subsections.purpose: `PtySession` starts the CLI in a pseudo-terminal, keeps a virtual screen for prompt detection and browser attach, answers the terminal queries CLIs send at startup, and ends the CLI with a grace period. `TermLog` stores the raw bytes so the Terminal tab can replay an ended run.

owns: PTY, screen model, input queue, terminal query replies, termination, replay log.
does_not_own: The browser terminal view and WebSocket (server and web areas).

assumptions: The terminal size is clamped to 20 to 1000 columns and 5 to 500 rows (`MIN_COLS`, `MAX_COLS`, `MIN_ROWS`, `MAX_ROWS`), because vt100 0.16 panics on smaller screens that wrap; the default is 120 by 40.
Environment variables that tie a process to the harness session Ostra itself runs under (16 names in `PARENT_SESSION_ENV`) are removed, so Claude Code persists the session and it can be resumed.
`TERM` is `xterm-256color` and `COLORTERM` is `truecolor`.

business_flow.action: Calls `PtySession::spawn(plan, cols, rows, on_output)`.
business_flow.outcome: Threads start for reading, writing and waiting for exit; output feeds the screen, the broadcast stream for viewers, the query answerer and the `TermLog`.

business_flow.action: Receives terminal queries (cursor position, device attributes, colors, kitty keyboard, XTVERSION, mode queries).
business_flow.outcome: `answer_queries` writes the replies; only `?<digits>$` parameters are echoed, so program output cannot type into the program's input.

business_flow.action: Types a line with `type_line`.
business_flow.outcome: Bracketed paste of the text, 150 ms later Enter.

business_flow.action: Calls `terminate(grace)`.
business_flow.outcome: SIGTERM to the process group (closing the pseudoconsole on Windows), a kill after the grace period, then the sandbox members are dropped.

tables.title: Limits
rows: A full input queue refuses writes instead of blocking
A viewer that falls further behind resyncs from a snapshot
The log grows to twice the cap, then is rewritten with its last 2 MiB; the file is owner-only
Trailing bytes kept for a sequence the next read completes

concerns.responsibility: Process, screen, streams, termination.
Terminal query recognition and replies.
Sessions by execution id for viewers.
Append-only capped replay file; a failed write stops the log, not the run.

subsections.title: Sandbox wrapping of the CLI
subsections.purpose: `sandbox::wrap` runs the CLI under the execution's sandbox profile so the CLI's own shell tool and everything it starts inherit the sandbox. It allows the model API hosts, forwards the hook bridge into the sandbox, and protects the CLI's settings and hooks so a write cannot run later in the user's own CLI sessions.

owns: Which dirs are writable or protected per harness, which hosts are allowed, how the bridge URL is rewritten.
does_not_own: Backends, egress proxy and decoy implementation (sandbox area).

assumptions: Under bubblewrap the home folder is overlaid; Seatbelt has no overlay, so the rest of home stays read-only there and a CLI's write at its top level (Claude Code's `~/.claude.json`) fails, which the CLIs survive.
`sandbox::decide(cfg)` picks the backend or returns an unsandboxed warning; an `Err` means the config requires a sandbox this machine cannot provide and the launch fails.
The bridge address must be `http://<ip>:<port>`; with `bridge_socket` set, the sandbox reaches only `/internal/*`, not `/api`.
When the CLI is sandboxed, Claude Code's own sandbox is disabled in its settings, because macOS cannot nest Seatbelt sandboxes.

business_flow.action: Builds a profile with allowed hosts (the harness's model hosts, plus hosts of `*_BASE_URL` variables, Claude settings `env`, and Codex `model_providers`), starts the egress proxy and plants decoys.
business_flow.outcome: Model endpoints chosen by the user work even when they are on the LAN.

business_flow.action: Forwards the bridge port or socket and rewrites the URL inside plan files and `OSTRA_URL` to the forwarded loopback address.
business_flow.outcome: Hooks and the MCP shim reach the server from inside the sandbox.

business_flow.action: Marks the harness state dirs writable and their settings, instructions and hooks read-only; copies `~/.claude.json` into the config dir for Claude Code under bubblewrap.
business_flow.outcome: A CLI can save sessions but cannot plant code for later sessions.

business_flow.action: After the run calls `cleanup`.
business_flow.outcome: The Claude config copy, Grok's token-bearing config and the scratch `/tmp` are removed.

tables.title: Read-only entries inside each harness state dir
rows: settings.json, settings.local.json, CLAUDE.md, commands/, agents/, skills/, plugins/, hooks/, output-styles/

concerns.responsibility: Profile assembly and command wrapping.
Per-harness dirs and allowed hosts.
`CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR` and `SSL_CERT_FILE` (`/etc/ssl/cert.pem`) for macOS.

subsections.title: Usage following and session transcripts
subsections.purpose: A harness reports no token counts through hooks, so Ostra reads the CLI's own session file while the run is live and adds it up, which shows spend during the run as native runs do. At the end, the same reader supplies the final usage and the last assistant message.

owns: Per-harness usage arithmetic and file discovery.
does_not_own: Prices (`ostra_core::pricing`).
Showing usage (web and server areas).

assumptions: Session files are JSON Lines; a last line without a newline counts once it parses as JSON.
A file shorter than the last read offset was replaced or truncated and is read again from the start.
Antigravity records no token counts, so its follower returns at once and its usage stays zero.
The session path depends on a session id the CLI may report late; the follower looks again every 2 s until the file exists.

business_flow.action: Locates the session file, then watches its directory with `notify`.
business_flow.outcome: On a change, waits 500 ms for a burst to settle and reads the appended bytes; with no platform watcher it polls every 5 s.

business_flow.action: Emits `ExecutionDelta::Usage` when the tally changed.
business_flow.outcome: Tool calls are counted from hooks, not from the file.

business_flow.action: Stops the follower before building the final result.
business_flow.outcome: A late reading cannot overwrite the result.

tables.title: Usage arithmetic per harness
rows: One line per content block repeats the message usage, so usage counts once per message id; each message is priced with its own model and cache TTL split
`token_count` events hold running totals; each increase is normalized (input minus cached and written, output includes reasoning) and priced with the current turn's model
Each `turn_completed` update adds its usage; cost is `costUsdTicks` divided by 10^10
Only the last `PLANNER_RESPONSE` text is read

concerns.responsibility: Incremental reading and per-harness tallies.
Discovery, watching and emission.

subsections.title: Harness status, installers and the Antigravity integration
subsections.purpose: `setup.rs` reports whether each harness CLI is installed and logged in, names the login and installer commands the Terminal view runs, and installs the one global integration Antigravity needs. `command.rs` resolves a command name to a program Windows can start.

owns: Status detection, installer commands, Antigravity plugin files.
does_not_own: The setup terminal UI (web area) and the API routes (server area).

assumptions: Status probes run the CLI with a 15 s limit; a failed probe leaves `logged_in` unknown (`None`).
Antigravity reads hooks and MCP servers only from global config, so its integration must be installed before its first run and is idempotent.
The official installers put binaries in `~/.local/bin` and `~/.grok/bin` (Windows adds `AppData/Roaming/npm`); these join the server's `PATH` at start.

business_flow.action: Calls `harness_status` per harness.
business_flow.outcome: Installed (by `which`), version from `--version`, and login state from `claude auth status` (JSON `loggedIn`), `codex login status` (contains `Logged in`), the existence of Grok's `auth.json`, or Antigravity's token files.

business_flow.action: Before an Antigravity launch calls `ensure_agy_integration`.
business_flow.outcome: Writes `plugin.json` and `hooks.json` under `~/.gemini/config/plugins/ostra`, enables the plugin in `config.json`, and runs `agy mcp add ostra <binary> mcp-stdio` when `agy mcp list` does not show it.

concerns.responsibility: Detection.
Plugin, agent file, hooks JSON, tool list (only names from Ultracode's verified mapping, because one unknown name fails the session).
On Windows, finds a `PATHEXT` file and runs an npm shim's script with `node` directly; Unix uses the name as given.

sections.title: MCP client (ostra-mcp)
sections.purpose: The MCP client connects Ostra to a workspace's external Model Context Protocol servers over stdio or streamable HTTP, lists their tools, calls them, and signs in to remote servers with OAuth. The server crate owns the connections and the settings; this crate owns the protocol.

owns: Transports, handshake, tool listing, call result text conversion, OAuth discovery and token exchange.
does_not_own: Storing tokens and client credentials, opening the sign-in page, callback handling, settings and tool naming as `mcp__<server>__<tool>` (server area `src/mcp.rs` and core area `ostra_core::mcp`).
Permission decisions for MCP tools (policy section, Rule M1).

assumptions: Ostra declares no client capabilities (`capabilities: {}`), so it answers only `ping` from a server and returns error -32601 for any other server request.
The protocol version offered is 2025-11-25; a server may answer 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26 or 2024-11-05, and any other version fails the connection.
A stdio server speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdout and logs only to stderr; a non-JSON stdout line is skipped.
Every call has a caller-provided timeout; there is no default in this crate.

business_flow.action: Calls `Client::connect(endpoint, timeout)`.
business_flow.outcome: The transport starts, `initialize` runs, the version is checked, `notifications/initialized` is sent, and `server_info` holds name and version.

business_flow.action: Calls `list_tools`.
business_flow.outcome: Every page of `tools/list` (at most 50 pages) becomes a `ToolInfo`; `read_only` comes from `annotations.readOnlyHint`.

business_flow.action: Calls a tool through the server.
business_flow.outcome: `call_tool` sends `tools/call`; the result is `Ok(text)`, or `Err(text)` when the server sets `isError`.

business_flow.action: A call times out or is cancelled.
business_flow.outcome: The pending request is abandoned and `notifications/cancelled` is sent with the request id.

diagrams.title: Request with timeout and cancel
diagrams.source:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller
    participant Client
    participant Transport
    participant Server as MCP server
    Caller->>Client: call_tool(name, arguments, timeout, cancel)
    Client->>Transport: request(id, tools/call)
    Transport->>Server: JSON-RPC message
    Server-->>Transport: response with id
    Transport-->>Client: message
    Client-->>Caller: Ok(text) or Err(text)
    Client->>Transport: notify notifications/cancelled on timeout or cancel

tables.title: McpError variants
rows: HTTP 401, or 403 with an `insufficient_scope` challenge, after a refresh attempt
Start failure, bad header, bad body, unsupported version, other HTTP status, 403 without a Bearer challenge
Stdio process exited (with the last 5 stderr lines), the HTTP session ended (404 with a session id), or the event stream ended early

concerns.responsibility: Handshake, id allocation, timeouts, cancellation, pagination.
`request`, `notify`, `abandon`, `initialized`.
`alive` and `tools_changed` flags read through `is_alive` and `take_tools_changed`.
Bearer tokens with refresh, implemented by the server.

code_refs.note: Redirect policy: same origin only, at most 5 earlier hops.

Tests with a fake stdio child and a fake axum HTTP server: JSON and SSE answers, crash reporting, environment removal, OAuth sign-in and refresh, refusal of script and foreign-issuer metadata, redirect handling.

subsections.title: Stdio transport
subsections.purpose: The stdio transport starts the server as a child process and exchanges one JSON message per line. It keeps the last 4096 bytes of stderr to explain a crash and ends the whole process tree on drop, because `npx` and `uvx` servers run in grandchildren.

owns: Process start, line framing, pending request map, crash explanation.
does_not_own: The sandbox around the server (server area).

assumptions: `Endpoint::Stdio.env_remove` lists Ostra variables the server must not inherit, such as provider credentials.
`Endpoint::Stdio.guard` is held as long as the server runs, so the caller's sandbox processes are cleaned up with it.
A batch (JSON array) on stdout is processed element by element.

business_flow.action: Spawns with piped stdio, `kill_on_drop`, and a new process group or job from `ostra_core::proctree`.
business_flow.outcome: Failure to start is `Transport(could not start <program>: ...)`.

business_flow.action: Routes responses to waiting requests by id, and replies to server requests through `on_server_message`.
business_flow.outcome: At end of stdout the client is marked not alive and pending requests fail.

business_flow.action: A write fails or the process is gone.
business_flow.outcome: Waits up to 500 ms for stderr to end, then returns `Closed(the server exited: <last 5 stderr lines joined by ' / '>)`.

concerns.responsibility: Process and tasks.
Terminates the tree.

subsections.title: Streamable HTTP transport
subsections.purpose: Each JSON-RPC message is a POST. The server answers with a JSON body or an SSE stream; the client reads until the response with its request id. The transport keeps the `mcp-session-id` and, after initialize, sends `mcp-protocol-version` on every request.

owns: HTTP framing, session and version headers, refresh-once authentication flow.
does_not_own: Token storage and refresh (the `TokenSource` implementation in the server area).

assumptions: Configured headers must be valid header names and values, or construction fails with a Transport error.
Requests carry `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`; the user agent is `ostra/<version>`; connect timeout is 15 s.
A 404 while a session id is held means the server ended the session.

business_flow.action: Posts with the current bearer token.
business_flow.outcome: A success response stores the session id from its header.

business_flow.action: Receives 401, or 403 with `insufficient_scope`.
business_flow.outcome: Asks `TokenSource::refused(token)` once; a fresh token retries the post; otherwise returns `NeedsAuth` with the `WWW-Authenticate` header.

business_flow.action: Receives 403 without that challenge.
business_flow.outcome: Returns a Transport error with the first 300 characters of the body.

business_flow.action: Reads an SSE response.
business_flow.outcome: Events with other messages are handled as side messages (server requests answered by a separate POST, `notifications/tools/list_changed` sets the changed flag); the matching response ends the read.

concerns.responsibility: Auth retry and status handling.
JSON or SSE response reading.

subsections.title: Tool results as text
subsections.purpose: `content::result_text` converts a `tools/call` result into the text a tool result carries. Tool results are text, so images and audio become a placeholder with their size.

owns: Content part conversion and the size cap.
does_not_own: Wrapping into provider blocks (native executor and tools area).

assumptions: Image and audio byte counts are estimated as base64 length times 3 divided by 4.
When every part is blank and `structuredContent` exists, the pretty-printed structured content is used.

business_flow.action: Converts each content item by type.
business_flow.outcome: Text is kept; `[image <mime>, N bytes, not shown because tool results are text]`; resource text or `[binary resource <uri>]`; `[resource <uri> <name>]`; any other item as its JSON.

business_flow.action: Caps the joined text at `MAX_RESULT` (100 KiB) on a character boundary.
business_flow.outcome: The rest is replaced by `... (N more bytes cut)`.

business_flow.action: Applies `isError`.
business_flow.outcome: `Err(text)`, or a fixed message when the text is empty.

concerns.responsibility: Conversion and truncation.

subsections.title: OAuth sign-in for remote servers
subsections.purpose: The oauth module implements the MCP authorization flow: protected resource metadata (RFC 9728), authorization server metadata (RFC 8414 and OpenID discovery), dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), PKCE with S256, and the `resource` parameter (RFC 8707). It is a set of functions; the server decides when to call them.

owns: Discovery, registration, PKCE, authorization URL, code exchange, refresh.
does_not_own: The callback route, state storage, token persistence and the `TokenSource` implementation (server area).

assumptions: Every OAuth URL Ostra fetches or sends the browser to must be `https`, or `http` on a loopback host or on the MCP server's own origin; anything else (for example `javascript:`) is refused, because the browser would run it on Ostra's origin (`check_endpoint`).
Authorization server metadata must name the same issuer it was fetched for (trailing slash ignored); a different issuer is refused (RFC 8414 section 3.3).
A server with no OAuth metadata at all is treated as pre-RFC 9728 and gets the defaults `/authorize`, `/token`, `/register` on its origin, with `guessed = true`.
A token counts as expired 60 seconds before `expires_at` (`Tokens::expired`).
Redirect URIs, `state` and PKCE verifiers are supplied by the caller; `random_token` produces 256 random bits, URL-safe.

business_flow.action: Calls `discover(http, server_url, challenge)` after a `NeedsAuth` error.
business_flow.outcome: Candidate metadata URLs are tried in order: the challenge's `resource_metadata`, `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource<path>`, then the same without the path; the first document with `authorization_servers` wins and its first server is the issuer.

business_flow.action: Fetches the issuer's metadata from `oauth-authorization-server` and `openid-configuration` URLs (path-aware forms when the issuer has a path).
business_flow.outcome: An `AuthServer`; scopes come from the challenge, else resource metadata, else server metadata.

business_flow.action: Calls `register` when no `client_id` is configured.
business_flow.outcome: A public client (`token_endpoint_auth_method: none`) named Ostra for the redirect URI; an absent registration endpoint says to set `oauth.client_id`.

business_flow.action: Builds `authorization_url` with `response_type=code`, client id, redirect URI, state, `code_challenge` (S256), `resource` and optional `scope`.
business_flow.outcome: The URL is checked again, so a discovery record saved before checks existed is still refused.

business_flow.action: Calls `exchange_code`, later `refresh`.
business_flow.outcome: `Tokens` with `expires_at = now + expires_in`; a refresh response without a new refresh token keeps the old one.

diagrams.title: Discovery order
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
    A[server URL and 401 challenge] --> B[try resource_metadata URL]
    B --> C[try well-known protected resource with path]
    C --> D[try well-known protected resource at origin]
    D --> E{document with authorization_servers}
    E -->|yes| F[issuer is first authorization server]
    E -->|no| G[issuer is the server origin]
    F --> H[fetch authorization server metadata]
    G --> H
    H --> I{metadata found}
    I -->|yes| J[check issuer and endpoints]
    I -->|no and no resource metadata| K[guess default endpoints]
    I -->|no and resource metadata| L[fail]

tables.title: Token endpoint client authentication
rows: Has a secret and the server lists only `client_secret_basic`

concerns.responsibility: Metadata discovery with checks.
Client identity and request construction.
Token endpoint calls.
Reads `resource_metadata` and `scope` from a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` header, quoted or not.

sections.title: Web Push (ostra-notify)
sections.purpose: The notify crate sends a browser push message without OpenSSL. It encrypts the message with RFC 8291 in the RFC 8188 `aes128gcm` content coding, authenticates to the push service with an RFC 8292 VAPID JWT (ES256), and posts it. The server uses it to tell the user that a gate needs them.

owns: Encryption, VAPID keys and JWT, delivery and its outcome classification.
does_not_own: Storing subscriptions and VAPID keys, choosing when to notify and what text to send (server area `src/app.rs`, `src/services.rs`).
The `PushSubscription` type (core area `ostra_core::api`).

assumptions: The subscription's `p256dh` key is an uncompressed P-256 point and `auth` is the subscriber's auth secret; both are URL-safe base64 with or without padding (`b64_decode`).
The endpoint URL is `http` or `https`; the JWT audience is its origin (`origin_of`).
The VAPID subject is a `mailto:` or `https:` contact URI supplied by the caller.
The whole message fits one record: the plaintext limit is 3993 bytes (`MAX_PLAINTEXT`), so the body stays within 4096 bytes.

business_flow.action: Creates `Notifier::new(keys, subject)` with `VapidKeys::generate()` or keys restored by `from_private_bytes`.
business_flow.outcome: The public key in URL-safe base64 is the browser's `applicationServerKey`.

business_flow.action: Calls `Notifier::send(subscription, notification)`.
business_flow.outcome: The `Notification` (title, body, url, tag) is serialized to JSON, encrypted with a fresh sender key and a random 16-byte salt, and posted.

business_flow.action: Posts with `Authorization: vapid t=<jwt>, k=<public key>`, `Content-Encoding: aes128gcm`, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, `TTL: 86400`, `Urgency: high`.
business_flow.outcome: The JWT expires 12 hours after signing; the client timeout is 20 s.

business_flow.action: Classifies the answer.
business_flow.outcome: 2xx is `Delivered`; 404 or 410 is `Gone`, and the caller removes the subscription; other statuses and network errors are `Failed` with the status and up to 500 characters of the body.

diagrams.title: Encrypting one push message
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
    A[plaintext JSON up to 3993 bytes] --> B[ECDH of sender key and p256dh]
    B --> C[HKDF with auth secret gives 32 byte key material]
    C --> D[HKDF with salt gives 16 byte key and 12 byte nonce]
    A --> E[append 0x02 delimiter]
    D --> F[AES 128 GCM encrypt]
    E --> F
    F --> G[body: salt, record size 4096, key id length, sender public key, ciphertext]

tables.title: NotifyError
rows: Endpoint not a URL or not http or https

concerns.responsibility: P-256 key pair, public key encoding, JWT and Authorization value; `Debug` prints only the public key.
RFC 8291 encryption; `encrypt_with` takes explicit key and salt so the RFC test vector can be checked.
HTTP delivery and outcome classification.

code_refs.note: RFC 8291 Appendix A vector, round trip, size limit, JWT verification, audience and padded base64.

sections.title: Crate layers and public API
sections.purpose: Explains how ostra-sandbox is split so that an operating system difference lives in one file, and lists what the crate exports. A caller builds a Profile, asks a Backend to wrap a program, and runs the returned command. Read this section first to find which file owns a behavior.

owns: The split between Profile (what to enforce), Backend/Enforcer (how one backend renders it), and sys (kernel calls).
The crate's public exports in lib.rs.
The rule that code outside a backend's module asks `Backend::enforcer()` instead of matching on the backend.
does_not_own: Judging tool calls by path, guards, and permissions: owned by the ostra-policy area.

Sandbox config types (`SandboxConfig`, `SandboxMode`, `SandboxNetwork`, `LoopbackAccess`, `WorkspaceSandbox`), `paths::*`, `HOME_CREDENTIALS`, and the `ExecutionHost` trait: owned by the ostra-core area.
Starting executions and deciding when to sandbox a spawn: owned by the ostra-exec-native, ostra-exec-harness, and ostra-engine areas.

On macOS `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` must be owned by root with no group or other write bit (`mode & 0o022 == 0`), because the Homebrew prefix on `PATH` is user-writable (sys/macos/mod.rs).

sections.title: Profiles and mount rules
sections.purpose: A `Profile` describes one execution's boundary as an ordered set of mount rules plus environment, egress policy, decoys, forwards, scratch dir, and terminal settings. It is built once per execution (`for_execution`) or once per project program (`for_program`), and is rendered by a backend into a command. The same rules give the same boundary on bubblewrap and Seatbelt.

owns: Which paths are writable, read-only, or hidden for an agent execution and for a project program.
The built-in lists `PERSISTENCE_IN_HOME`, `UNSET_VARS`, and `DOCKER_SOCKETS`.
Rule ordering and conflict resolution (`Profile::ordered`).
The `SandboxedCommand` returned to callers.
does_not_own: Rendering rules into bubblewrap arguments or SBPL: sandbox-bubblewrap and sandbox-seatbelt sections.
Which harness state dirs a CLI may write and which of its settings files stay read-only: ostra-exec-harness area (`sandbox.rs`), which uses `Profile::writable`, `protect`, `home_overlay`, and `link`.
The contents of `ExecContext`: ostra-core area.

assumptions: Rules are added only for paths that exist: `writable`, `hidden`, and `writable_file` call `real()` (canonical path) and skip a missing path silently (profile.rs).
`read_only` on a missing path records the path through `real_or_missing`, the longest existing ancestor plus the missing rest, so a placeholder can be created later (profile.rs).
An empty path in `ExecContext` (`workspace_root`, `repo_root`, `session_root`, `session_dir`) means the context has no such root, and no rule is added for it (profile.rs `for_execution`).
The Ostra data dir holds an `assets` subdirectory that agents read, so it is revealed read-only inside the hidden data dir (profile.rs `common`).
Path names are UTF-8 without control characters where Seatbelt is used; `sbpl_str` returns an error otherwise (seatbelt.rs).

business_flow.action: Calls `Profile::for_execution(ctx, cfg, home)` for an agent, or `Profile::for_program(roots, cfg, home)` for a project program.
business_flow.outcome: A profile holds the writable roots, hidden paths, read-only paths, caches, and an egress policy built from `cfg`.

business_flow.action: Adds execution-specific settings: `scratch`, `start_egress`, `watch_decoys`, `forward` or `forward_socket`, `allow_hosts`, `writable`, `protect`, `home_overlay`, `link`, `tty`, `new_session`.
business_flow.outcome: The profile reflects this execution's needs.

business_flow.action: `Profile::ordered()` sorts all mounts by path depth, then path, then restrictiveness, and keeps the most restrictive rule when two share a path.
business_flow.outcome: A deeper rule overrides a shallower one and, at one path, hidden beats read-only beats writable.

business_flow.action: Calls `profile.command(backend, chdir, program, args)`.
business_flow.outcome: A `SandboxedCommand` is returned, or an error string when a path cannot be named in a Seatbelt policy or the helper is missing.

subsections.title: Rule ordering and conflicts
subsections.purpose: `Profile::ordered` makes both backends apply rules in the same order so that the deepest rule for a path wins, and at one path only the most restrictive rule remains.
assumptions: Seatbelt applies the last matching rule, and bubblewrap applies mounts in argument order; both rely on shallow-before-deep ordering (profile.rs `ordered`, seatbelt.rs `seatbelt`).
When `home_overlay` is set, the home directory's entries are read at render time with `read_dir`; entries created later are not bound.

business_flow.action: Collects the profile's mounts and, if a home overlay is set, adds a `HomeTmpfs` and one `HomeEntry` per top-level entry of home (with its symlink target when it is one).
business_flow.outcome: The full rule list exists.

business_flow.action: Sorts by (path component count, path, rank).
business_flow.outcome: Shallow paths come first; at one path the lowest rank comes first.

business_flow.action: Walks the list and, when a rule has the same destination as the previous one, removes the previous one.
business_flow.outcome: At one path the highest rank, the most restrictive rule, remains.

subsections.title: Tool caches
subsections.purpose: The sandbox gives each session its own tool caches instead of the user's, so one session's downloads cannot feed a later session's builds, and the user's `~/.cargo`, `~/.npm`, and `~/.cache` stay read-only. Project programs share one cache per project root.
assumptions: The cache base is `$OSTRA_SANDBOX_CACHE` when set, else `<home>/.cache/ostra/sandbox` (cache.rs `cache_base`).

Cache names on disk use SHA-256 (`stable_hex`: first 8 bytes of a hash over `salt`, a NUL byte, and the path, as 16 hex digits), not `DefaultHasher`, because that algorithm may change between Rust releases and move the directories.
A user cargo settings file is linked into the sandbox `CARGO_HOME` only if it is a file and the link does not exist yet; cargo credentials are never linked.

business_flow.action: Chooses the cache root: `session-<session id>` under the base for a session, `keyed_cache(home, "agents", workspace_root or repo_root)` for a run without a session, `keyed_cache(home, "", first root)` for a project program.
business_flow.outcome: A root directory path is chosen.

business_flow.action: `add_caches` creates `<root>/tmp` owner-only, creates one subdirectory per `CACHE_ENV` entry, and sets the variable to it.
business_flow.outcome: Tools write their caches inside the sandbox-owned root.

business_flow.action: Links `config.toml` and `config` from `~/.cargo` into `<root>/cargo`, then makes the root writable.
business_flow.outcome: Builds keep the user's linker and registry settings.

business_flow.action: Calls `remove_session_cache(session)` when a session ends or is deleted.
business_flow.outcome: A thread named `ostra-cache-remove` deletes the session directory; failure is logged as a warning.

code_refs.note: Variables, cache base, stable hash, removal.

subsections.title: Git protection
subsections.purpose: A writable repository lets an agent plant a hook, a `core.fsmonitor`, a credential helper, or a `commondir` that makes git run programs outside the sandbox, for example in the user's later commits. The profile keeps the files that choose programs read-only and undoes the one plant it cannot block.
assumptions: Repositories are found by walking each root; the walk does not enter symlinks, `node_modules`, or directories holding `CACHEDIR.TAG` (for example Cargo's `target/`).
The walk stops after `GIT_WALK_DIRS` = 20000 directories or `GIT_WALK_REPOS` = 128 repositories and logs a warning that repositories below the stop point keep a writable `.git/config` (git.rs).
A `.git` file is read up to 4096 bytes and must start with `gitdir:` (git.rs `GitDir::of`).
`git_dirs` follows submodule git dirs under `modules/` up to 256 entries.

`commondir` cannot be protected with an empty placeholder because git refuses to open a repository whose `commondir` is empty, so `repair_git_dirs` covers it after the fact (git.rs comment on `GIT_PROTECTED`).

business_flow.action: `protect_git` finds repos under the roots with `git_repos`.
business_flow.outcome: A list of work trees, shallowest first.

business_flow.action: For each repo, resolves its git dir; a `.git` file is made read-only so it cannot name a planted git dir.
business_flow.outcome: The git dir location is fixed.

business_flow.action: For each git dir and submodule git dir, protects `config`, `config.worktree`, `hooks/`, `info/`, and each linked worktree's `config.worktree`.
business_flow.outcome: Those paths are read-only; a missing one gets an empty read-only placeholder under a writable directory.

business_flow.action: After an execution, calls `repair_git_dirs(repos)`, and gives the agent `git_repair_note(path)` for each path changed.
business_flow.outcome: A `commondir` in a repository's own git dir is removed; a linked worktree's `commondir` that is not `../..` is restored.

sections.title: Bubblewrap backend (Linux)
sections.purpose: Renders a profile as `bwrap` arguments on Linux. The sandbox gets its own mount, pid, IPC, and (unless the network is `host`) network namespaces. The first process inside is `ostra sandbox-init`, which forwards the sandbox's loopback to Ostra's sockets and loads the seccomp filter before starting the command.

owns: The argument list passed to `bwrap`, including mount order.
Placeholders for missing protected paths and self-binds of directories above protected mounts.
Decoy placement under bubblewrap.
Locating the helper binary (`set_helper`, `helper`).
does_not_own: The helper's runtime behavior: sandbox-helper section.
The proxy and splice implementations: sandbox-egress section.
The profile content: sandbox-profile section.

assumptions: `bwrap` can create unprivileged user namespaces on this machine; the probe verifies this once.

The helper is the `ostra` binary: set with `set_helper`, else `ostra` beside the current executable or one directory up, which finds `target/debug/ostra` from a test binary in `target/debug/deps` (bwrap.rs `helper`).
Paths in the profile are canonical, because bubblewrap mounts at real paths (profile.rs `real`).
The egress socket directory (`<data dir>/egress`) is inside the hidden data dir, so only sockets bound explicitly are reachable (egress.rs `socket_dir`).
A socket path is limited to 107 bytes; a long data dir path makes `bind` fail with advice to keep the data dir path short (egress.rs `bind`).

business_flow.action: Finds the helper. Uses the profile's egress listener, or starts a log-only proxy when the policy needs one and the profile has none.
business_flow.outcome: An egress listener or none.

business_flow.action: When the network is private, adds a forward for every loopback port the policy lists (`loopback_ports`) that is not already forwarded.
business_flow.outcome: Listed loopback services such as `127.0.0.1:8317` are reachable at the same port inside the sandbox.

business_flow.action: Emits `--ro-bind / /`, `--dev /dev`, `--proc /proc`, then `/tmp` (the scratch dir bound, else `--tmpfs /tmp`), then every planned mount sorted by path depth, then decoy read-only binds, `--unsetenv` for each `UNSET_VARS`, `--setenv` for the profile's variables, `--unshare-pid --unshare-ipc`.
business_flow.outcome: The mount and namespace part of the command.

business_flow.action: When the network is private, adds `--unshare-net` and binds each proxy and forward socket at its own path. Then adds `--die-with-parent`, `--new-session` (when set), `--chdir`, and a `--bind` per writable file.
business_flow.outcome: Only the bound sockets lead out of the network namespace.

business_flow.action: Appends `-- <helper> sandbox-init [--proxy <socket>] [--forward <port>=<socket>]... -- <program> <args>`.
business_flow.outcome: A `SandboxedCommand` whose program is the `bwrap` binary, with `Members` holding the listeners and decoys.

subsections.title: Directory pins
subsections.purpose: A bind mount point cannot be renamed, but the directories above it can: `mv repo r && git init repo` would leave a protected `.git` behind under another name. `Profile::plan` binds each directory between a writable bind and a mount inside it onto itself, so those directories are mount points too.
assumptions: Only directories that exist (`symlink_metadata(...).is_dir()`) are pinned (bwrap.rs).
Home overlay entries, links, and the home tmpfs are not pinned (bwrap.rs `plan`).

business_flow.outcome: Candidate directories below a writable self-bind.

business_flow.action: Keeps the candidates only when the enclosing mount is a writable self-bind, or an already pinned directory.

business_flow.action: Adds a `Writable {src: p, dest: p}` for each pin.

subsections.purpose: Chooses where a decoy file can be bound in without writing to the host.
assumptions: `in_tmpfs(path)` looks at the deepest mount that strictly contains `path`; only `Hidden` and `HomeTmpfs` count, because their tmpfs can hold a new file (bwrap.rs `decoys`).
An existing decoy target must be a regular file; a directory is skipped.

business_flow.action: For each wanted `(relative path, kind)`, resolves `home/rel` with `real_or_missing`.
business_flow.outcome: The path the sandbox sees.

business_flow.action: Accepts the path if it is an existing regular file, or if it is missing and lies inside a hidden directory or the home tmpfs.
business_flow.outcome: The decoy replaces an existing file or fills a hidden directory; the host is never written.
