sections.title: Seatbelt backend (macOS)
sections.purpose: Renders a profile as an SBPL policy passed to `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -p`. Seatbelt has no mount namespace, so a hidden path answers EPERM instead of looking empty, `/tmp` is denied instead of private, a harness gets no disposable home, and every sandbox shares the host's loopback.

owns: The SBPL policy text: the base policy, per-mount rules, network rules, decoy refusals, and unlink pins.
`sbpl_str`, which keeps a path from rewriting the policy.
Seatbelt environment changes: `TMPDIR`, `TMPPREFIX`, proxy variables, removed variables.
The server port that no Seatbelt sandbox may connect to (`set_server_port`).
does_not_own: The macOS calls (`sandbox_check`, `log stream`): sandbox-os-layer and sandbox-decoys sections.
Choosing the loopback mode and blocked ports: ostra-core config and workspace settings (validated in the sandbox-validate section).

assumptions: Seatbelt applies the last matching rule, so rule order matters and follows `Profile::ordered` (seatbelt.rs `seatbelt`).
Paths are UTF-8 and free of control characters; otherwise `sbpl_str` returns an error naming the path, because a path that ends its string early would rewrite the policy.
`set_server_port` is called once at server start; the port is denied only when the network is private (seatbelt.rs).
The base policy was measured with git, cargo, npm, go, pip, clang through xcrun, and the four harness CLIs; the allowed mach services are the ones those tools need (seatbelt.rs `SEATBELT_BASE`).
Behavior of `process-info*` and `sysctl-read` was measured on macOS 26 (seatbelt.rs comments).

business_flow.action: Uses the profile's proxy or starts a loopback proxy with a credential when the policy needs one; builds `Members` from the forwards and proxy listeners.
business_flow.outcome: `Members` carries the per-invocation and group mach markers.

business_flow.action: Starts from `SEATBELT_BASE`, allows `mach-lookup` of the two marker names, denies reads and writes in `/private/tmp`, `/private/var/tmp`, and the per-user temp dir.
business_flow.outcome: Shared temp directories are unreachable.

business_flow.action: For each ordered rule: writable dirs get allow read/write plus `network-bind network-outbound` (so Unix sockets inside them work); read-only rules deny `file-write* network-bind` (and allow read when revealed); hidden paths deny read, write, and network bind/outbound.
business_flow.outcome: Filesystem rules in depth order.

business_flow.action: Allows `file-read-metadata` on every ancestor of every reachable path, adds the TTY rule when `tty` is set, and adds network rules.
business_flow.outcome: Allowed paths are reachable through `stat`, and the PTY works.

business_flow.action: Adds `(deny file-read-data (literal <decoy>) (with message <tag>))` per decoy, then `(deny file-write-unlink ...)` for every writable ancestor directory of a protected path.
business_flow.outcome: Decoy reads are logged by the kernel, and protected files cannot be carried away by renaming a parent.

business_flow.action: Returns program `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` with `-p <policy> <program> <args>`, the environment, and `env_remove` of `UNSET_VARS`.
business_flow.outcome: A `SandboxedCommand` to run.

sections.title: Egress proxy and network policy
sections.purpose: The egress proxy is the one way out of a private network sandbox. It reads an HTTP proxy request (`CONNECT host:port` or an absolute-form `http://` request), checks the destination against the execution's policy, resolves the name itself, and connects to the address it checked. Every allowed or refused destination is reported, and each refusal names the setting that would allow it.

owns: Host rule syntax and matching (`HostRule`).
The per-execution `Policy`: network mode, trusted and built-in hosts, upstream proxy, loopback choice, blocked ports.
The proxy protocol handling, TLS server name check, and connection limits.
Listener types: proxy, splice, loopback proxy, loopback splice, served-elsewhere.
`DEFAULT_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `model_hosts`, `proxy_env`, `socket_dir`, `remove_stale_sockets`.
does_not_own: The `SandboxNetwork` and `LoopbackAccess` enums and the config keys: ostra-core area.
Where the proxy is reached from inside the sandbox: the bubblewrap helper (sandbox-helper section) and the Seatbelt loopback rules (sandbox-seatbelt section).
Showing decisions to the user: ostra-engine and web areas, through the `ExecutionDelta::Egress` event (sandbox-report section).
The WebFetch tool's private-address check reuses `egress::is_private` from ostra-tools (`crates/ostra-tools/src/web.rs`); that tool is owned by the ostra-tools area.

assumptions: The proxy speaks HTTP/1.x only. A request line must have exactly three space-separated parts and a version beginning `HTTP/1.` (egress.rs `parse_request`).
The egress runtime is one process-wide Tokio multi-thread runtime with 2 worker threads named `ostra-egress`, started on first use (egress.rs `runtime`).

A client on a bubblewrap sandbox reaches the proxy only through its own Unix socket, which is the only socket bound into that sandbox. Under Seatbelt the client reaches it on `127.0.0.1:<port>` and must present the Basic credential, because sandboxes that open the loopback can reach other executions' proxy ports.
Loopback addresses and names are never sent through the proxy by clients (`NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1`), so a loopback entry in `allowed_hosts` works only as a forwarded port.
`OnDecision` callbacks run on the proxy runtime and must not block (egress.rs `OnDecision`).

business_flow.action: Sends `CONNECT host:port` (HTTPS) or `GET http://host/path` (plain HTTP) to the proxy.
business_flow.outcome: The proxy reads the request head.

business_flow.action: Parses the request, asks `Policy::route`, and either refuses (403 with a reason naming the setting) or selects a direct route or an upstream route.
business_flow.outcome: A checked set of addresses, or an upstream proxy.

business_flow.action: Connects to the checked address (10 seconds per address), or tunnels through the upstream proxy with CONNECT.
business_flow.outcome: A connection to the destination, or 502.

business_flow.action: For CONNECT, answers `200 Connection established` and compares the TLS server name with the CONNECT host.
business_flow.outcome: A tunnel that carries traffic only to the host that was allowed.

business_flow.action: Reports the first allowed connection and the first refusal per host and port.
business_flow.outcome: One event per destination, so a retry loop does not flood the log.

diagrams.title: Handling one proxy connection
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  A["Read request head"] --> B{"Complete within 8 KiB and 30 s?"}
  B -- no --> E400["400 Bad Request or close"]
  B -- yes --> C{"Loopback proxy credential correct?"}
  C -- no --> E407["407 Proxy Authentication Required"]
  C -- yes --> D["parse_request"]
  D -- invalid --> E400
  D -- valid --> F{"Policy route"}
  F -- refused --> E403["403 Forbidden with reason, report refusal"]
  F -- direct --> G["Connect to checked address, 10 s each"]
  F -- upstream --> H["CONNECT through the upstream proxy"]
  G -- fails --> E502["502 Bad Gateway"]
  H -- fails --> E502
  G --> I{"CONNECT tunnel?"}
  H --> I
  I -- yes --> J["200 Connection established, check TLS server name"]
  I -- no --> K["Send origin-form head with Connection: close"]
  J --> L["Copy both directions"]
  K --> L

subsections.title: Policy: network modes, access classes, and address checks
subsections.purpose: `Policy::new(cfg)` builds the set of trusted and built-in hosts for a network mode. `Policy::route` turns a requested host and port into a list of addresses to connect to, an upstream route, or a refusal.
assumptions: Trusted hosts are chosen by the user (`allowed_hosts` and base URLs a harness launch passes) and may resolve to any address; built-in hosts must resolve to public addresses (egress.rs `Policy`).
Entries of `allowed_hosts` that do not parse are dropped silently at policy build; they are reported earlier by `validate` at save time.

`is_private` covers IPv4 loopback, private, link-local (including the cloud metadata address), unspecified, broadcast, multicast, `0.0.0.0/8`, CGNAT `100.64.0.0/10`, `198.18.0.0/15`, and `240.0.0.0/4` and above; IPv6 loopback, unspecified, multicast, unique-local `fc00::/7`, link-local `fe80::/10`, site-local `fec0::/10`, IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96`, and local-use NAT64 `64:ff9b:1::/48`.
A name is local when it is `localhost`, has no dot, or ends in `.localhost`, `.local`, `.internal`, `.lan`, or `.home.arpa`.

business_flow.action: Classifies the destination: a trusted rule match gives `AnyAddress`; network `public` or a built-in match gives `PublicOnly`; otherwise `Refused`.
business_flow.outcome: An access class.

business_flow.action: For `PublicOnly` with a local-only name, refuses without a lookup, because the lookup would go out on the LAN (multicast DNS for `.local` takes seconds to fail on macOS).
business_flow.outcome: Refusal flagged `local`.

business_flow.action: Resolves a name with the system resolver (`tokio::net::lookup_host`), canonicalizing mapped addresses; an IP destination is used as given.
business_flow.outcome: A list of socket addresses, or a refusal `Check the host name ... it does not resolve`.

business_flow.action: For `PublicOnly`, removes private addresses; refuses with the `local_refusal` text if none is left. For `AnyAddress`, keeps all.
business_flow.outcome: The addresses the proxy connects to, and never resolves a second time.

business_flow.action: With `[sandbox] upstream_proxy` set, sends public destinations through the upstream; a trusted host on a private address is connected directly, because an internal mirror is rarely behind the corporate proxy.
business_flow.outcome: `Route::Direct` or `Route::Upstream`.

subsections.title: Request parsing, upstream proxy, and TLS server name check
subsections.purpose: Describes how the proxy reads plain HTTP and CONNECT requests, how it reaches an upstream proxy, and how it checks that a tunnel goes to the host that was allowed.
assumptions: Plain HTTP requests are rewritten to origin form with `Host: <authority>`, all `Proxy-*`, `Host`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` headers removed, and `Connection: close` added; only the first request on a connection is served (egress.rs `parse_request`).
When the route is an upstream proxy, the plain HTTP head is turned back into absolute form (`absolute_form`).
A TLS client speaks first. When the destination speaks first (for example an SSH banner), the tunnel is not TLS, the banner is passed on, and the server name check is skipped.
The server name check runs only for CONNECT to a name, not to an IP address, and only when the upstream returned no early bytes.

business_flow.action: After sending `200 Connection established`, reads the first bytes from the client with `read_hello` until `client_hello_name` decides (30 s limit).
business_flow.outcome: `Name(sni)`, `NoName`, or `Invalid`.

business_flow.action: Compares the server name (lower-cased, trailing dot removed) with the CONNECT host.
business_flow.outcome: A different name is refused, reported as a refusal, and the connection is closed; the refusal text is `Connect to <sni> by its own name, because the sandbox refuses a TLS server name that differs from the CONNECT host <host>.`

business_flow.action: An unreadable or oversized handshake is refused with `Send a standard TLS ClientHello to <host>, because the sandbox could not read the server name in this one.`
business_flow.outcome: A CDN that routes by SNI cannot carry an allowed tunnel to any other site it serves.

business_flow.action: A non-TLS first byte, or a ClientHello without a server name, passes.
business_flow.outcome: The buffered bytes are sent to the destination and both directions are copied.

The host name of the `server_name` extension (type 0).
A record that is not a handshake, an empty or over-long record, a handshake that is not a ClientHello (type 1), a body over 32 KiB, or a body that does not parse.

sections.title: sandbox-init helper and seccomp filter (Linux)
sections.purpose: `ostra sandbox-init` is the first program inside a bubblewrap sandbox. The sandbox has a network namespace of its own, so the helper listens on the sandbox's loopback and forwards each connection to a Unix socket that Ostra bound in. It then loads a seccomp filter, starts the command, and exits with the command's status.

owns: The helper's argument grammar and exit codes.
The loopback listeners and connection copying inside the sandbox.
The seccomp filter program and the decision to load it before any helper thread starts.
does_not_own: Starting the helper: the bubblewrap wrapper (sandbox-bubblewrap section).
The Unix sockets the helper connects to: egress proxy and hook bridge (sandbox-egress section; the bridge itself is in the ostra-server area).
Dispatching the `sandbox-init` subcommand from the CLI: `crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs` calls `ostra_sandbox::init::main`.

assumptions: Only Linux runs the helper; macOS and other systems return an error `the sandbox helper runs on Linux only` from `run_helper`.
The helper uses std threads only and no async runtime (init.rs docs).
The seccomp filter is built for x86_64 and aarch64 only (`cfg(any(target_arch = ...))`); on other architectures the helper runs without it and `known_gaps` reports it.
The filter is loaded while the helper has one thread, because a filter applies to the calling thread and to what it starts afterwards (helper.rs, seccomp.rs `install`).
Fixed forward ports are bound before the proxy's free port so the proxy cannot take one of them.

business_flow.action: Parses `[--proxy <socket>] [--forward <port>=<socket>]... -- <program> [args...]`.
business_flow.outcome: `Args` or an error printed as `ostra sandbox-init: <error>` with exit status 125.

business_flow.action: Binds `127.0.0.1:<port>` (and `[::1]:<port>` on a best-effort basis) for every `--forward`.
business_flow.outcome: Fixed ports such as the hook bridge are listening inside the namespace.

business_flow.action: With `--proxy`, binds `127.0.0.1:0` and sets the command's proxy environment to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`.
business_flow.outcome: The command's HTTP clients use the local proxy port.

business_flow.action: Installs the seccomp filter (sets `no_new_privs`, then loads the filter).
business_flow.outcome: The helper and everything it starts inherit the filter.

business_flow.action: Starts one thread per listener that copies each accepted connection to the Unix socket, then spawns the command.
business_flow.outcome: Traffic flows to Ostra's proxy or bridge.

business_flow.action: Ignores SIGINT, SIGQUIT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP, SIGTSTP, SIGTTIN, and SIGTTOU, and waits for the command.
business_flow.outcome: The command receives terminal signals through its process group; the helper remains to report the status.

business_flow.action: Returns the command's exit code; if the command died by signal, restores the default action, re-raises the signal, and returns 128 plus the signal number.
business_flow.outcome: The caller sees the same status the command had.

sections.title: Decoy credential files (Rule P3)
sections.purpose: Decoys are fake credential files at paths an agent has no reason to read. Opening one from inside the sandbox is a containment signal: a Bash `cat` is seen as well as a tool call, because the kernel reports it. The first open of each decoy is reported once to the execution's host as a decoy event.

owns: The built-in decoy list, decoy contents, placement rules per backend, and detection.
The decoy base directory `<data dir>/decoys` and stale cleanup.
Validation rules for a workspace's own decoys (`decoy::invalid`).
does_not_own: What happens after a decoy is opened (event handling, user notification): ostra-engine area, through `ExecutionDelta::Decoy`.
The workspace setting `sandbox_decoys`: ostra-core and ostra-workspace areas; its validation calls `decoy::invalid`.

assumptions: Common tools do not open the built-in decoys on their own, except `ssh`, which reads its keys when it authenticates; SSH key decoys are therefore skipped when the policy reaches port 22 (profile.rs `watch_decoys`).
`~/.netrc` is deliberately not a built-in decoy, because Python `requests` and Go module downloads read it on every fetch (decoy.rs).
On macOS only existing regular files can be decoys, because Seatbelt reports no refusal for a missing file and cannot bind a file in; the log stream is readable to admin-group users only (gid 80).
The decoy base directory is under the data dir, which every sandbox hides; `remove_stale` is called while no other server of the data dir runs.
A workspace adds decoys and cannot remove built-in ones (`wanted`).

business_flow.action: Calls `Profile::watch_decoys(backend, home, workspace decoys, on)`.
business_flow.outcome: The wanted list is the four built-in decoys followed by the workspace's entries, minus SSH keys when SSH is reachable.

business_flow.action: Places decoys where the backend can: bubblewrap binds a fake file read-only over an existing file or into a hidden directory; Seatbelt refuses reads of existing files.
business_flow.outcome: A `Decoys` value, or `None` when nothing fits or the backend cannot watch.

business_flow.action: `Decoys::plant` writes each fake file into a private directory `<data dir>/decoys/<16 hex>/<index>` and adds an inotify `IN_OPEN` watch on it.
business_flow.outcome: The first open of a decoy calls `on(path inside sandbox)` once, and the watch on that file is removed.

business_flow.action: `Decoys::refuse` registers a tag `dev.ostra.decoy.<16 hex>` per file; the policy denies `file-read-data` with that message; a `log stream` reader reports the kernel's message.
business_flow.outcome: The first refusal calls `on(path)` once.

business_flow.action: `Decoys` is dropped: the watch stops first, then the decoy directory is deleted.
business_flow.outcome: No decoy files remain on the host.

sections.title: Invocation lifetime: Members and leftovers
sections.purpose: `Members` is what one sandboxed invocation holds while it runs: its egress proxy and forward listeners, its decoys, and two marker names used to find and kill processes that outlive their shell. Dropping it ends the invocation's listeners and kills stragglers.

owns: Marker names and the kill loop.
Keeping listeners and decoys alive exactly as long as the invocation.
`kill_leftovers` for processes of earlier servers.
does_not_own: The pid namespace and `--die-with-parent` on Linux: bubblewrap itself (sandbox-bubblewrap section).
Calling `kill_leftovers` at server start: ostra-server area (`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`).
Holding `Members` for the lifetime of a PTY program or language server: ostra-exec-harness and ostra-code areas.

assumptions: Seatbelt has no pid namespace and no `--die-with-parent`, so a child that calls `setsid` or double-forks outlives its shell; the policy's two mach names let the OS find every such process (`Os::marked`). Under bubblewrap no process is marked (members.rs).

Each invocation's policy allows looking up two names that no daemon registers: its own `dev.ostra.sandbox.<uuid>` and a group name `dev.ostra.sandbox.d<hash of the data dir>` shared by every sandbox of this data dir.
`kill_leftovers` is called once at server start, before any execution starts (members.rs).

business_flow.action: Creates `Members::new(listeners, decoys)` with fresh markers.
business_flow.outcome: The invocation's resources are held together.

business_flow.action: Holds `members` until the program exits, then drops it.

sections.title: Browser sign-in and cookies
sections.purpose: Auth gives one browser at a time access: the server prints a URL carrying a one-time token in the fragment, the page exchanges the token once for an HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookie, and every later API call and WebSocket carries the cookie. Tokens and cookies are stored only as SHA-256 hashes in the registry, so sign-ins survive a restart and the CLI can mint tokens for a running server (HANDOVER 15).

owns: Registry keys `auth:token:HASH`, `auth:cookie:HASH`, and `server:private_host`.
The allowed Host list, the Origin rule, the private `.localhost` name, and the failed-exchange limiter.
The revoke broadcast that closes open WebSockets.
does_not_own: Applying the Host, Origin, and cookie checks to requests (server-http-guard section).
Closing sockets on revoke (server-websocket section).
The registry implementation (ostra-store area).

assumptions: The registry key-value table supports atomic compare-and-replace (`kv_replace`); the one-time token claim depends on it.
The cookie value is 32 random bytes in hex; the token is also 32 random bytes in hex, so guessing is not feasible and loopback peers are exempt from the failure limit.
`X-Forwarded-Proto` is never read; `Secure` is set only when the request `Origin` starts with `https://`.
Legacy sign-in rows hold only a creation time as a decimal number; `parse_record` reads them and they are rewritten as JSON records with a new id.
A revoke made by the CLI or another process reaches a running server only through the registry re-read, at most 5 seconds (`RECHECK`) later.

business_flow.action: `sign_in_url` / `request_url` calls `mint_token`
business_flow.outcome: A token valid for 15 minutes is stored as `auth:token:SHA256(token)` with its expiry in seconds; the URL is `http://HOST/#token=TOKEN`.

business_flow.action: Posts {"token": ...} to /api/auth/exchange
business_flow.outcome: On success the server answers 204 with `Set-Cookie: ostra_session=...; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/; Max-Age=2592000`.

business_flow.action: Marks the token `used:TIMESTAMP` with `kv_replace` before checking its expiry
business_flow.outcome: A second use answers `Used { seconds_ago }`; an expired token answers `Expired`; an unknown one `Unknown`.

business_flow.action: Calls `check_cookie` on each API call
business_flow.outcome: A cookie is trusted from memory for 5 seconds, then the registry row is read again; `last_seen` is written at most once per 60 seconds.

business_flow.action: Revokes a sign-in from settings, `ostra sessions`, or signs out
business_flow.outcome: The registry row is deleted; a revoke from this server also broadcasts the cookie hash so open sockets close with code 4401.

sections.title: Request guard and security headers
sections.purpose: One middleware, `guard`, wraps every route. It rejects unknown Host headers (DNS rebinding), redirects a loopback-IP page to the private name, applies Origin and fetch-metadata rules to API calls, demands the session cookie, restricts /internal to local non-browser callers, and adds security headers to every response including refusals.

owns: The ordering of Host, private redirect, /internal rules, Origin and fetch-metadata rules, and cookie check.
The exact header set: Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, Referrer-Policy no-referrer, X-Frame-Options DENY, and Cache-Control no-store on API paths.
does_not_own: Cookie and Host validity rules (server-auth section).
Bearer-token checks on /internal (ostra-exec-harness `LiveRegistry`; server-harness-bridge section).

assumptions: `ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>` is available on requests because the server is started with `into_make_service_with_connect_info`; when it is absent the /internal peer check is skipped (the bridge Unix socket has no peer address and serves only `internal_routes`).
Browsers always send `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` on requests made by a web page, so their presence on /internal means a page, not a harness.
`Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site` is refused on API paths because a page on another localhost port is same-site and would carry the SameSite cookie.
The CSP string must equal the `<meta>` CSP in site/vite.config.ts and web/vite.config.ts (project rule in CLAUDE.md); tests/browser/specs/site.spec.ts checks the site's copy.

business_flow.action: Looks up the Host header in the allowed list
business_flow.outcome: A request with another Host receives 421 `This host is not allowed.`

business_flow.action: Checks for a private host name
business_flow.outcome: A page request on 127.0.0.1, localhost, or [::1] is redirected with 307 to the private name keeping path and query; an API request there receives 421 with the URL to open. /internal is exempt.

business_flow.action: For /internal/*: requires a local peer and no Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site header
business_flow.outcome: Otherwise 403 `This endpoint accepts local connections only.` or `This endpoint is for Ostra's harness bridge, not for web pages.`

business_flow.action: For /api/* and /ws: checks Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Dest
business_flow.outcome: A foreign Origin, a cross-site or same-site fetch, or a destination other than empty, websocket, or document receives 403 `This origin is not allowed.`

business_flow.action: Checks the cookie on every API path except /api/auth/exchange
business_flow.outcome: Missing or unknown cookie receives 401 `Sign in with the URL the ostra command printed.` and an info log line with request facts but no token or cookie values.

sections.title: WebSocket: channels, pushes, and terminal streams
sections.purpose: `/ws` carries one socket per browser tab. The client subscribes to named channels; the server forwards engine notices and its own pushes to the sockets subscribed to the matching channels, streams harness terminals as binary frames, and answers editor hints. The socket re-checks its sign-in and closes when the cookie is revoked.

Per-socket limits and the terminal frame layout.
Cancellation of a socket's streams and pending hint tasks when it ends.
does_not_own: PTY sessions and transcripts (ostra-exec-harness area).
Hint computation (`Code::complete`, `signature`, `navigate`; server-code-navigation section).
Message type definitions `ClientMsg` and `ServerMsg` (ostra-core area).

assumptions: The upgrade passes through `guard`, so Origin and cookie have been checked before `handler` runs; `run` checks the cookie once more after subscribing to the revoke channel to cover a revoke that happened in between.
A client that falls behind the hub (8192) or push (1024) broadcast receives `{type: error, message: lagged}` and is expected to refetch its REST snapshot.
Terminal streams assume `PtyRegistry::inserted()` notifies when a PTY is added, so a subscription made before the PTY starts waits for it.
The stored transcript of an ended harness run is read from `paths::terminal_transcript` under the session root and is sent once when no live PTY exists at first subscribe.

business_flow.outcome: The server records the channel and answers `subscribed`; subscribing to `home` first sends the harness status list.

business_flow.action: Delivers a HubMsg
business_flow.outcome: `route` maps it to channels; the frame is sent only when the socket subscribed to one of them.

business_flow.action: Send a `Pushed` (git progress, project changes, tree patches, activity, workspace updates)
business_flow.outcome: Sockets subscribed to any of the pushed channels receive the message.

business_flow.action: Sends term_input or term_resize
business_flow.outcome: Input up to 64 KiB is written to the PTY; a size outside the PTY limits is refused with an error message.

business_flow.action: Revokes the sign-in
business_flow.outcome: The socket sends close code 4401 `Signed out` and ends.

sections.title: Harness bridge: policy hooks and Ostra MCP tools
sections.purpose: Harness executions (Claude Code, Codex, and other CLIs) run outside the server. This module registers each live execution's policy, tools, and host when it starts, and answers the callbacks the harness makes: the per-tool-call hook on /internal/policy and Ostra's own MCP tools on /internal/mcp. The same `ExecutionPolicy::check` decides every call, as for native runs.

owns: The `Running` record per live harness execution (policy, tool environment, host, memory database, repo, inspect flag).
The MCP tool table `MCP_TOOLS`: report, document, memory, memory_recall, docs_search, `code_<op>` for each `CODE_TOOLS` entry, the project management tools, and the coordination tools.
Policy inputs from the project profile: build commands (build, test, test_one, lint, typecheck) and test commands (test, test_one).
Telling the file watcher about successful harness writes.
does_not_own: Bearer tokens, hook scripts, PTYs, and adapters per harness (ostra-exec-harness area).
Guard and permission rules (ostra-policy area).
Tool implementations (ostra-tools area).

assumptions: The per-execution bearer token is verified by `LiveRegistry::authorize` inside `HarnessBridge` (ostra-exec-harness); `ServerBridge::authorize` only confirms the execution is registered as running here.

`/internal/*` is served on the TCP router (local peers only) and on a Unix socket file in the egress directory for sandboxes with their own network namespace (`serve_bridge_socket`, Unix only); the socket serves nothing else.
Hook callbacks for a workspace MCP tool or a management tool pass without a check because the MCP handler checks, logs, and asks once when it runs the call (Rules M2 and O1).
`ctx.permissions.allow` supplies private hosts for WebFetch through `ostra_tools::webfetch_hosts`.
A resumed execution with `resume.inspect` is a read-only reopening of an ended run: every tool call is refused and no MCP tools are offered.

business_flow.action: Starts a harness run: opens the workspace MCP tools, builds policy and `ToolEnv`, inserts `Running` under the execution id
business_flow.outcome: Callbacks for this execution can be authorized; MCP notes are emitted as Status deltas.

business_flow.action: Calls the hook before a tool
business_flow.outcome: `policy_check` logs ToolCall and Policy deltas and returns Allow, Ask, or Deny with the correction first.

business_flow.action: Receives an Ask
business_flow.outcome: `resolve_ask` calls the host's `ask_permission`; an `AlwaysInWorkspace` answer adds a session allow rule from `allow_rule_suggestion`.

business_flow.action: Calls one of Ostra's MCP tools
business_flow.outcome: `mcp_call` maps the name to the native tool, checks the canonical call, asks if needed, executes it with `ostra_tools::execute`, observes the outcome, and returns the text with policy notes appended.

business_flow.action: Observes a finished call
business_flow.outcome: A successful write call sends a `Touch` to the file watcher; policy observations add notes or up to 5 recalled lessons for failures like this one.

business_flow.action: Harness run ends
business_flow.outcome: The `Running` record is removed, so later callbacks for it are unauthorized.

sections.title: MCP gateway and OAuth sign-in
sections.purpose: Ostra is the only MCP client (HANDOVER 10.6). `McpGateway` keeps one connection per workspace MCP server, signs in to remote servers with OAuth, discovers tools, and exposes them to native runs directly and to harness runs through Ostra's MCP server, so one policy and one allowlist cover every executor.

owns: Connection cache keyed by (workspace root, server name), invalidated when the config or sandbox settings change (fingerprint).
Pending OAuth logins keyed by `state`, and the registry secret `mcp_oauth:ROOT:NAME` holding discovery data, client credentials, redirect URI, and tokens.
Per-execution tool lists with read-only flags and disabled tools.
does_not_own: The MCP protocol client, transports, and OAuth primitives (ostra-mcp area: `Client`, `Endpoint`, `oauth`).
Workspace trust and approval (ostra-workspace area).
Policy classification of MCP tools (ostra-policy area).

assumptions: Servers are configured in the workspace settings (`mcp_servers`); a server runs only from the approved copy of the workspace file (Rule A1), otherwise the error is `ostra_workspace::trust::PENDING_MESSAGE`.
A stdio server is the workspace's own program and starts under the agent sandbox through `ostra_sandbox::host_command` with the workspace root as its writable member.

`env` and `headers` values may use `${VAR}` expansion from the Ostra server's environment, or the marker `mcp::SAVED_SECRET` for a value stored sealed in the registry; provider keys, bridge tokens, and OAuth client secrets are never expanded or inherited (`credential_env`).
The OAuth redirect URI is the browser-visible origin of this server plus `/mcp/oauth/callback`; the guard has already validated the Origin or Host used to build it.
A refresh token may be single-use, so token refreshes are serialized per server by a mutex.

business_flow.action: Calls GET .../mcp
business_flow.outcome: `status` connects to every enabled server in parallel and reports state Disabled, Connected, NeedsAuth, or Error, server info, sign-in state, and tools with `enabled` and `read_only`.

business_flow.action: Starts login for a remote server
business_flow.outcome: `login` discovers the authorization server, registers a client when none is configured or saved, builds a PKCE authorization URL, stores a pending login for 600 seconds, and returns the URL.

business_flow.action: Redirects the browser to /mcp/oauth/callback with code and state
business_flow.outcome: `callback` removes the pending login, exchanges the code, saves the record, resets the connection, and the page shows `Signed in`.

business_flow.action: Opens an execution
business_flow.outcome: `Connector::open` connects to each enabled server that serves the agent, merges tools (first canonical name wins, disabled tools skipped), and returns notes for servers that failed.

business_flow.action: Calls an MCP tool
business_flow.outcome: `ExecMcp::call` restarts a dead server once, calls with the server's `timeout_secs`, and maps auth errors to the sign-in instruction.

code_refs.note: Connect, list, cache, and retry-window logic.

sections.title: Git credentials, clone, and pull
sections.purpose: Users save git credentials in the browser and clone or pull projects over https or ssh. Credentials reach git only through the process environment and one-off `-c` options, never through a repository's `.git/config`, and every output line is redacted of the secret.

owns: Credential validation and matching (host prefix, kind, plain http exclusion).
The claim registry `WorkspaceRt.cloning` usage (`claim`/`Claim`) that serializes git work per key and folder.
Clone planning and execution, pull, and progress pushes.
does_not_own: Importing the cloned folder as a project and the destination folder rules (`import_project`, `new_folder_issues`, `key_and_stack`; ostra-workspace area).
Sealing of registry secrets (server-secrets section and ostra-store).
Git dock commands (server-git-dock section).

assumptions: The `git` executable is on PATH; if missing the error is `Install git on the machine that runs Ostra, because cloning and pulling run the git command.`
Git has no terminal: `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, SSH runs with `BatchMode=yes` and `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`, and on Windows `GCM_INTERACTIVE=never`.
An ssh key saved as a credential has no passphrase (a key containing `ENCRYPTED` is refused when newly entered).
A `commondir` planted in a repository could load another repository's config, so `run_git` calls `ostra_sandbox::repair_git_dirs` before running git in a directory.
Secrets are stored sealed in the registry under `git_credential:ID` with ids of the form `gc_` plus a UUID v7 in simple form.

business_flow.action: Saves a credential (host, kind https or ssh, optional username, secret, label)
business_flow.outcome: `apply` normalizes the host (scheme, user info, and trailing slash removed; host lowercased), validates, and stores the record; the view never returns the secret.

business_flow.action: Posts a clone request (url, key, stack, path, branch, credential)
business_flow.outcome: `clone_plan` validates every field and reports problems by field name; on success a spawned task runs `git clone --progress`.

business_flow.action: Runs git
business_flow.outcome: Progress lines are pushed to `workspace:ID` as `git_progress` at most every 250 ms; failure empties or removes the destination (`clear_failed`); success imports the folder and pushes `workspace_updated`.

business_flow.action: Pulls a project
business_flow.outcome: Refused with 409 when a session works in it; otherwise `git pull --ff-only` with the credential matching the upstream remote URL; the answer reports branch, before, after, and whether it updated.

diagrams.title: Clone request
diagrams.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Browser
  participant Api as API
  participant Git as git module
  participant Proc as git process
  participant Ws as WorkspaceRt
  Browser->>Api: POST /api/workspaces/WS/clone
  Api->>Git: clone_plan validates url, key, stack, path, branch, credential
  Api->>Git: clone in a spawned task
  Git->>Git: claim(key, dest)
  Git->>Proc: run_git clone --progress
  Proc-->>Git: progress lines
  Git-->>Browser: git_progress at most 4 per second
  Git->>Ws: import_project
  Git-->>Browser: workspace_updated
  Api-->>Browser: WorkspaceDetail

tables.title: Constants
rows: 12 lines of output kept for errors

tables.title: Remote URL rules (parse_remote)
rows: Accepted; http to a non-loopback host sets `plain_http`, which never matches a saved credential.
Local path, file://, ext::, other schemes, leading `-`, whitespace or control characters
Refused with `Use an https:// or ssh:// URL, or git@host:owner/repo.git.`
Refused: `Remove the user name and token from the URL and save them as a git credential ...`

tables.title: Credential matching
rows: ssh remote needs an ssh credential; https remote needs an https credential.
Credential host equals the remote host or is a path prefix (`github.com/acme` matches `github.com/acme/shop`, not `github.com/acmeish/shop`); a credential host without a port matches any port.
The matching credential with the longest host string.

tables.title: HTTPS authentication
rows: Drops the user's helpers so git does not copy the token into them; the helper answers only for the credential's own host.
The token goes directly over verified TLS whatever the repository config names.
Written to a private temp dir under the data dir `tmp` with mode 0600, used with `IdentitiesOnly=yes`, deleted with the `GitAuth`.

concerns.responsibility: Validated records and their views without secrets.
Remote parsing and credential choice.
Process environment, timeout, output capture, redaction.
Workflow and busy rules.

sections.title: Git dock commands
sections.purpose: The Git dock shows a project's branch, upstream, ahead and behind counts, and staged, unstaged, and conflicted changes, and runs stage, unstage, commit, fetch, push, and branch switch or create. It is the browser-driven counterpart of the git steps the engine runs itself.

owns: Status parsing (`parse_status`), branch listing, and the command wrappers in `repo::Op`.
The 2,000-entry cap per change list and the 500-branch cap.
does_not_own: Credential selection, `run_git`, and claims (server-git-remote section).
File marks in the tree (server-files section), which read `git status` separately.

assumptions: Every changing command refuses while a session in status running, waiting, or paused works in the project or an init session targets it (`session_in`), because the engine runs its own `git add`.
`git status --porcelain=v2 --branch -z` output is parsed with paths relative to the repository root; entries outside the project's prefix are dropped.
`--literal-pathspecs` is passed to local commands, and each path is checked to stay inside the project with `files::tree::contain`.
A project outside any git work tree answers `is_git: false` and changing commands fail with `` `KEY` is not in a git repository. Run git init in it first. ``

business_flow.action: Opens the dock
business_flow.outcome: `status` answers branch, head, upstream, ahead, behind, staged, unstaged, conflicted, `staged_elsewhere`, `truncated`, and `busy` text.

business_flow.action: Stages or unstages paths (none means the whole project)
business_flow.outcome: `git add -A --` or `git restore --staged --` (or `git rm --cached -r` before the first commit).

business_flow.action: Commits
business_flow.outcome: Refused when the message is empty, nothing is staged, or conflicts remain; otherwise `git commit --no-edit -m MESSAGE`.

business_flow.action: Fetches or pushes
business_flow.outcome: The remote is the branch's configured one, else `origin`, else the only remote; fetch uses `--prune`; push sends `HEAD:MERGE` or `HEAD:refs/heads/BRANCH` with `--set-upstream` when none was set.

business_flow.action: Switches or creates a branch
business_flow.outcome: `git switch`, `switch -c NAME [START]`, or `switch --track REMOTE/NAME`; every change is announced so the Files dock reloads.

tables.title: Constants
rows: 5 minutes (hooks may run formatters and tests)

tables.title: Refusals
rows: 409 `Stop session S or wait for it to finish, then try again, because it is working in `KEY`.`
Branch name fails `branch_ok` or ends in `/` or `.lock`
400 `` `S` is not a commit or branch name. ``
Create with an existing local name
400 `Set an upstream for this branch with git, because the repository has several remotes: ...`
400 `Switch to a branch first, because HEAD is detached ...`

concerns.responsibility: Read-only facts through `files::git::run`.
Holds the claim, runs git with local authentication, announces the change, and returns the new status.

sections.title: Project files, diffs, and change attribution
sections.purpose: The Files dock reads project folders, files, file-name indexes, git marks, per-file diffs, and the list of files that sessions changed, and lets the user save one file from the browser editor. It attributes each changed file to the execution that last wrote it, and pushes `project_fs_changed` when files change.

owns: Caches: file index (30 s), git status (5 s), attribution (3 s), live writes (at most 5,000 per project), user edits, and the directory-browse cache (2 s).
The save protocol with `base_hash` and atomic write.
Read-only rules for `.git`, Ostra runtime state, and memory.
does_not_own: Session state and `file_changes` (ostra-engine area).
Workspace artifact rules (server-artifacts-books section), which this module calls for hidden units and room checks.
Code index content (server-code-navigation section).

assumptions: Every path from the browser is relative to a canonical project root and passes `tree::contain`, which resolves symlinks of the longest existing prefix and refuses anything outside the root (the same rule as the write-scope guard).
The key `artifacts::TAG_ROOT` is not a project: it addresses the workspace artifacts, whose visible folder and hidden folder are listed together and whose files have no git marks or diffs.
Git calls are read-only, take no optional locks (`--no-optional-locks`, `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0`), and time out after 15 seconds, so they never contend with the engine's `git add`.
Text files are UTF-8 or reported binary; NUL in the first 8000 bytes means binary, as git does.
A running execution's writes are known to the server through `Touch` messages; attribution of finished work comes from the session fold via `ostra_engine::view::file_changes`.

business_flow.action: Requests a tree with path, depth (1 to 4), and hidden flag
business_flow.outcome: `tree::list` returns folders before files, never `.git`, dotfiles only with `hidden`; ignored and symlinked folders are listed but not entered; each row carries git mark, staged flag, whether anything under a folder changed, `changed_by`, and `hidden_from_agents`.

business_flow.action: Reads a file
business_flow.outcome: Up to 1 MiB of text with `hash` (SHA-256 of the whole file, only when complete valid UTF-8), `truncated`, `binary`, and a `read_only` reason.

business_flow.action: Saves a file with the `base_hash` it opened
business_flow.outcome: The write happens only when the disk still hashes to `base_hash`; a new file needs no hash and an existing one requires it.

business_flow.action: Requests a diff against `base` (default HEAD)
business_flow.outcome: A unified diff parsed into hunks, capped at 4 MiB; an untracked file diffs against `/dev/null`; a repository with no commit compares HEAD to the empty tree.

business_flow.action: Requests changes
business_flow.outcome: Files attributed to sessions that still differ from HEAD, with added and removed line counts, at most 500.

diagrams.title: From a write tool call to a pushed change
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  a["Native ToolResult notice or harness policy_observe"] --> b[Touch sent on the touches channel]
  b --> c[run_touches batches for 150 ms]
  c --> d[absorb resolves each path to the deepest project root]
  d --> e[Invalidate index, git, and attribution caches]
  d --> f[Code index touch]
  d --> g[Record live write with execution id]
  e --> h["Push project_fs_changed, at most 500 paths"]

tables.title: Constants
rows: 4,096 pending write calls (map cleared when full)
Directory browse: CACHE_TTL / DEFAULT_LIMIT / MAX_LIMIT / MAX_SCAN

tables.title: Read-only reasons (read_only_reason)
rows: `Files under .git are read-only here. Use git to change them.`
Inside the workspace runtime folder (except artifacts) or a project's memory folder
`Ostra's own state is read-only here. Change workspace settings on the Settings screen ...`
A running execution last wrote the file
`A running execution is writing this file. Edit it after the execution ends ...` (409 on save; other reasons 403)

tables.title: Save conflicts
rows: 409 on `base_hash`: `The file changed on disk after you opened it. Reload it ...`
409 on `base_hash`: `... already exists. Open it and edit that version.`
Path is a folder or empty
400 `Name a file with path. Folders cannot be saved.`

concerns.responsibility: Caches, tree, file, mkdir, save, diff, changes, attribution.
Containment, ignore-aware walking (same ignore sources as Grep and Glob), capped reads.
Read-only git status, diff, numstat, and their parsers.
Pairs native write tool calls with successful results into `Touch` values.
Folder picker listing and mkdir, including Windows drive lists and `~` expansion.

sections.title: Code navigation providers, hints, and file watching
sections.purpose: This module serves the Files view's code features (display tokens and outline, usages, dependencies, symbol search, the dependency graph, completion, signature help, and navigate) and the agents' code tools. It chooses each project's providers per request and feeds file changes to the index and language servers. The index and LSP client themselves live in ostra-code.

owns: Per-request provider chain construction and the validation of symbol, path, line, column, and limit parameters.
`Code` state: the per-project indexes, the LSP pool, and the watches.
`CodeTools`, which resolves an agent's repo root to a project and runs `ostra_code::tools::run`.
does_not_own: Tokenizer, index, LSP client, and provider implementations (ostra-code area).
The file-name index that feeds the code index (server-files section).

assumptions: Providers are chosen on every request in this order: the project's own `code_provider` command, then each configured language server, then the built-in `NativeProvider` index; the first to answer wins (`provider::ask`).
A language server answers for a file only after it has started; hints wait at most 3 seconds (`HINT_WAIT`) and the index answers completions meanwhile.
`external_server` answers only for URIs that a language server of the project pointed at since the server started, so the browser cannot name arbitrary files.
The watcher watches each folder that holds a listed file, not the whole tree, so ignored build output adds no watches; folders refused by the OS fall back to the periodic disk check (30 s index TTL).
`CodeTools` is bound to the `App` after construction (`OnceLock<Weak<App>>`); a call before binding or during shutdown answers `The Ostra server is shutting down.`

business_flow.action: Requests code/file, usages, deps, or symbols
business_flow.outcome: `Code::ask` builds a `ProviderRequest` with protocol version, project root, and a contained relative path; the chain answers or the error becomes 400.

business_flow.action: After each answer, ensures a watch on the project
business_flow.outcome: Outside edits (editor, shell, checkout) reach the index within about 250 ms to 2 s.

business_flow.action: Delivers a batch
business_flow.outcome: Structural changes invalidate the file list; changed files are touched in the index and servers; the browser receives `project_fs_changed` (with an empty path list when more than 200 paths changed).

business_flow.action: Sends code_complete, code_signature, or code_navigate over the socket
business_flow.outcome: Completion tries each language server then the index; signature help tries servers only; navigate tries the index first and then servers.

business_flow.action: Calls a code tool
business_flow.outcome: The innermost project containing the repo root is found among open workspaces and the tool runs on its index in the blocking pool.

tables.title: Limits
rows: Usage results; requested limit is clamped to 1..MAX.
A symbol has no whitespace or control characters.
Wait for a starting language server.
A batch closes after a quiet spell or the maximum wait.
More changed paths push an empty list, meaning reload.

tables.title: Graph queries (GET .../code/graph)
rows: 400 `Give either package or path, not both.`
404 `That package, file, or symbol is not in the code index ...`

concerns.responsibility: Provider chain, hints, external files, graph, reindex, watch management.
Per-request language servers and the index fallback inputs for editor hints.
Debounced filesystem watcher honoring .gitignore and .git/info/exclude.
Agent-facing code navigation over the same indexes.

sections.title: Sessions tree, search, and workspace activity
sections.purpose: The redesigned console shows a Sessions tree, a search box over the whole workspace, and an activity summary of running executions, open gates, and spend. `Nav` rebuilds changed tree nodes from engine notices at a fixed tick and pushes patches; search merges ranked hits from several sources; activity counts spend from local midnight.

owns: `Nav` per-workspace state: cached nodes, dirty sets, activity cache, and push cadence.
Search scoring and merging.
Activity window calculation.
does_not_own: The content of tree nodes (engine `tree_session`).
The full-text tables and cost queries (ostra-store area).
Settings key catalog `SETTING_KEYS` (ostra-core area).

assumptions: Engine notices mark sessions and executions dirty; a lagged hub marks everything dirty so the next tick rebuilds every session.
`engine.tree_session` builds a session's node; two equal nodes are not pushed again.

Artifact headings are indexed into the workspace database full-text index (`index_artifact`) while nodes are built, skipping files whose label and mtime are unchanged; files over 4 MiB are indexed by label and file name only.
`spend_since` returns dollars since a UTC instant; the day and week windows are local midnight today and local midnight six days earlier (daylight-saving gaps fall back to the first existing hour).

business_flow.action: Arrives through the attach forwarder
business_flow.outcome: `Nav::observe` marks the session or execution dirty; tool calls and status messages also dirty the execution's summary line.

business_flow.action: Runs every 250 ms on the blocking pool
business_flow.outcome: `flush` rebuilds dirty nodes, pushes `tree_patch` for each node that differs, and builds activity when due.

business_flow.action: Searches with q and limit
business_flow.outcome: An empty query returns recent sessions; otherwise hits from projects, settings keys, executions, artifacts, sessions, file names, and lessons are scored 0 to 1, merged, deduplicated by id, and cut to the limit.

diagrams.title: Dirty marking to pushes
diagrams.source:
flowchart TD
  a[Engine notice] --> b[Nav.observe marks session or execution dirty]
  b --> c[Ticker every 250 ms]
  c --> d[flush rebuilds dirty nodes]
  d --> e{Node differs from cached node?}
  e -->|yes| f[Push tree_patch]
  e -->|no| g[Drop]
  c --> h{"Activity dirty and 500 ms since last?"}
  h -->|yes| i[Build activity]
  i --> j{Changed?}
  j -->|yes| k[Push activity]

tables.title: Constants
rows: 250 ms (at most four patches a second per session)
500 ms (at most two activity messages a second per workspace)
200 rows read from the text index
0.45 score for an index match the in-memory scorer cannot place

tables.title: Text score (Needle::text_score)
rows: All words of a multi-word query present
minus 0.0005 per extra character, at most 0.05

tables.title: Source adjustments
rows: Exact file name 1.0, name prefix 0.88, name substring 0.74, path substring 0.6, name subsequence 0.4, path subsequence 0.3
as is; last segment times 0.95; description times 0.85
plus 0.03 minus 0.0001 per rank; heading times 0.95

concerns.responsibility: Dirty tracking, tree cache, flush, artifact indexing.
Needle scoring and per-source ranking, merge, and the async `search` entry.
Running executions, open gates, and spend windows.

sections.title: Workspace artifacts and books
sections.purpose: Workspace artifacts are files the user keeps for every session of a workspace. Visible artifacts live in `<workspace>/.ostra/artifacts/` and every agent reads them. The user can hide a folder or a file as one unit; hidden content lives in Ostra's data dir where no agent, harness, or sandboxed command can read it (Rule W2). Books are documentation books under the workspace, listed, read, and deleted through the same API style.

owns: Locating, listing, uploading, hiding, showing, moving, deleting, and downloading artifacts.
The hidden-units file.
does_not_own: Path normalization, size limits, and listing helpers (ostra-core `artifacts` module).
The Files dock's display of artifacts (server-files section).
Book file format, validation, and listing (ostra-core `book` module); the server only calls `list`, `read`, `remove`, and `book_dir`.

assumptions: Invariant: a path is stored in the hidden folder exactly when it is within a hidden unit; every change (upload, hide, show, move, delete) keeps it.

Hidden units are a JSON array of relative paths in `artifacts::hidden_units_file(workspace id)`; when that file is absent (a workspace that hid files before units were recorded) each hidden file is its own unit.
Rule W4: artifacts are deleted or moved only while no session is running, waiting, stalled, or paused and no execution runs, because an agent may be reading the file.
Artifact paths are normalized by `ostra_core::artifacts::normalize` and contained under the visible or hidden root with `tree::contain`.
The data dir can be on another file system than the workspace, so a move falls back to copy then delete when rename fails.

business_flow.action: Uploads a file to a path
business_flow.outcome: Refused over 25 MiB, when it exists, or when 2,000 artifacts exist; otherwise saved in the hidden root when a hidden unit holds the path, else the visible root.

business_flow.action: Hides or shows a unit
business_flow.outcome: Showing something inside a hidden folder is refused with `Show the folder `F` instead ...`; otherwise files are relocated between the roots and the unit list is saved.

business_flow.action: Moves an artifact or folder
business_flow.outcome: All targets are checked before anything moves; what was hidden stays hidden and what lands in a hidden folder becomes hidden.

business_flow.action: Deletes an artifact
business_flow.outcome: Refused while work runs; otherwise the file and emptied parent folders are removed and its unit entry is dropped.

business_flow.action: Deletes a book
business_flow.outcome: Refused with 409 while work starts; the book folder is removed and the remaining list returned.

tables.title: Limits and rules
rows: 2,000 per workspace, visible and hidden together
Move to a path inside itself
409 `Stop session S or wait for it to end, then delete|move, because its agents may be reading the artifact.`
409 `Wait for execution E to finish, then ..., because it may be reading the artifact.`

concerns.responsibility: All artifact operations and the W2 and W4 rules.
List, read, and delete books with the work lock.

sections.title: Project skills and commands
sections.purpose: The project screen lists, reads, writes, deletes, and adopts skills, and edits the project's build, test, lint, and run commands stored in `.ostra/project.toml`. Both apply to the next execution, because engine and policy read the profile fresh per execution.

owns: Scanning skills from three places: the `skills` list in project.toml, directories under `paths::SKILL_DIRS`, and harness directories.
Validation and cleaning of command strings.
does_not_own: How skills are loaded into prompts (ostra-agents and ostra-tools areas).
The format approval of commands (`trust::saved_format` in ostra-workspace).

assumptions: Skill names and kinds are checked on every change: a name is 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, `-`, `_`, starting with a letter or digit, because it becomes a directory name; kinds are `convention`, `creation`, `test`, or `other`.
Skill paths come from project.toml, which the repository can supply, so every path is resolved inside the project with symlinks followed (`in_project`) before reading or writing.
Ostra writes skills only under `.agents/skills/` (`paths::SKILLS_DIR`) and `.ostra/`; a skill located elsewhere must be edited in the Files tab.
Skills and commands cannot change while the project folder is missing or an init session runs, because the initializer writes them.
The commands file must exist (initialize first) and parse; otherwise the answer is 409.

business_flow.action: Saves a skill (kind, content, optional component type)
business_flow.outcome: SKILL.md is written (non-empty, at most 512 KiB) and a project.toml entry is inserted or updated.

business_flow.action: Adopts a skill found in a harness directory (.claude/skills, .codex/skills, .grok/skills, .gemini/skills, .ultracode/skills)
business_flow.outcome: The directory is copied (symlinks skipped) to the project's skills dir under the chosen name and registered with source `adopted`.

business_flow.action: Deletes a skill
business_flow.outcome: The profile entry and every skill directory of that name are removed; 404 when neither existed.

business_flow.action: Saves commands
business_flow.outcome: Each field is trimmed; blank or `—` becomes unset; a newline, control character, or more than 2,000 characters is an issue on `commands.FIELD`; `before` format command and the new one go to `trust::saved_format`.

tables.title: Command fields
rows: build, test, test_one, format, lint, typecheck, run
One line, no control characters, at most MAX_COMMAND_LEN (2,000) characters; issues are returned together as 422 `Fix the commands and save again.`

concerns.responsibility: Scan, read, save, delete, adopt, front-matter description parsing.
Clean and save the `commands` table of project.toml.

sections.title: Master key and saved provider credentials
sections.purpose: Provider credentials, git credentials, MCP OAuth records, and the push signing key are stored as sealed secrets in the registry. The master key that seals them lives in the OS keychain when one is reachable, otherwise in an owner-only file. Provider credentials entered in the browser never reach config.toml or a response body.

owns: Key selection and `unlock`, which also seals plaintext secret rows left by older versions.
The provider credentials record under `provider_credentials:NAME` and its validation.
does_not_own: The `Sealer` cipher and `secret_*` methods (ostra-store area).
Provider construction from config and credentials (ostra-providers area).

assumptions: Backend choice is recorded under the registry key `secrets:backend` as `keychain` or `file`; once `file` is recorded the keychain is not consulted again.
A keychain call can block on an unlock prompt or a dead D-Bus, so it runs on a thread abandoned after 10 seconds (`KEYCHAIN_TIMEOUT`).
Keychain entries are named by service `ostra` and account `master-key DATA_DIR`, so separate installs keep separate keys.
The key file holds 64 hex characters; on Unix it is created with mode 0600 and loosened modes are tightened, but a read-only mount that cannot be changed is left alone with a warning.
A key that opens nothing sealed so far means credentials were saved under another key; they read as not set and the check value (`secrets:check`, sealing the text `ostra`) moves to the current key.

business_flow.action: Starts and calls `master_key::unlock`
business_flow.outcome: A key is loaded or created; the registry gets a sealer; `seal_plaintext_secrets` encrypts rows stored in plaintext and logs how many.

business_flow.action: Saves provider credentials in settings
business_flow.outcome: `apply` merges the edit onto the saved record (`None` keeps, empty clears, other replaces), validates, stores, and `reload_providers` rebuilds the providers.

diagrams.title: Master key selection

tables.title: Provider credential rules
rows: http or https with a host and no user name, password, or query, because the URL is shown in settings.
No whitespace or control characters, because they are sent as HTTP headers.
Only `anthropic` and `openai`, and present in the global config.

tables.title: Registry keys
rows: Sealed JSON `SavedCredentials`; an empty record deletes the key

concerns.responsibility: Key discovery, creation, permission tightening, check value.
Provider credentials storage, merge, validation, and `Shared::reload_providers`.

sections.title: Environment check, first-run setup, harness setup terminals, and model prices
sections.purpose: These modules tell the console what the machine has (harness CLIs, providers, sandbox, shell), create a workspace in one call during first-run setup, run a harness's official installer or login in a browser-attached terminal, and keep model prices fresh for cost accounting.

owns: `EnvStatus` and its 60 second freshness rule.
Setup terminal ids `setup_HARNESS_ACTION` and their lifecycle.
The price cache file `models-dev.json` in the data dir.
does_not_own: Install scripts, login commands, and PTYs (ostra-exec-harness area).
Pricing math (ostra-core `pricing`).
Workspace creation rules (`ostra_workspace::create`).

assumptions: Harness detection uses `which` for each `HarnessKind::ALL` command from the global config and runs `COMMAND --version` with an 8 second timeout.

`logged_in` is `Some(true)` from an API key variable or credential file, `None` for Grok and Agy, and `None` for Claude when only the OS keychain could hold the login, because absence of a marker means unknown, not logged out.

Setup terminals run in the user's home directory in a PTY of 100 columns by 30 rows; the installer needs `curl` (or `npm` on Windows) and prints an install message with exit code 127 when the tool is missing.
The prices catalog comes from the models.dev JSON at `ostra_core::pricing::MODELS_DEV_URL`; setting `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` to an empty value disables fetching.

business_flow.action: Calls GET /api/environment
business_flow.outcome: The harness list is refreshed when older than 60 seconds; the answer holds providers, harnesses, stack names, sandbox status, and shell status.

business_flow.action: Posts a workspace from the setup wizard
business_flow.outcome: `setup::create` registers the workspace, attaches it (recovering its sessions), and marks the machine onboarded.

business_flow.action: Starts a harness install or login
business_flow.outcome: The same terminal is returned if still running; a login needs the CLI on PATH (`Install NAME first ...`); when the terminal exits, harnesses are detected again and `harness_status` is pushed to `home`.

business_flow.action: Starts the price task
business_flow.outcome: The cached catalog is installed at once; a fetch runs when the cache is older than 24 hours, and a failed fetch retries after 1 hour keeping the cached prices.

tables.title: Price refresh rules

sections.title: Workspace database
sections.purpose: `WorkspaceDb` is the SQLite database at `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db`. It holds the append-only session event log, which is the source of truth, and the tables the engine materializes beside it so the console can list sessions, executions, gates, decisions, transcripts, and activity without folding events. The engine and the workspace runtime are its callers.

owns: The schema and its migrations (`MIGRATIONS` in `crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs`).
Assigning event, message, and activity sequence numbers per session or execution.
File permissions and the `.gitignore` of the `.ostra` folder.
Full-text search over sessions and artifacts, the spend sum, and the cost report.
does_not_own: What an event means or how events fold into session state: the engine area (`SessionState::fold`).
Deciding when to append an event or update a materialized row: the engine runner (`Inner::append`).
The registry and credentials: section `store-and-2-more-store-registry`.

assumptions: One `WorkspaceDb` value wraps one connection behind an `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`; every method takes the mutex, so calls in one process never overlap. A poisoned mutex is recovered with `into_inner` (`WorkspaceDb::lock`).
The workspace id is written to the `meta` table with `set_workspace_id` before sessions are read; `workspace_id_of` returns an empty id when none is stored.
Timestamps are RFC 3339 strings with millisecond precision in UTC (`util::now`), and they sort correctly as text, which the `started_at >= ?` comparisons in `spend_since` and `cost_report` rely on.
Enum columns hold the serde string of a unit-variant enum (`enum_str`, `enum_from`); a stored value that no longer parses returns `StoreError::Json`.
On Unix the process can `chmod` its own files; on other systems `restrict` does nothing.

subsections.purpose: This piece describes how the database file is opened and how the schema evolves. It runs once when a workspace opens and once per process for in-memory test databases.
assumptions: `user_version` is the count of applied migrations. `migrate` applies every entry of `MIGRATIONS` from index `user_version` onward, each in its own transaction, and sets `user_version` inside that transaction, so a failed migration leaves the version unchanged.
A migration never edits an earlier entry; new columns and tables are new entries (the second entry adds `sessions.title` and `executions.summary`).
`open_in_memory` runs the same migrations but sets no pragmas, creates no folder, and writes no `.gitignore`.

subsections.title: Event log append and read
subsections.purpose: This piece stores the session event log. The engine's `Inner::append` calls `append_event` for every state change, and recovery after a restart reads the events back with `events` or `events_after`.
assumptions: `SessionEvent` serializes to a JSON object with a string `type` field; `append_event` stores `unknown` as the type column when it is absent.

The sequence number is `MAX(seq) + 1` for the session, computed inside an `IMMEDIATE` transaction, so two writers in one or several processes never get the same number (test `concurrent_appends_get_distinct_seqs`).
The caller passes an existing session id; the `events` table has no foreign key, so an event for an unknown session is stored without error.

business_flow.action: Calls `append_event(session, event)`.
business_flow.outcome: The store opens an immediate transaction and reads the next `seq`.

business_flow.action: Inserts the row with the JSON payload and a millisecond timestamp, and sets `sessions.updated_at` to the same timestamp.
business_flow.outcome: The session moves to the top of recently updated lists.

business_flow.action: Commits and returns a `StoredEvent` with `seq`, `at`, and the event.
business_flow.outcome: The engine folds, broadcasts, and wakes its driver with the stored event.

business_flow.action: Calls `events(session)` or `events_after(session, n)` on recovery or when a client catches up.
business_flow.outcome: Events return in `seq` order and each payload parses back to a `SessionEvent`.

sequenceDiagram
  participant Engine
  participant WorkspaceDb
  participant SQLite
  Engine->>WorkspaceDb: append_event(session, event)
  WorkspaceDb->>SQLite: BEGIN IMMEDIATE
  WorkspaceDb->>SQLite: SELECT COALESCE(MAX(seq), 0) + 1 FROM events
  WorkspaceDb->>SQLite: INSERT INTO events
  WorkspaceDb->>SQLite: UPDATE sessions SET updated_at
  WorkspaceDb->>SQLite: COMMIT
  WorkspaceDb-->>Engine: StoredEvent with seq and at

subsections.title: Materialized tables and their methods
subsections.purpose: This piece describes the tables the engine writes beside the event log: sessions, executions, messages, activity, gates, decisions, tool calls, and projects. The console reads them directly. They are a cache of facts the engine also records as events or execution results, so a reader who needs the authoritative state folds the event log.
assumptions: `update_session` changes only fields set to `Some`; a `category` or `title` of `Some(None)` clears the column. It returns `StoreError::NotFound` when the session row does not exist, and it always sets `updated_at`.
`create_session` starts every session at status `Running`, lane `Research`, stage label `Intake`, and cost 0.

`finish_execution` keeps the stored `native_session_id` when the result carries none (`COALESCE`), and `reopen_execution` (Rule P2) clears `error` and `ended_at` and keeps usage, transcript, and activity so a resumed run adds to them.

`ExecutionView.can_resume` is true only for a harness executor with a stored native session id; `has_transcript`, `has_terminal`, `pending_gate`, and `repo_root` are left empty here and filled by callers.
The `run_label` of a view is the first-run label; the engine numbers repeated runs from the fold.
`upsert_gate` on an existing id refreshes title, explanation, and payload but keeps `opened_at` and any answer.

subsections.title: Search, spend, and cost report
subsections.purpose: This piece answers three read questions: which sessions and artifacts match a typed text, how much money executions spent since a time, and how spend splits by session, stage, agent, and executor. The console search box, the budget check, and the cost page call them.
assumptions: Session rows enter the search index through SQL triggers (`sessions_search_ai` and `sessions_search_au`), so the session title and request stay searchable without application code; the third migration backfills sessions that existed before it.
Artifact rows enter only when a caller invokes `index_artifact`, which stores the file's modification time in milliseconds so the caller can skip unchanged files.
`fts_prefix_query` splits text on every non-alphanumeric character, quotes each word, doubles embedded quotes, appends `*`, and joins words with a space, so every word must match as a word prefix.
`cost_report` parses each execution's stored `usage` JSON; an unparsable row fails the whole report with `StoreError::Json`.
`spend_since` and `cost_report` count an execution by its `started_at`, not by when the money was spent.

business_flow.outcome: The server calls `search_text(text, limit)`.

business_flow.action: Builds the prefix query; an empty query returns no hits. Otherwise it joins `search_fts` to `search_docs` and orders by `bm25(search_fts, 4.0, 1.0)`.
business_flow.outcome: Label matches weigh four times as much as body matches; lower rank is better.

business_flow.outcome: Each group sorts by cost descending then key; each row carries `cache_reads_per_tool_call`, which is cache read tokens divided by tool calls and is 0 when there are no tool calls.

sections.title: Machine registry
sections.purpose: `RegistryDb` is the database at `~/.local/share/ostra/registry.db` (the data directory of the machine). It lists registered workspaces, stores Web Push subscriptions, keeps a key-value table used by authentication, command approvals, and credentials, and records first-run onboarding. The server and `ostra-workspace` use it.

owns: The `workspaces`, `push_subscriptions`, and `kv` tables and their migration.
The uniqueness of a workspace root and the atomic compare-and-swap `kv_replace`.
The rule that credential rows go through `secret_*` methods and need a `Sealer`.
does_not_own: Which `kv` keys exist and what they mean: the callers, for example `ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs` for `trust:*` and `workspace_access:*` keys and `ostra-server` for `auth:*` keys.
Where the master key comes from: `crates/ostra-server/src/master_key.rs`.
The encryption format: section `store-and-2-more-store-secrets`.

assumptions: `RegistryDb::open` returns a registry with no sealer; `secret_get`, `secret_set`, `secret_scan`, and `seal_plaintext_secrets` return `StoreError::Locked` until `with_sealer` supplies one.
`open_in_memory` gives the registry an ephemeral key that lives as long as the process; it applies only `MIGRATIONS[0]`.
Opening sets `secure_delete = ON`, so freed pages are zeroed and a replaced plaintext credential does not stay in the file.
Callers pass only keys listed in `SECRET_KEYS` to `secret_get` and `secret_set`; a `debug_assert!` checks it in debug builds only.

A workspace root is stored as the lossy string of the path the caller passes; callers pass the canonical root so the `UNIQUE` constraint on `root` matches (`create::register` canonicalizes before `add_workspace`).

diagrams.title: Sealing plaintext credentials at startup
diagrams.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Server
  participant RegistryDb
  participant Sealer
  participant SQLite
  Server->>RegistryDb: with_sealer(sealer)
  Server->>RegistryDb: seal_plaintext_secrets()
  RegistryDb->>SQLite: kv_scan with empty prefix
  RegistryDb->>Sealer: seal(key, value) for each plaintext secret row
  RegistryDb->>SQLite: kv_replace(key, old, sealed)
  RegistryDb->>SQLite: VACUUM and wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)
  RegistryDb->>SQLite: kv_set(secrets_vacuumed, 1)

sections.purpose: The `secrets` module seals credential values stored in the registry so a copy of `registry.db` does not reveal them. `RegistryDb` uses a `Sealer` built from the machine's master key. The module also lists which registry keys hold credentials.

sections.title: Project lesson memory
sections.purpose: `MemoryStore` keeps durable lessons that agents record for a project and recall in later runs. The file is `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3`; the path the tools use comes from `ToolEnvConfig.memory_db`. It follows the schema of Ultracode's `mcp/lib/memory.js`: one lesson per (area, lesson) pair, area sub-scopes written `area::sub`, bm25 ranking, and targeted forgetting. Lessons are never capped and never expire.

owns: The `lessons` table, its FTS5 index `lessons_fts`, and the recall ordering.
Deduplication on (area, lesson).
does_not_own: The `Memory` and `MemoryRecall` tool arguments and output text: section `store-and-2-more-tools-agent-io`.
The lesson gate that refuses a report until a lesson is recorded: `crates/ostra-policy`.
The memory browser routes: `crates/ostra-server`.

assumptions: Every method opens a fresh connection with a 5000 ms busy timeout and runs `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` for the schema, so parallel executions wait on the SQLite file lock and never share a handle.
`recall`, `forget`, `list`, and `delete` return empty or false when the database file does not exist and do not create it; `record`, `update`, and `open` do create the folder and file.

`update` marks the lesson source as `user` and resets `created_at`; it fails with `StoreError::NotFound` when no row matches the id after the update, and with `StoreError::Sqlite` when the new (area, lesson) pair already exists because of the `UNIQUE` constraint.
The recall query text splits on non-alphanumeric characters and matches any token (`OR`); this differs from the workspace search, where every word must match.

business_flow.action: Calls `record(area, lesson, source)`.
business_flow.outcome: The pair is inserted, or an existing pair gets the new source and time; the method returns the total lesson count.

business_flow.action: Calls `recall(area, query, limit)`.
business_flow.outcome: Lessons return in buckets: (1) the area and its `area::%` sub-scopes, ranked by bm25 when a query exists and by newest first otherwise; (2) global text matches as fill; (3) with neither area nor query, the newest lessons overall. Duplicates by (area, lesson) are dropped and the list stops at `limit`.

business_flow.action: Calls `forget(area, lesson)` for a confirmed-stale lesson.
business_flow.outcome: The exact pair is deleted; the method returns false when it is absent.

business_flow.action: Uses `list(query, limit, offset)`, `update(id, area, lesson)`, and `delete(id)`.
business_flow.outcome: Lessons list newest first (or by bm25 with a query), can be edited, and can be deleted.

sections.title: Tool environment and call dispatch
sections.purpose: `ToolEnv` holds the per-execution state of the native tools, and `execute` runs one tool call against it and returns a `ToolOutput`. Native executions call `execute` directly, and the server's harness bridge calls it for harness tool calls that map to native tools. Tool names and input shapes follow Claude Code's tools because the agent prompts are tuned to them.

owns: Dispatch from tool name to implementation, the `Unknown tool` and cancellation results, and the duration measurement.
Path resolution against the shell's working directory, including `~/` expansion and the sandbox `/tmp` mapping.
The set of files read in this run, which gates Write and Edit.
Coercing JSON-string arguments to the schema's types before running.
does_not_own: Permission and guard checks: `crates/ostra-policy` (`ExecutionPolicy::check`), called by `crates/ostra-exec-native` and the harness bridge before `execute`.
The agent loop and provider calls: `crates/ostra-exec-native`.
Sandbox profile construction: `crates/ostra-sandbox`.

assumptions: The caller builds the call with `ToolEnv::canonical_call` and passes that same call both to the policy and to `execute`, so the policy and the tool see one target (`exec-native` line 937 and `server/src/bridge.rs` line 415 do this).
`ToolEnv` is created once per execution: its working directory starts at `repo_root` and its read set starts empty.
`ToolEnvConfig.workspace_root` is empty outside a workspace; `DocsSearch` and workspace-artifact skills depend on it.
Private hosts for `WebFetch` come from `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` allow rules through `with_private_hosts`; without the call the list is empty.
`scrub_env` is computed when the environment is created from `config.toml` (`configured_secret_vars`), so a change to credential variable names applies to the next execution.

business_flow.action: Builds `ToolEnvConfig` (agent, repo root, workspace root, session dir, report file, memory database, memory source, skill resolver, and optional code, MCP, manage, and coordination handles) and calls `ToolEnv::new`, then `with_private_hosts`, `with_scrub_env`, and `with_sandbox`.

business_flow.outcome: Relative paths become absolute, shell calls get `cwd`, and a WebFetch URL becomes its parsed form.

business_flow.outcome: The tool runs.

business_flow.action: Looks up the tool's input schema for the agent and coerces string values to the schema's types, then dispatches by name.
