subsections.title: classify, sufficiency, track and stakes
subsections.purpose: These four judges decide the shape of a session before any code is written: its category and scope, whether research is finished, and how much of the pipeline an implementation runs.
assumptions: classify sees only the pinned projects when the user pinned any, and must return exactly those because Ostra drops any other key (Rule O6).
RESEARCH, SPEC, PLAN and IMPLEMENT always get at least one explore task (Rule D1), one per project in scope (Rule M1); every other category gets an empty list.
Each explore task names, by absolute path, every attached file, folder and upload that bears on it, because the researcher reads only its task.

business_flow.action: Reads what the request asks Ostra to produce, not its first verb, and picks one category; a request that changes files is a changing category.
business_flow.outcome: Category, projects, explore tasks, opt-ins and a title.

business_flow.action: Asks for each Not covered item whether the request depends on it; an item a later document covers is not needed.
business_flow.outcome: A research task for every needed item; the spec stage starts only when none is left (Rule D2).

business_flow.action: Defaults to light and picks full only for one of 6 research findings.
business_flow.outcome: light: one reviewed phase per project built from the research. full: spec, fact-check, plan and approvals (Rule D1).

business_flow.action: Reads the approved spec's counts, Delivery Order, Contracts and Data Impact.
business_flow.outcome: low skips the plan (one inline phase per project); medium and high run it.

tables.title: Category rules worth knowing
rows: Only when a developer could make the edit without reading beyond the lines it touches; it skips research, spec, plan and review. A decision, more than a few lines, a behavior other code depends on, or a request for tests or docs makes it IMPLEMENT.
Any edit to an AI prompt, SKILL.md, agent file or judge prompt under assets/, even when the edit is spelled out, because prompt-generation applies the prompt writing rules.
A documentation book about existing code; the docs stage writes into the workspace and changes no project file. Changing a docs page, README or code comments in a project is IMPLEMENT.
Writing, extending or fixing tests for existing code; always sets opts_in.tests. DOCS always sets opts_in.docs.
Starts on the light track; do not pick PLAN or SPEC only because a change looks large.

tables.title: Conditions that make the track judge pick full
columns: Why the spec and plan help
rows: The request leaves a behavior or rule open that the user must settle
Open questions reach the user before code is written.
A contract other code consumes changes (public API, wire format, event, shared library, cross-project contract)
The spec pins the contract and fact-check checks every caller.
A schema, migration or stored data changes
The plan sequences it and the user approves it.
The change spans modules or areas that must land in a set order
The plan orders phases and review checks each.
Security, authentication, permissions, payments or data deletion is involved
The user approves requirements before code touches them.
The request needs a new codebase no project in scope holds
Only an approved plan can put phases in a project that does not exist yet (Rule O2).

tables.title: Stakes levels
rows: One deliverable in one project, isolated to one area, easy to revert, no schema or data change, no contract change.
Several files in one area, a change to an existing contract, a new integration point, or more than one deliverable.
Architectural change, schema or data migration, cross-module or cross-project change, shared-library change, or external integration change.

subsections.title: route-answer, feedback and yolo-answer
subsections.purpose: These judges decide where a human's words go, and, under YOLO, what answers in the human's place. The user's words win over any recommendation; Ostra's own rules are the only limit.
assumptions: Ostra's own rules apply whatever the decision: guards, the session budget, fact-check PASS before approval, the review cap count, BLOCKER removal, and a plan built only from an approved spec. The judge delivers such an answer as written and names the rule in the reason.
Exactly one item per answer: each open question's ID, or the ID answer for a gate with one text. One answer is never split into several items.
A remembered note never changes a requirement; an answer that changes what the system must do is deliver, so the spec records it.
Nothing can be kept for the plan agent because it reads only the spec.
YOLO changes who answers, never what must be true.

business_flow.action: Answers a gate, adds context to a running session, or sends feedback after a build.
business_flow.outcome: Text reaches the judge before any agent.

business_flow.action: Assigns each item a disposition (deliver, remember, discard), names later stages (implement, tests, docs) that also receive a note, lists kept notes to forget, adds up to three research tasks, and picks a route.
business_flow.outcome: Engine delivers, keeps or drops the text and starts any research first.

business_flow.action: When YOLO is on and a gate would wait for the user, answers by gate kind.
business_flow.outcome: The answer and reason are recorded and listed under 'Decided for you' in the completion report.

tables.title: Dispositions
rows: The answer settles what the stage asked or changes what the agent must do now. Default.
The asking agent receives it as written.
The whole answer is only for a later stage.
Nothing reaches this stage; the note reaches the named stages.
The user says to ignore it, in their own words.
Nothing reaches any agent; the text stays in the session log.

tables.title: Routes
rows: At a phase gate, stops the phase and re-runs generate-spec with the answer, asks for spec approval again and plans again (Rule D10). In feedback, writes the change into the spec, fact-checks it, asks for approval, then builds.
Passes the answer to the implementer as an instruction, or builds the revision directly; the spec is unchanged. Always chosen when the session has no spec.
Runs the chosen optional stages, such as tests or docs at the closing gate; the spec is unchanged (Rule T5).

tables.title: YOLO answers by gate kind
rows: Each question's recommended option unless research or code gives a specific reason for another; name the reason.
Approve only with a latest fact-check PASS; decline and give feedback if the artifact plainly omits something the request asked for.
No tests and no docs unless the request already asked for that stage (Rule T3).
Another pass while the open-finding count is falling, else stop.
State a fact if the context supplies one, else leave the phase blocked.
Allow unless the call matches one of the user's explicit deny rules.
Re-route the execution to the native executor.
Accept every default disposition the proposal set.

code_refs.note: Items, dispositions, forget, research (at most 3), route, context the user added.
Route, targets, disposition answer, forget, research.

subsections.title: rescue, resolve-review and completion
subsections.purpose: These judges handle exits from the normal flow: an agent that returned STUCK, a review loop that ran out of budget under YOLO, and the end of a session.
assumptions: A plain retry of a stuck agent is never an option, because the same instructions reproduce the same failure and spend the budget twice (Rule D9).
Under YOLO the review loop budget is 10 passes; BLOCKER security findings never reach resolve-review and loop without a cap until removed.
The completion judge reports only what the input records: a command, check or test the input does not show running did not run.

business_flow.action: Reads the stuck diagnostic, need, project, recalled lessons and the number of earlier rescues.
business_flow.outcome: rerun with a fact quoted from its source, explore with a self-contained research task, or gate to ask the user.

business_flow.action: Reads the ledger to find why findings recur: a fix that never landed, a fix that caused the next finding, contradictory findings, a re-raised WONTFIX, or a missing fact.
business_flow.outcome: fix with one exact instruction per open finding (file, line, exact change, why earlier attempts failed), then one fix pass and one verification review; or block so the phase is marked blocked and independent work continues.

business_flow.action: Writes Markdown sections Summary, Phases, Checks, Not run, Blocked (omitted when empty) and Decided for you (YOLO only).
business_flow.outcome: The report states every stage that did not run and how to run it later, and quotes blocked phases' diagnostics and ledger paths verbatim.

tables.title: Rescue actions
rows: The fact is in the lessons, phase file, spec or diagnostic.
Re-runs the agent with the diagnostic and the quoted fact.
The fact is findable in code or outside documentation and nothing given states it.
Runs the research task, then re-runs the agent with the findings.
Only the user can supply it: intent, business rule, credential, unreachable environment, spec question; or two rescues of this phase with the same diagnostic failed.
Asks the user; under YOLO the phase is set aside and independent work continues.

sections.title: Stack references, the inventory contract and the meta-author skill
sections.purpose: assets/refs/ and assets/skills/ are the standards the initializer and prompt-generation agents read while they create a project's skills, INVENTORY.md and project.toml. A stack reference tells the scout which component types recur in a language and framework and what commands and review rules to seed; the inventory contract fixes the two output files; the meta-author skill fixes how instruction files are written.

owns: The content of the 4 stack references, the generic fallback, inventory-and-profile.md, skill-archetypes.md and the meta-author skill

does_not_own: Parsing project.toml into ProjectProfile: ostra-core and ostra-workspace (core and workspace areas)

assumptions: Seed references start with the heading '# Stack Reference:'; stack_names() lists exactly those whose file name does not start with '_', so _generic (the fallback), inventory-and-profile and skill-archetypes are not offered as stacks. The result is go, java-spring, python, typescript-node.
A project's stack is free text in kebab-case; it never has to match a reference name, and it is never the word generic.
TOML has no null: a key with no value is omitted, never written as null, because Ostra cannot parse a file that contains it and initialization fails.
project.toml has no routing table; which executor and model each agent uses is a workspace setting resolved per execution.
SEC-BLOCK-* and PHASE-REQ-* rule IDs never appear in the profile's review rules; the code-reviewer defines them itself.

sections.title: Site: homepage and docs
sections.purpose: site/ is the npm package @ostra/site. It builds two static pages with Vite: a homepage that introduces Ostra and embeds a mock console, and a docs page that renders the repository's own Markdown (README.md, HANDOVER.md, CLAUDE.md, tests/browser/README.md and every file under docs/) at build time. It needs no server, because both pages use relative paths and carry their Content Security Policy in a meta tag.

The Markdown content: README.md, HANDOVER.md, CLAUDE.md and docs/: docs area
The server's CSP header in crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs, which the site policy must equal (server area)
The browser tests that check the built site: tests/browser/specs/site.spec.ts (tests area)

assumptions: The site is built from the repository root as part of the npm workspace (workspaces design, web, site); @ostra/design resolves through that workspace.

npm run build runs build:console first, which builds web/ in shot mode (vite build --mode shot --base ./ --outDir ../site/public/console --emptyOutDir) so the homepage iframe has a console to load; dist and public/console are git-ignored.
A missing console/ build must 404 in the iframe, which is why vite uses appType mpa with no SPA fallback.
The dev script runs vite and the dev server listens on port 5174 with file access allowed for the repository root, because docs pages import Markdown above the package.
The CSP meta tag is injected only in builds (the dev server injects an inline script); frame-ancestors has no meta form and is not set.
Node.js 24 and npm ci at the repository root are needed, as the install text on the homepage states.

sections.title: Engine conformance fixtures
sections.purpose: tests/conformance/main.rs holds 126 #[test] functions, one or more per HANDOVER or Ultracode rule, each of which builds a session event history, folds it, and asserts the exact steps the planner returns. It is the fastest way to test pipeline behavior because it needs no runner, provider or server. Every change to a rule or a new rule adds or changes a fixture in the same change.

owns: The fixture helper H and the canned flows (classify, explore, spec_approved, plan_approved, pass_phase, accept)
The expected Step::summary() lists for each rule
The submit payload builders used by fixtures (explore_submit, spec_submit, fact, plan_submit, phase, impl_submit, finding, review, report)
does_not_own: SessionState::fold and SessionState::apply (engine area, crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs)
next_steps and the Step type (engine area, crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs)
The runner that performs steps (engine area, runner.rs); crates/ostra-engine/tests/runner.rs covers it
Event and submit types (core area)

assumptions: Fixtures import only ostra_core and ostra_engine; they never start a runner, database or executor.

SessionState::fold is a pure function of the stored events, so a fixture can reproduce any session by listing events with consecutive seq numbers starting at 1 (H::ev assigns seq = len + 1 and at = Utc::now()).

Step::summary() strings are stable identifiers: spawn steps read `spawn <agent> <purpose>` (for example `spawn generate-spec spec#1`), plus `gate <kind>`, `judge <name>`, `command <purpose> <project>`, `autofix phase N`, `blocked phase N`, `yolo-answer`, `fail`, `write-book <id>`, `deliver answer`. Fixtures compare against these literal strings.
A fixture finds a spawn step by prefix with H::spawn_step and panics with all summaries when none matches, so a renamed purpose breaks many fixtures at once.

H::start records ExecutionStarted with executor Native, model mock:m and params {auto_fixable_ids: [C1]}, because the fold cannot read project.toml and needs AUTO_FIXABLE_PARAM in the event (repo pattern 1).
Project paths are /code/<key>, the workspace root is /ws and the session root is /ws/.ostra/sessions/s1 in every fixture.
PlanCtx::default() carries no budget; fixtures set ctx.budget_usd or ctx.format_commands directly. H::new registers format command fmt-<project> for each project.

business_flow.action: Chooses the rule ID and builds the history with H (for example H::plan_approved for a session whose plan is approved)
business_flow.outcome: The history is a list of StoredEvent values in order.

business_flow.action: Calls h.summaries() or h.spawn_step(prefix)
business_flow.outcome: The planner runs on the folded state and returns steps.

business_flow.action: Drives the next step as the runner would: h.start, h.finish, h.run, h.open_gate, h.answer, h.deliver
business_flow.outcome: The matching events (ExecutionStarted, ExecutionFinished, GateOpened, GateAnswered, DecisionMade) are appended.

business_flow.action: Asserts the summaries, the SpawnRequest inputs, or folded state fields
business_flow.outcome: A rule violation fails the test with both lists printed by pretty_assertions.

sections.title: Browser security suite
sections.purpose: tests/browser is a Playwright suite that runs in real Chromium against a scratch ostra server. It proves the browser-facing defenses: untrusted text from agents and repos never runs as script, terminal escape sequences stay in the terminal, other origins cannot use the API, the one-time sign-in token is spent, uploads never render, and browser storage holds no secrets. It covers the console (desktop and phone layouts), the documentation books and the site.

owns: The scratch world under /tmp/pw-browser, the fake model, the stub harness and MCP server, the attacker server, the static site host
The guard fixture and the DOM audit
The spec files and the assertions in them
does_not_own: The server's guard, headers, CSP and routes (server area, crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs)
The console's rendering code (web area) and the site's (site area)
The CSP meta tags the site and console shot carry (site/vite.config.ts and web/vite.config.ts), which must equal the server's CSP
The real provider clients (providers area)

assumptions: All state lives under ROOT = /tmp/pw-browser; global-setup throws when ROOT does not start with /tmp/, then removes ROOT recursively.
The suite runs one worker with fullyParallel false because one scratch server and one PTY exist per run.
Chromium resolves any *.localhost name to loopback, and the private ostra-<hex>.localhost origin of the server ends with .localhost:<port>; global-setup throws `unexpected sign-in origin` otherwise.
lib/env.ts overrides dns.lookup in the Node process so *.localhost names resolve to 127.0.0.1 (the machine resolver may answer ::1 only while the server listens on 127.0.0.1).
The hostname evil-ostra.test is mapped to 127.0.0.1 only inside Chromium through --host-resolver-rules and stands for another site.
stopOld kills the previous server only when /proc/<pid>/cmdline contains both `ostra` and `serve` (Linux only).

The server reads config from OSTRA_CONFIG, data from OSTRA_DATA_DIR, the master key from OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE, HOME from ROOT/home, and sets OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL to empty so no price catalog is downloaded; nothing leaves the machine.
The console is built with npm run build in web/ and the server with cargo build -p ostra-server using CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target-browser unless PW_SKIP_BUILD is set.

subsections.title: Guard fixture and DOM audit
subsections.purpose: lib/guard.ts extends Playwright's test with a guard fixture that every spec uses, and lib/audit.ts checks what a render path left in the DOM. Together they turn any executed or loaded test string into a failed test.

owns: Finding kinds, origin allow-lists, dialog and popup policy
domProblems rules and payload link clicking
does_not_own: The CSP itself (server area; the guard only observes violations)

assumptions: An init script runs in every frame before page scripts; it defines window.__pwned as a non-configurable accessor that reports a finding when set, and listens for securitypolicyviolation in the capture phase. Findings travel through console.log with the prefix __PW_FINDING__ because a CSP cannot block the console.
CSP violations count only on origins in guard.cspOrigins (the app by default); an attacker page's own violations are expected.
Main-frame navigation must stay on an origin in guard.origins (the app and about:blank by default); a subframe may not navigate to javascript:, data: or vbscript: URLs.
More than one page in the context counts as a popup unless guard.allowPopups is true.
After the test body the fixture waits 500 ms for late loads before calling check().

business_flow.action: Attaches to the browser context before the first page exists and watches console, dialogs, frame navigations and new pages
business_flow.outcome: Findings of kind pwned, csp, dialog, navigation, popup are collected.

business_flow.action: Calls audit(page, guard, marker, where)
business_flow.outcome: The marker text must be visible, domProblems must return [], every visible link whose text matches js link, data link, vbscript link, ref link, entity link, raw anchor or cell is clicked, and its href must not start with javascript:, vbscript: or data:.

business_flow.action: Closes popups that a sanitized link opened and checks each is about:blank or on the page's origin
business_flow.outcome: The page stays on its origin.

business_flow.action: Adds a canary finding for each canary hit since the fixture started and expects no findings
business_flow.outcome: The test fails with a list of every finding.

subsections.title: Cross-origin and rebinding checks
subsections.purpose: cross-origin.spec.ts serves attacker pages from another port on 127.0.0.1 (same-site, so a SameSite=Strict cookie would ride along) and from evil-ostra.test (another site), and sends every kind of request the browser allows. It asserts the server refuses each one, nothing is readable, and the server's state is byte-for-byte unchanged.

owns: Attack page generation, response recording and the state comparison
does_not_own: The server's Host, Origin, Sec-Fetch and cookie checks (server area, guard in api.rs); the Rust test the_browser_boundary_refuses_page_content_and_other_sites pins the 403 per header

assumptions: lib/routes.ts parses the route list from the source of crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs between `pub fn router(` and `.merge(crate::bridge::internal_routes())`, splitting on `.route(`; it throws when fewer than 60 routes parse. A router written in another style breaks the parser.
The OAuth callback path is read from CALLBACK_PATH in crates/ostra-server/src/mcp.rs, defaulting to /mcp/oauth/callback.

Placeholders are filled with this run's ids: {ws}, {key} app, {name} pw, {harness} claude, and {id} as the session id under /api/sessions/, the first execution id under /api/executions/, else pw-id; query strings are added per route so a request that passed the guard would do real work.
Outside /api, /internal and /ws the app shell and assets are public, so the server may answer them; the forged-state OAuth callback is refused with 400 and changes nothing.
A second sign-in is created before the attack so a forged revoke-others would change the list of sign-ins.

business_flow.action: For every GET route loads an img and a script tag and fetches with credentials in cors and no-cors modes
business_flow.outcome: The browser or server refuses each.

business_flow.action: For each of 21 POST targets sends a no-cors text/plain POST, a no-cors form-encoded POST, a cors JSON POST and a PUT, then submits a text/plain form into a hidden iframe
business_flow.outcome: Every request is refused or blocked by the browser.

business_flow.action: Opens WebSocket /ws and sends subscribe home
business_flow.outcome: The socket never opens and no message arrives.

business_flow.action: Navigates the top level to every GET route
business_flow.outcome: /api routes and /ws answer 403; other GET routes answer 400.

business_flow.action: Takes a snapshot before and after
business_flow.outcome: Sign-ins, workspaces, UI state, session status, onboarding, settings, git status, refs, file tree under ROOT, data dir listing, model call count and harness run count are equal.

sections.title: Live evals and their fixtures
sections.purpose: tests/evals holds the data for four evals that run real models: judge routing, the init advisor, subagent coordination and the test stage. The runners are Rust tests in crates/ostra-server/tests. Each runner is #[ignore]d because it costs money, plus one offline test per data set that checks the cases are well formed. The evals exist to compare a prompt or model before and after a change, because model output varies from run to run.

The case design rules: counter-cases, rubrics, expected facts
does_not_own: The runners judge_evals.rs, advisor_evals.rs, coordination_evals.rs, test_stage_evals.rs (server area)

assumptions: Live tests are run with OSTRA_EVAL_MODELS set to a comma-separated list such as anthropic:claude-opus-5-5,anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5; the tests never fail on a wrong model answer, only when calls fail (judge evals), when every run fails to finish (advisor), or when no live run finished (coordination and test stage).
Reports are written to target/evals/.
Scenarios are laid out under CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR, never /tmp, because the sandbox mounts its own /tmp.
Run each case several times per model before judging a prompt change, and add a counter-case with each fix (CLAUDE.md).

sections.title: Windows sandbox probes
sections.purpose: tests/windows-probes is a standalone Rust program named winprobe, built outside the workspace, that measured which assumptions of the Windows sandbox design hold. It creates two local probe users, builds an ACL test tree, runs confined checks as a probe user, and writes a results table. The recorded results in results-full.md come from Windows Server 2025 build 26100 and feed the Phase 3 design. It contains no Ostra code.

owns: The probe program, its 17 numbered checks ('verify' numbers) and results-full.md
does_not_own: The real Windows sandbox implementation (sandbox area, crates/ostra-sandbox)
WINDOWS_HANDOVER.md (git-ignored design document)

assumptions: Run only on a throwaway VM, as an administrator over SSH: setup creates users OstraProbeA and OstraProbeB, sets passwords, edits HKLM, and grants ACLs; cleanup deletes them.
The exe is built with crt-static (.cargo/config.toml) so it runs on a bare VM without the Visual C++ runtime, and release builds use opt-level z, lto, strip and panic abort.
Layout is fixed in defs.rs: ROOT C:\ostra-probe, OUT C:\ostra-probe\out, REPO C:\ostra-probe\repo, PASS_FILE C:\ostra-probe\pass.txt readable only by Administrators and SYSTEM.
The probe password is generated from the clock and pid in the form Aa1!<16 hex>#Zz9, which meets default complexity; it is not cryptographically random.
Findings travel from the confined role to the host as tab-separated lines (verify, status tag, name, expected, observed) with tabs and newlines in fields flattened to spaces.
The VM is headless, has no Git, Node or harness CLIs, so checks 9 (desktop isolation), 13 (ConPTY), 14 (Git Bash) and 15 (mitigation policies) are recorded as NEEDS_CLIENT.

business_flow.action: Runs winprobe setup as administrator
business_flow.outcome: Probe users exist and the test repo has an inheritable Modify grant for OstraProbeA, deny ACEs on .git (write, delete, append, EA write, attribute write) and .git\hooks, a FILE_DELETE_CHILD deny on the repo root, and a read deny on secret.

business_flow.action: Runs winprobe run
business_flow.outcome: The host grants BUILTIN\Users access to the session's window station and desktop, spawns `winprobe asuser` as OstraProbeA through CreateProcessWithLogonW, runs a medium-integrity caller probe, the network filter probe, the ACL cost probe and notes, and writes results.md.

business_flow.action: Runs the check groups: restricted-token spawn, Job Objects, process access, registry, credentials, ACL, reads, hard links, escapes
business_flow.outcome: Findings are written to C:\ostra-probe\out\findings_a.tsv.

business_flow.action: Runs winprobe cleanup
business_flow.outcome: Users, registry entries, profiles, firewall rules named OstraProbe* and the ROOT tree are removed.

tables.title: Main results recorded in results-full.md
rows: CreateProcessWithLogonW and CreateProcessAsUserW with a restricted token work from a medium-integrity caller; the confined user holds only SeChangeNotifyPrivilege and SeIncreaseWorkingSetPrivilege
A Job Object kill terminates the child and a nested-job grandchild
The host user's profile is unreadable; C:\Program Files, C:\Windows and System32 are readable
Writes to .git and .git\hooks are denied by canonical, case-folded, trailing-dot, trailing-space, ADS and 8.3 short names; rename and rmdir of .git are denied; the hidden secret is unreadable
Hard links inside the tree work; a link to a hidden file still cannot be read; a link to a write-protected file is denied

Windows Firewall does not filter loopback or the host's own addresses, so limiting the sandbox user to the proxy port on loopback needs a raw WFP filter (FAIL); DNS through Dnscache is not filtered per user (INCONCLUSIVE)
Processes of different users cannot open each other; same-user siblings can (FAIL), and restricting SIDs cannot isolate them, so isolation needs one user per execution slot
A probe user writes its own HKCU and is denied HKLM Run
schtasks and BITS do not fire for a non-logged-on sandbox user; WMI Win32_Process.Create and out-of-process COM run as the sandbox user outside the job, so the policy denylist must block them
The sandbox user has no stored credentials and cannot read the host's profile
icaclss /t granted a Modify ACE over 8000 files in 40 directories in 1273 ms, favoring persistent per-workspace grants
The unsigned exe ran under Defender without detection; Kaspersky's reaction is not measured

areas.title: agents, code
areas.overview: This part covers two crates. `ostra-agents` embeds the repo's `assets/` folder in the binary and turns it into what every execution receives: the agent definition from `agent.toml`, the system prompt rendered with the tool names of the executor, the typed `Label: value` spawn block, and the repo brief appended to the first message. `ostra-code` is the code navigation layer: a table-driven tokenizer for 22 languages, an incremental per-project index of names, definitions and imports, a dependency and reference graph, the eight code tools agents call, and a provider chain (a project's own command, language servers over LSP, then the built-in index) that serves the Files view and the editor. `ostra-engine` (`factory.rs`) builds each spawn from `ostra-agents`, `ostra-workspace` reads agent definitions to validate settings, and `ostra-server` wires `ostra-code` into the REST API and into the `CodeNav` trait that native and harness executors use. `ostra-agents` depends only on `ostra-core`; `ostra-code` depends on `ostra-core` and `ostra-sandbox`, because language servers and command providers run under the workspace sandbox. The prompts, judges, references and skills themselves belong to the assets area; this part describes how they are loaded and rendered.

areas.title: core
areas.overview: ostra-core is the shared domain crate of Ostra. It depends on no other Ostra crate, and every other crate (store, sandbox, policy, tools, providers, agents, engine, executors, MCP, code index, workspace, server) builds on its types. It defines identifiers, agent names, capabilities, executor kinds, pipeline enums and stages, the append-only session event log and gate payloads, the `submit_<agent>` payload schemas, the `Executor` and `ExecutionHost` traits, global and workspace settings with route resolution and save-time validation, the project profile, every path Ostra derives, the canonical tool-call and policy-decision shapes, MCP tool naming, subagent coordination and project management tool inputs, typed research/spec/plan documents, documentation books with BM25 search, code navigation contracts, workspace artifacts, model pricing, and the REST and WebSocket data types that ts-rs exports to `web/src/api/gen/`. The crate also holds small OS helpers: process-tree control, shell lookup, and git config overrides. Its functions are synchronous and pure except where a section says it reads or writes files or starts a process; async code lives in the crates that call it.

areas.title: engine
areas.overview: ostra-engine is the code that runs one Ostra session, which is one user request taken through research, spec, fact-check, plan, build, review, test, and documentation. A session is an append-only event log; `SessionState::fold` turns the log into state, the pure function `next_steps` turns state into the next steps, and the `Engine` runner performs those steps and appends the events that result. Models do the work inside stages through executors, and they answer a small set of named judgment questions (judges); code holds every gate and every limit. The crate knows no executor, provider, or HTTP server: it reaches them through the `Services`, `SpawnFactory`, and `Executor` traits, and ostra-server wires the real implementations. It depends on ostra-core (events, DTOs, traits), ostra-store (SQLite), ostra-agents (prompts and typed spawn blocks), and ostra-sandbox (host commands and git repair). Its sections below cover the fold, the planner, judges and YOLO, the runner, subagent coordination, the init flow, the spawn factory, the view projections, and the tests.

areas.title: exec-harness, exec-native, mcp, notify, policy, providers
areas.overview: This area holds the crates that run one leaf agent and keep it inside Ostra's rules. `ostra-policy` decides, for every canonical tool call, whether it is allowed, needs the user, or is denied. `ostra-providers` streams model responses from Anthropic and OpenAI behind one neutral interface. `ostra-exec-native` is the native agent loop built on those two plus `ostra-tools`. `ostra-exec-harness` runs the same agents inside installed CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Antigravity) under a PTY and routes every tool call back through the policy by a hook bridge. `ostra-mcp` is the client for workspace MCP servers with OAuth sign-in, and `ostra-notify` sends Web Push messages without OpenSSL. The engine reaches executors only through the `Executor` trait of `ostra-core`, and `ostra-server` wires these crates to HTTP routes, the approval cards, the MCP connections and the push subscriptions.

areas.title: sandbox
areas.overview: ostra-sandbox is the kernel-enforced boundary under every command Ostra runs for an agent or a project. The policy layer (ostra-policy) judges tool calls by the paths they name, which a shell can hide; this crate makes the operating system enforce the same boundary: the host is read-only, only an execution's own roots are writable, Ostra's data and the user's credentials are hidden, and the network leads out only through an egress proxy that Ostra controls. It has three layers. A `Profile` describes one execution's boundary without naming a backend. A `Backend` (bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt through `sandbox-exec` on macOS) renders the profile into a wrapped command. The `sys` module is the only code that calls the kernel, with one `Os` implementation per operating system. Around these sit the egress proxy (`egress.rs`), the `ostra sandbox-init` helper with its seccomp filter (Linux), decoy credential files that signal a containment probe, process tracking (`Members`), host commands for programs Ostra starts for a project, and save-time validation of sandbox settings. The crate depends on ostra-core for config types, paths, and the `ExecutionHost` trait. It is called by ostra-exec-native and ostra-tools (the native Bash tool), ostra-exec-harness (harness CLIs), ostra-engine (format commands and cache cleanup), ostra-code and ostra-server (language servers, code providers, MCP stdio servers, startup cleanup, the `sandbox-init` subcommand), and ostra-workspace (settings validation and status). Those areas are documented by their own writers.

areas.title: server
areas.overview: The server area is the `ostra` binary and library in crates/ostra-server. It is the only process an Ostra user starts. It binds an HTTP listener (default 127.0.0.1:7878), authenticates browsers with a one-time token that is exchanged for an HttpOnly cookie, serves the embedded React console, and exposes the REST API under /api, the multiplexed WebSocket at /ws, and the local-only harness callbacks under /internal. It wires the real implementations of the traits the engine (ostra-engine), workspaces (ostra-workspace), and tools (ostra-tools) declare: Services, WorkspaceHost, CodeNav, McpConnector, ManageConnector, and CoordConnector. It owns the server-side features that need process-wide state: the sign-in registry, the per-workspace engine hub, the MCP gateway with OAuth, the git clone and git dock commands with saved credentials, the project file views with change attribution, the code-index providers, the Sessions tree and search, workspace artifacts, the master key that seals stored secrets, and harness setup terminals. Other areas own the engine, executors, policy, sandbox, tools, providers, code index, MCP client, workspace logic, and storage; this area calls them and names them in each section's boundaries.

areas.title: store, tools, workspace
areas.overview: This area covers three Rust crates. `ostra-store` keeps Ostra's durable state in SQLite: each workspace's database (the session event log plus the tables materialized beside it for the console), the machine-wide registry (workspace list, push subscriptions, key-value rows, encrypted credentials), and each project's lesson memory. `ostra-tools` implements the native tools that agents call (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob, WebFetch, Skill, Report, Document, Memory, MemoryRecall, DocsSearch, and the Windows PowerShell and Cmd shells), their JSON-schema definitions, and the traits through which the server supplies code navigation, MCP, project management, and subagent coordination. `ostra-workspace` owns one open workspace: its settings and validation, its projects, the approval records that keep commands from folder files from starting, workspace creation and deletion, and the stored console layout. The crates depend downward on `ostra-core`; `ostra-engine` and `ostra-exec-native` use the store and tools, and `ostra-server` wires the real implementations into `WorkspaceHost`, the connector traits, and the registry's encryption key.

areas.title: web
areas.overview: The web console is the React 19 single-page app in web/. It is the browser UI of the ostra server: a person uses it to start tasks, answer gates, watch executions and terminals, read specs, plans and documentation books, browse and edit project files, change workspace settings, and set up a workspace. It is built with Vite into web/dist, which the ostra binary embeds (crates/ostra-server/src/assets.rs) and serves next to the REST API under /api and the WebSocket at /ws. All types come from ts-rs bindings generated by ostra-core into web/src/api/gen, and all visual components come from @ostra/design. The code splits into an API layer (client.ts, socket.ts, mock/), shared live data (lib/store.ts, lib/live.ts), a desktop shell with editor-style tabs (shell/), a mobile shell for viewports up to 720 px (mobile/), one screen per resource type (screens/), and feature modules (features/context, features/docs, features/gates). Per the project rules the UI is kept compiling against API changes and is not polished, because it will be redesigned later.

areas.title: design, site, assets
areas.overview: This part covers three folders that contain no Rust logic: assets/ (the text Ostra gives to models), design/ (the @ostra/design React component library and CSS tokens), and site/ (the public homepage and docs site). The assets folder holds 14 agent prompts with their agent.toml definitions, 10 judge prompts, 7 stack references, the meta-author skill, a capability-to-tool mapping, and 3 prompt fragments; the ostra-agents crate embeds them in the binary, renders each prompt for the executor that will run it (native, claude, codex, grok or agy), and writes references, skills and rendered agent instructions under the data directory. The design package is imported by web/ (the console) and by site/, never the reverse, and it also holds the Markdown and Mermaid renderer that the site docs and the console documentation books share. The site builds two static pages, a homepage with an embedded mock console and a docs page that renders the repository's own Markdown at build time. Other areas own the engine that spawns agents and asks judges, the core submit schemas the prompts describe, the server that embeds the web build, and the browser tests that check the site.

areas.title: tests
areas.overview: The tests/ folder holds four independent suites. tests/conformance/main.rs is the engine conformance binary: 126 fixtures that build an event history for a session, fold it with SessionState::fold, and assert the exact list of next steps the pure planner returns, one or more per HANDOVER or Ultracode rule. tests/browser is a Playwright suite that starts a scratch ostra server, a fake Anthropic API, an attacker web server and a static copy of the site, and proves that agent text, repo text, terminal output, cross-origin requests, the sign-in token, uploads and browser storage cannot run script or change server state. tests/evals holds TOML and fixture data for four live, paid evals (judges, advisor, coordination, test stage) that are run by test files under crates/ostra-server/tests. tests/windows-probes is a standalone Rust program, outside the cargo workspace, that measured the Windows sandbox design on a throwaway VM. The suites talk to the other areas only through their public surfaces: the engine crate API, the ostra binary and its REST routes, the embedded web build, and the site build.

areas.title: docs, other files
areas.overview: This part of the book covers everything in the ostra repository that is not a crate, a browser package, the agent assets or the tests: the 34 Markdown files in docs/, the three root design documents (README.md, HANDOVER.md, CLAUDE.md), the Cargo and npm workspace configuration, the build and run scripts, the login-service installers for Linux, macOS and Windows, and the Docker image. Readers are people who build, install, run or document Ostra, and agents that need to know where a fact is written and which command produces the binary. The docs are plain Markdown that GitHub shows as it is and that the site package renders at build time through a navigation list in site/src/docs/pages.ts. HANDOVER.md is the behavior spec, CLAUDE.md holds the contributor patterns, and the scripts turn the npm workspace (design, web, site) and the Cargo workspace (15 crates) into one release binary, target/release/ostra, that embeds web/dist. This area describes the crates, web, design, site, assets and tests only at their boundary with these files; the other areas of the book document them.

glossary.definition: A per-harness translator between hook payloads and canonical tool calls and decisions.
A workspace created in a folder that already held a `workspace.toml`; nothing in that file is approved and its mode and YOLO are ignored.
The agent that reads a failed step of a created project's init (Rule O5) and chooses retry with guidance or escalate to the user.
A model run with a prompt, tier and capability list defined by assets/agents/<name>; 14 exist.
The data of one agent from `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml`: description, default tier, effort per executor, capabilities and timeout.
Context the user added after the session started, delivered by Queue or Now.
The server object holding Shared, the open workspaces, the hub and push channels, auth, file and code caches, and navigation.
One slice of the repository that a single documentation writer covers; this part covers docs/ and root files.
A module name that scopes a lesson, with sub-scopes written `area::sub`; recall by an area also returns its sub-scopes.
A file in a session directory (spec, plan, report, ledger, upload) or a workspace artifact under .ostra/artifacts.
An `ArtifactTrack`: generation and fact-check state of the spec or the plan.
A file under assets/ that is embedded in the ostra binary and read as a prompt, judge, reference, skill or mapping.
The folder on disk, `<data_dir>/assets` by default, where references, skills and per-agent instructions are materialized.
The mapping from a project file to the execution that last changed it, shown in the Files dock.
The mechanism that enforces a profile on this machine: `Bubblewrap` on Linux or `Seatbelt` on macOS.
The name an external MCP tool has on Ostra's own MCP server, `<server>__<tool>`, at most 52 characters.
A documentation book written by the docs stage, with one part per project, rendered as pages.
The /internal endpoints through which harness CLIs report tool calls for policy checks and call Ostra's MCP tools.
A Unix socket file that serves only the internal routes to sandboxes that have their own network namespace.
The Linux tool (`bwrap`) that starts a program in new mount, pid, IPC, and optionally network namespaces.
The count of consecutive failing build or test commands in one execution, with warnings at 3 and a refusal at 5.
A Docker build feature that keeps the Cargo registry, git data, target folder and npm cache between builds.
A package registry, source host, or model API host that Ostra allows under `allowlist` and that must resolve to public addresses.
A URL of the form <fake>/canary/<id> inside a test string; any request to it means the string loaded, and the guard fails the test.
A tool call with paths made absolute, the shell `cwd` set, and the WebFetch URL parsed, so the policy check and the tool see the same target.
A `ToolCall` that uses Claude Code tool names and input shapes, which is the only form the policy reads.
A named kind of tool an agent may use, such as read, shell or code; each maps to a tool name per executor.
A WebSocket subscription name: session:<id>, execution:<id>, term:<execution>, workspace:<id> or home.
A guard that marks a project key and folder as in use by a git command, released on drop.
A component that answers file, usages, deps or symbols requests for the Files view: a project command, a language server, or the built-in index.
The ordered providers tried for a code navigation request: project command, language servers, then the built-in index.
Replacing the conversation with a provider-made summary when the context nears its window.
A plan phase's Low, Medium, or High value, which routes the model tier of implementer and write-test runs.
A test in tests/conformance/main.rs that builds an event history and checks the planner's expected steps for one rule ID.
The homepage iframe that loads the console built in shot mode with mock data and is driven by postMessage.
A read-only run that continues a finished subagent's conversation to answer another subagent's question.
An execution event showing an attempt to leave its sandbox; three from one execution pause the session.
A project an agent created during a session that the plan named as new; it gets an init before its phases run (Rules O3, O4).
A file named by OSTRA_ENV_FILE whose `export NAME=value` lines run.sh and the service launcher apply.
Content Security Policy; the site carries it as a meta tag because a static host sends no headers.
The per-user directory that holds registry.db, server.json, server.log and master.key; it is overridden by OSTRA_DATA_DIR.
A fake credential file whose first open by a sandboxed command is reported as a containment signal (Rule P3).
A shippable group of at most 6 criteria in a spec, in a single repo.
One streamed item of an execution, an `ExecutionDelta`, persisted and sent to the Activity view.
HANDOVER.md, the specification of Ostra's behavior, whose section numbers key several site pages.
A CSS custom property such as --accent or --space-2 defined in design/src/tokens.
A directory above a protected mount that is bound onto itself so it cannot be renamed or removed.
The Docs class that builds pages, anchors, links and a search index from Markdown sources.
The tool through which the explore, generate-spec, and plan agents write a typed research document, spec, or plan that Ostra renders as Markdown.
The per-project documentation Ostra's docs stage writes into the workspace, searchable with DocsSearch.
The per-session tokio task that plans, starts steps, and waits to be woken after each appended event.
Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax: the five requirement templates (ubiquitous, event-driven, state-driven, unwanted behavior, optional feature) that generate-spec uses.
A link from one file to another carrying import lines and the names the first file uses from the second.
Settings with registry overlay applied and, while approval is pending, MCP servers disabled and code providers, language servers, allow rules, and outside projects removed.
The reasoning effort level low, medium, high, xhigh, or max sent to a model.
The HTTP/CONNECT proxy that is the only network path out of a private sandbox and enforces the host policy.
The crate-private trait each backend implements to wrap programs, start listeners, and place decoys.
The execution path analyzer agent (execution-path-analyzer) that lists the paths a change creates or alters so write-test can cover them.
The execution-path-analyzer's verification plan: paths, system flows, regression suites and a test level per check.
A live, paid test that runs real models on cases from tests/evals and reports pass counts instead of failing on a wrong answer.
The append-only `events` table of a workspace database; the state of a session is the fold of its events.
The hostname evil-ostra.test that Chromium maps to 127.0.0.1 to stand for another site.
What an execution is for (explore, spec, fact-check, plan, implement, review, and so on); the fold keys on it.
One run of one leaf agent, identified by an `ExecutionId`, started by the engine with an `ExecutionSpec`.
How an execution is shown: activity for native runs, terminal for harness runs.
What runs an agent: the native loop or a CLI harness (claude, codex, grok, agy); its tier table selects tool names and effort.
The spec table whose E{n} rows carry an established fact, a binding rule, a source URL and a version or date.
An agent pass that verifies a spec or plan against its sources and returns PASS, FAIL, or Error.
PASS, FAIL or ERROR; PASS requires zero HIGH or MEDIUM findings.
The local HTTP server in tests/browser/lib/fake-model.ts that answers /v1/messages with scripted SSE responses for every agent and judge.
Text of the form @project/path that names a project file or an artifact (@_artifacts/path) in a request.
The pure function `SessionState::fold(id, events)` that builds session state by applying events in order.
A point where the pipeline waits for a user answer or, under YOLO, a judge answer.
A reference analysis (epa.md) or reference tests kept under tests/evals/test_stage/goldens/ that stand in for a live agent.
The model named by OSTRA_EVAL_GRADER (default anthropic:claude-opus-5-5) that scores an eval run against a case's rubric.
The middleware that applies Host, Origin, fetch-metadata, and cookie checks and adds security headers.
The Playwright fixture that records executed or loaded test strings, CSP violations, dialogs, popups and off-app navigations and fails the test on any.
The test helper struct in tests/conformance/main.rs that appends events and drives planner steps the way the runner would.
An installed agent CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Antigravity) that Ostra runs in a terminal as an executor.
A spec or plan gate answer stored until the Route answer judge decides where its parts go (Rule J1).
A workspace artifact folder or file hidden as one unit; its content is stored in the data dir out of agent reach (Rule W2).
An editor request for completions, signature help or a base class or implementation jump, sent over the socket with the unsaved text.
The channel through which a harness reports each tool call so the policy can decide; its decisions appear in the Tool calls tab.
A program launch for a project or workspace, sandboxed when configured, with credential variables removed.
One `allowed_hosts` entry: a host name, `*.domain`, or IP address with an optional port.
The broadcast channel `App.hub` that carries every engine notice with its workspace id.
An index module such as `lib.rs`, `index.ts` or `__init__.py`, or a file with `export * from`, which re-exports other files.
A read-only reopening of an ended harness execution in which every tool call is refused.
The reason the engine cancelled a running execution: Pause, Context, or ProjectCreated.
A project's .ostra/INVENTORY.md: commands, skills with paths, file-type to skill mapping, module map and review rules.
A short model call with a fixed system prompt from assets/judges that answers one named question with a decide call.
The system prompt of one of the ten named judgment questions, loaded from `assets/judges/<name>.md`.
One of the nine pipeline progress positions: research, requirements, verification, design, build, review, test, docs, done.
A group of languages that share definition and import rules: Rust, Js, Python, Go, Jvm, C, Ruby, Lua, Shell, Data.
The program, arguments, environment, files and links that start one harness execution.
The generated script ostra-service that applies the credentials file and then starts the server for a service manager.
A policy check that no permission, user answer or YOLO setting overrides.
The policy stage that applies modes and allow, ask and deny rules in Claude Code's model.
A one-line durable note that an agent records under an area for a project and later runs recall.
The guard that refuses a report or an ok submit after a verified recovery until a lesson is recorded with the Memory tool or waived with a reason.
The in-memory state of a running harness execution, including its bridge token and recorded submit.
The Ostra mark component with eight arcs (one per stage) and a center pearl whose state shows pipeline progress.
The workspace choice (`open` or `listed`) of which host loopback ports a Seatbelt sandbox may connect to.
The set of running language servers keyed by project and command, with idle and count limits.
A mach service name in a Seatbelt policy that lets the OS find every process of an invocation or of this data dir.
The 32-byte key that seals registry credentials; the server loads it from the OS keychain or an owner-only file.
Write embedded references, skills and rendered agent instructions to the assets directory on disk.
A table such as `sessions`, `executions`, or `gates` that the engine writes beside the event log so the console can read current state without folding events.
Model Context Protocol, a JSON-RPC protocol through which a client lists and calls tools of a server.
The server component that connects to each workspace MCP server, handles OAuth, and serves its tools to executors.
The `ostra mcp-stdio` subprocess that serves Ostra's tools to a harness CLI by forwarding to `/internal/mcp`.
What one sandboxed invocation holds while it runs (listeners, decoys, process markers) and whose drop kills leftover processes.
One way a file uses a name: bare, qualified by a name or `self`, and whether it follows `.` or `->`.
Running the console on in-memory fixtures with VITE_MOCK=1.
The public price and limits list at `https://models.dev/api.json`, installed in memory by the server.
One rule of a profile: writable, read-only, hidden, home tmpfs, home entry, or link.
A textual replacement in a fixture source file that an adequate test suite must fail; write-test output is graded by whether it kills every mutant.
The ordered list of sidebar groups and pages that decides which Markdown file or section is a docs page.
A `Block` value that represents conversation content independent of the model vendor.
The list of touched-but-uninvestigated items in a research document; the sufficiency judge decides whether each needs another pass.
A reminder to submit, either as a blocked Stop or as a line typed into the terminal after silence.
Applying the permission mode, YOLO, limits, tool enforcement, and sandbox choices from the registry onto settings read from a folder file (Rule A2).
The nearest folder with a manifest (Cargo.toml, package.json, go.mod and similar) that owns a file.
Two agents that alternate on one artifact, such as author and fact-checker, where each continues its own conversation.
One project's overview and sections inside a book.
Commands found in folder files (MCP servers, language servers, code providers, format commands, allow rules, projects outside the workspace) that do nothing until the user approves them.
One of Default, AcceptEdits, Plan or Bypass, which sets what happens when no rule decides.
One unit of planned build work with a project, complexity, test policy and dependencies, implemented and reviewed on its own.
A finding that the code misses, deviates from, or exceeds a requirement of the phase file (MISSING, DEVIATION, SCOPE).
Proof Key for Code Exchange: a random verifier whose SHA-256 hash (S256) is sent with the authorization request and the verifier with the code exchange.
An empty read-only file or directory created so a protected path that does not exist cannot be created by the sandboxed command.
The pure function `next_steps` that returns the steps that can start from a given state.
The single italic tab that the next preview open replaces until the user keeps or pins it.
A host named exactly by a `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` allow rule, which WebFetch may reach even when it resolves to a private or loopback address.
A backend-neutral description of one execution's mounts, environment, egress policy, decoys, and forwards.
The per-project store of names, definitions and imports per file, without file text.
One of Missing, Initializing, Initialized, or NotInitialized, derived from the folder, running init sessions, and the project inventory file.
A lowercase slug `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*` that names a project in a workspace.
A project's .ostra/project.toml, the machine-readable twin of the inventory.
The pair of workspace id and project key that identifies a project in caches.
An RFC 9728 document at a `.well-known` URL that names the authorization servers of an MCP server.
A pseudo-terminal that hosts the harness CLI and exposes its screen and input.
A string from `purpose_key` naming one work loop, review loop, or stage, used to find a run to resume or wake.
A message the server originates for browsers, carrying the channel names it should reach.
The temporary file `ostra-pwd-<uuid>` that a Bash call's EXIT trap writes so the next call starts in the final directory.
Write to an existing file and Edit require that the file was read in the same execution.
A hostname other than the app's private name that reaches the app's own port; the server answers 421 for it.
The per-machine SQLite database `registry.db` that lists workspaces, push subscriptions, and key-value rows including encrypted credentials.
The block appended to an execution's task that carries the project's commands, skills, module map and review rules, resolved from project.toml.
The one document an explore run writes; it cites every external fact by URL and date and lists what it did not cover.
The table built from the file list and manifests that maps an import spec to a project file or folder.
A string such as session:<id> or file:<key>:<path> that names anything the console can open in a tab and maps one to one to a URL.
The session-dir file in which the code-reviewer and the fix agents record findings, fixes and WONTFIX rationale per iteration.
The executor and model an agent or the judge uses, resolved from settings by `resolve_route`.
A short label such as D3a or J1 defined in HANDOVER.md, cited in code comments and tested by a conformance fixture.
The rule that artifacts are deleted or moved only when no session or execution may be reading them.
The form agent[:kind][#n] that coordination eval cases use to name one run of an agent.
A YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS timestamp from date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S used in research and spec file names.
`auto`, `required`, or `off`: whether a missing sandbox is tolerated, refused, or not wanted.
The `ostra sandbox-init` subcommand that runs first inside a bubblewrap sandbox, forwards loopback to Ostra's sockets, loads seccomp, and starts the command.
A program, arguments, environment, working directory, and `Members` handle ready to run inside the sandbox.
The text `${ostra_secret}` that replaces an MCP header or env value in settings when the real value is held in the encrypted registry.
The Sandbox Profile Language in which a Seatbelt policy is written.
A private host directory mounted at `/tmp` in a bubblewrap sandbox, or named by `TMPDIR` under Seatbelt.
The ostra serve process that the browser suite starts under /tmp/pw-browser with its own config, data directory, master key and HOME.
A throwaway Ostra run with its own config and data folder set through OSTRA_CONFIG and OSTRA_DATA_DIR.
The object that encrypts and decrypts registry credential values with AES-256-GCM under the machine's master key.
The macOS sandbox, driven by an SBPL policy given to `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`.
A BLOCKER finding from the code-reviewer's mandatory security scan; it cannot be waived and loops until the code is removed.
A kernel system-call filter loaded by the helper that refuses new user namespaces, terminal input injection, and calls that widen the kernel surface.
The filter that keeps Grep and Glob walks out of credential stores and Ostra's data folder.
The part of a Markdown file under one `##` heading, selected by number or name in a NAV entry.
Token classes that a language server computes with type information and that Ostra overlays on the built-in tokens.
The file the server writes to the data folder at start with its port, URL host and process id; installers and the url and stop commands read it.
The trait through which the engine reads settings, gets executors, runs judge calls, and sends notices.
One user request taken through the pipeline, stored as an append-only event log and identified by a `SessionId`.
The per-session directory under the sandbox cache base that holds tool caches for agents of one session.
A Markdown index of the session rewritten from the fold for revisions and the implementation review gate (Rule F2).
The `ostra_session` HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookie valid for 30 days, stored hashed as a sign-in record.
The scratch directory where a session's documents, reports and ledgers are written.
One entry of a session's append-only log, a `SessionEvent`.
A PTY that runs a harness installer or login and is streamed to the browser like a harness execution.
The process-wide state every workspace uses: config, registry, providers, executors, notifier, MCP gateway, and environment status.
A cache of one value per key that has one fetch and one socket subscription however many components read it.
The workspace chrome: title bar, left dock, tab strip, center screen, quick-question dock and status bar.
The console build embedded in the site's homepage, driven by postMessage and using fixtures.
A Vite mode that builds the console with mock data into site/public/console for the homepage.
A 15 minute, single-use random value in the sign-in URL fragment, stored hashed in the registry.
A one-time link with a token in its fragment that signs a browser in; `ostra url` prints a new one.
A SKILL.md file with a name and description that an agent loads by reading it; per-project skills live in .agents/skills.
A place in the workspace-wide limit `limits.max_parallel_executions`; an execution holds one while it runs.
The host name a TLS client writes in its ClientHello; the proxy compares it with the CONNECT host.
The fact-check spawn line citations or refetch that decides whether cited pages are fetched again.
The Label: value lines that start an agent run and carry its required parameters.
A listener whose every connection is copied to a fixed target, used to forward a host address or Unix socket into a sandbox.
An assets/refs file that seeds the initializer with a stack's detection signals, slicing, commands, component catalog and review rule seeds.
low, medium or high; low skips the plan stage.
One action the planner asks the runner to perform, such as a judge call, a spawn, or a gate.
The stable string returned by Step::summary(), such as `spawn generate-spec spec#1` or `gate closing_gate`, that fixtures compare.
The shell script installed as ROOT/bin/claude that prints hostile terminal sequences and logs the input it receives.
A conversation of one or more runs identified by its first execution's ID, which other runs can ask questions.
The id of the first execution of a conversation, used to address that conversation in `SubagentAsk`.
The structured result an agent returns by calling `submit_<agent>`; the engine reads only this.
The single tool call, named submit_<agent>, through which an agent returns its structured result; Ostra reads nothing else.
The category of a definition: function, method, class, enum, interface, type, module, constant, variable, field or macro.
Markdown, HTML or text built in tests/browser/lib/payloads.ts that would set window.__pwned or request a canary if it ran or loaded.
A model class (fast, balanced, advanced, frontier) that a tier table maps to a concrete model per executor.
The closeness of a candidate defining file to a mentioning file, from 0 (imported) to 3 (in an imported package).
The display category of a token in the Files view, one of 11 classes such as keyword, type, function.
A {{tool_*}} placeholder in a prompt that render_prompt replaces with the executor's tool name.
The opening section of a harness prompt that lists each capability's tool and how to load skills and call Ostra's MCP tools.
The per-execution state of native tools: working directory, files read, HTTP client, scrubbed variable names, and sandbox handle.
The result of one tool call: text, error flag, exit code, duration, optional diff, and a `RunEnd`.
A record of files that one successful write tool call changed, sent to the file watcher.
The path an IMPLEMENT request takes: light (research then reviewed phases) or full (spec, fact-check, plan and approvals).
A `tree_patch` message that replaces one session node of the Sessions tree.
The rule that programs named by `workspace.toml` or `project.toml` start only while the user has approved exactly their current content; approvals are hashes in the registry.
A host the user chose (`allowed_hosts` or a harness base URL), which may resolve to any address.
The ts-rs setting in .cargo/config.toml that sends generated TypeScript types to web/src/api/gen.
A research, spec, or plan document stored as JSON and rendered to Markdown.
The Ultracode plugin at ../ultracode, the source of rules and measured facts that Ostra re-implements.
The stored console layout of a workspace, merged from PATCH bodies and capped at 64 KiB.
An HTTP proxy named by `[sandbox] upstream_proxy` through which the egress proxy reaches public destinations.
Part of an answer the judge kept for the implement, tests, or docs stage, with an ID such as N1.
A `path` and `message` pair that names the settings or request field a problem is about.
Voluntary Application Server Identification: an ES256 JWT and public key that identify the sender to a push service.
The index 1 to 17 of a Windows sandbox design assumption checked by winprobe and listed in results-full.md.
Delivery of an encrypted message to a browser through the push service named in its subscription.
The standalone Windows probe executable in tests/windows-probes that verifies sandbox design assumptions on a throwaway VM.
A `WorkLoop`: the implement or test pass with its review, fix, rescue, and staging steps, driven by `LoopNext`.
The trait through which a workspace reaches the process that opens it: registry, global config, environment, provider and harness status, and engine services.
The runtime of one open workspace: root, database, engine, host, clone list, and work lock.
A session mode in which the engine answers permission asks and gates, except those it must never answer such as the budget gate.
